blocks.h: 1. What an oil tanker carries, and under which convention

blocks.p: A tanker's certificates fall into four families, and grouping them by instrument rather than reciting them as a list is what earns limb (a): the examiner is asking which convention issues each one. Everything below is for a tanker on international voyages.

rows: Cargo Ship Safety Construction Certificate
SOLAS I/12, chapters II-1 and II-2
5 years
Cargo Ship Safety Equipment Certificate + Record of Equipment (Form E)
SOLAS I/12
5 years
Cargo Ship Safety Radio Certificate + Form R
SOLAS I/12, chapter IV
5 years
(Alternative) Cargo Ship Safety Certificate, Form C - the three above combined
SOLAS I/12
5 years
Safety Management Certificate; Document of Compliance held by the Company
SOLAS chapter IX / ISM Code
5 years each
International Ship Security Certificate
SOLAS chapter XI-2 / ISPS Code
5 years
Continuous Synopsis Record
SOLAS XI-1/5
no expiry - amended as particulars change
Minimum Safe Manning Document
SOLAS V/14
no fixed expiry - reissued when manning changes
Exemption Certificate, where granted
SOLAS I/12
not beyond the certificate it qualifies

blocks.p: An oil tanker is additionally subject to the Enhanced Survey Programme under SOLAS XI-1/2 and the ESP Code, which is not a certificate but a survey regime whose report file is carried on board and is what the Cargo Ship Safety Construction Certificate now rests on.

blocks.h: 3. MARPOL certificates - where the tanker differs most

rows: International Oil Pollution Prevention Certificate with Form B supplement
Annex I - Form B is the oil-tanker form; a non-tanker carries Form A
5 years
International Pollution Prevention Certificate for the Carriage of Noxious Liquid Substances in Bulk, or an IBC Code Certificate of Fitness, where so certified
Annex II
5 years
International Sewage Pollution Prevention Certificate
Annex IV
5 years
International Air Pollution Prevention Certificate + supplement
Annex VI
5 years
Engine International Air Pollution Prevention Certificate + NOx Technical File
NOx Technical Code under Annex VI
engine life, subject to survey
International Energy Efficiency Certificate
Annex VI regulation 24
ship's life, subject to change of flag or major conversion
DCS Statement of Compliance - fuel oil consumption reporting
Annex VI
issued annually

blocks.p: Garbage attracts no certificate under Annex V - only a Garbage Management Plan and Record Book. It is worth saying so expressly, because a candidate who lists an "IGPP certificate" invents one.

ul: International Load Line Certificate - Load Line Convention 1966 as modified by the 1988 Protocol. Five years.

International Tonnage Certificate (1969) - Tonnage Convention. No expiry: it stands until the ship's tonnage characteristics change or she changes flag. This is the standard trap in a validity question.

Maritime Labour Certificate and the Declaration of Maritime Labour Compliance, Parts I and II - MLC 2006, for ships of 500 GT and above on international voyages. Five years, with an intermediate inspection between the second and third anniversary.
International Anti-fouling System Certificate - AFS Convention. Valid for the life of the system unless it is changed.
International Ballast Water Management Certificate - BWM Convention. Five years.

Certificate of Insurance or other Financial Security in respect of Civil Liability for Oil Pollution Damage - CLC 1992, where the tanker carries more than 2,000 tonnes of persistent oil in bulk as cargo. Its validity is the period of the insurance, so it is usually one year and is the certificate most often found expired.
Bunker oil pollution damage insurance certificate - Bunkers Convention 2001, above 1,000 GT; and, where the convention applies, the wreck removal insurance certificate at 300 GT and above.
Ship Sanitation Control (Exemption) Certificate - International Health Regulations 2005, not an IMO instrument. Six months.

blocks.p: The Certificate of Class is deliberately not in any of these lists. It is issued under the society's own rules and is a commercial and contractual document, not a statutory one - although the same society, acting as a Recognized Organization, will normally have issued most of the statutory certificates above on the flag State's behalf.

blocks.h: 5. Harmonization under SOLAS 74/88 - what it actually changed

blocks.p: Before harmonization each convention ran its own survey clock. A ship could hold a SOLAS certificate surveyed in March, a Load Line certificate surveyed in September and an IOPP certificate surveyed in December, each with its own expiry, its own surveyor attendance and its own off-hire. The 1988 Protocols to SOLAS and to the Load Line Convention introduced the Harmonized System of Survey and Certification, in force 3 February 2000, and MARPOL was amended to match. Its four elements are:

ul: One anniversary date for the ship - the day and month corresponding to the expiry date of the certificate - which governs every harmonized certificate she holds.
A common five-year maximum period of validity for all of them, so they expire together.

A common survey pattern - initial, annual, intermediate, renewal, plus additional surveys after damage or repair - with a window of three months either side of each anniversary date in which the annual or intermediate survey may be held.
Flexibility on issue and extension, so that a genuine operational difficulty does not force a ship to trade uncertificated.

blocks.p: The purpose is economic as much as regulatory: one surveyor attendance discharges several conventions, off-hire falls, and the ship's certificates can no longer drift apart. Note the term of art - the intermediate survey takes the place of the second or third annual survey; it does not sit in addition to it.

blocks.h: 6. A certificate that has just expired, in a port that cannot survey

blocks.p: This is the practical half of limb (b) and it is answered from SOLAS regulation I/14. The first point to make, before any procedure, is the hard one: an expired statutory certificate is a detainable deficiency, and the ship does not sail on the strength of the Chief Engineer's opinion that she is fit. The regulation supplies three distinct reliefs and they are not interchangeable:

rows: Renewal survey COMPLETED, but the new certificate cannot be issued or placed on board before expiry
The Administration or a Recognized Organization acting for it may endorse the existing certificate, which is then accepted as valid
A further five months from the expiry date
Certificate expired and the ship is not in a port in which she is to be surveyed - the case in this question
The Administration may extend the period of validity, solely to allow the ship to complete her voyage to the port where she will be surveyed, and only where that is proper and reasonable
Three months, and no more
Ship engaged on short voyages, not covered above
A period of grace
One month from the stated expiry date

blocks.p: Two conditions on the three-month extension are routinely missed and both are worth a mark. First, it is granted for the voyage only: on arrival at the survey port the ship may not leave again on the strength of the extension - she must first hold the new certificate. Second, the extension does not buy time: when the renewal survey is completed, the new certificate is valid to a date not exceeding five years from the original expiry date, not five years from the survey. The lost time is lost.

blocks.h: 7. The actions to take, in the order you would take them

ul: Stop and establish the facts. Which certificate, which convention, the exact expiry date, whether the underlying survey has in fact been completed. The relief available depends entirely on that last question - a completed survey is a five-month endorsement, an uncompleted one is at best a three-month voyage extension.
Inform the Company and the Designated Person Ashore immediately. Under the ISM Code this is a non-conformity and it is reported as one; it is not a matter for the ship to resolve locally.

Apply to the flag Administration, through the Recognized Organization, for the appropriate relief - endorsement, extension or period of grace - stating the survey position, the port of intended survey and the voyage proposed. The RO cannot grant the three-month extension of its own motion; that power is the Administration's.

Request an occasional or additional survey where a surveyor can in fact attend, or arrange attendance at the next port. Inadequate facilities at this port is the premise of the question, not a permanent answer.
Notify the port State authority rather than let a PSCO discover it. A disclosed and covered expiry is a different conversation from a concealed one.

Notify the P&I club, the hull underwriters and the charterers. Trading with an invalid statutory certificate can prejudice cover and will usually put the ship off-hire; the club needs to know before the voyage, not after.

Satisfy yourself that the ship is materially compliant and record it. Testing and recording the machinery and equipment the certificate covers, and logging the result, is what makes the application for extension credible and is what a surveyor will look for on arrival.
Do not sail until the extension or endorsement is in hand and on board, and then sail only to the nominated survey port.

blocks.p: The principle underneath all of it: the certificate is evidence of compliance, not the compliance itself - but it is the only evidence a port State is obliged to accept, and the relief for an expired one comes from the Administration, in writing, before departure.

The limbs are 8 and 8, so the answer must be genuinely halved. Limb (a) is an enumeration and it is marked as one: the marks are in coverage and correct attribution, not in prose. Write it as tables grouped by instrument. Limb (b) is two questions welded together - a definition of harmonization and a scenario - and both must be answered. A candidate who explains harmonization beautifully and then writes two lines on the expired certificate throws away half of eight marks.
The question asks for validity, so the marks are in the exceptions, not the rule. Almost everything is five years. What is examined is what is not:

ul: International Tonnage Certificate (1969) - no expiry at all.
International Energy Efficiency Certificate - the ship's life, unless she changes flag or undergoes a major conversion.
International Anti-fouling System Certificate - the life of the system.
CLC and Bunkers insurance certificates - the period of the insurance, typically one year, renewed each 20 February with the club year.
Ship Sanitation Control (Exemption) Certificate - six months, and not an IMO instrument at all.
DCS Statement of Compliance - issued annually.
Continuous Synopsis Record and the Minimum Safe Manning Document - no expiry; they are amended or reissued on change.

blocks.h: Form A or Form B - the one-word tanker answer

blocks.p: If you write only one tanker-specific thing in limb (a), write this: the IOPP certificate carries a Form B supplement for an oil tanker and a Form A for a non-tanker. It is the cleanest demonstration that you have read the question's word "tanker" and not answered about ships in general. Add the Enhanced Survey Programme under SOLAS XI-1/2 and the CLC certificate above 2,000 tonnes of persistent oil, and the tanker point is fully made.

blocks.h: Harmonization: the number that carries the concept

blocks.p: One anniversary date, one five-year cycle, one three-month window. If you remember nothing else about the harmonized system, those three numbers reconstruct it. The 1988 Protocols to SOLAS and Load Lines brought it in, it took effect on 3 February 2000, and MARPOL was amended so that its certificates ran on the same clock.

blocks.h: Five months, three months, one month - keep them apart

rows: Five months
The renewal survey is COMPLETE but the certificate cannot be issued or placed on board
Paperwork relief - the ship has been surveyed and passed
Three months
The certificate has expired and the ship is NOT in a port where she can be surveyed
Voyage relief - to reach the survey port, and nothing else
One month
Short-voyage ships, where neither of the above applies
A period of grace

blocks.p: The question puts you squarely in the middle row. The examiner is testing whether you reach for the three-month voyage extension and whether you know its two conditions: it takes you to the survey port and no further, and the replacement certificate still runs five years from the original expiry date.

blocks.h: What is NOT on the list at this sitting

blocks.p: Do not list the International Certificate on Inventory of Hazardous Materials or a Ready-for-Recycling Certificate as statutory here. The Hong Kong Convention entered into force on 26 June 2025, a year after this examination. The EU Ship Recycling Regulation required an IHM on EU-calling ships before that, but it is a regional instrument, not a convention certificate, and the question asks for conventions.

ul: Listing certificates without naming the convention. The stem asks twice for the convention and its reference; an unattributed list cannot score full marks.

Including the Certificate of Class among the statutory certificates. It is a class document. The society may also be the RO, and saying so is what shows you understand the distinction rather than having missed it.
Giving every certificate five years, and so missing the Tonnage, IEEC, AFS, insurance and sanitation exceptions.
Answering limb (b) as though harmonization means only "all certificates expire together". The survey window and the common survey pattern are the operative parts.
Treating the expired-certificate scenario as an engineering problem. It is a certification problem: the answer is an application to the Administration, not a repair.
Sailing on the extension past the survey port. The regulation forbids exactly that.
"Who grants the extension?" The Administration. The RO may endorse a certificate where the survey is complete, but the three-month voyage extension is the flag State's power.
"How long is the new certificate valid after an extension?" Five years from the original expiry date - not from the survey. Candidates almost always give the survey date.
"Can she load and sail from the survey port on the extension?" No. On arrival she must have the new certificate before leaving.
"Does the intermediate survey replace an annual survey or add to it?" It replaces the second or third annual survey.
"What is the window?" Three months before to three months after the anniversary date.
"Which certificate expires most often in practice?" The insurance certificates - CLC and Bunkers - because they run with the policy year, not the harmonized cycle.
Show me the Form B supplement to the IOPP certificate and tell me what is in it.
Your Cargo Ship Safety Equipment Certificate expires next week and you are on a fourteen-day passage. What do you do, and who do you write to?
What is the difference between an annual, an intermediate and a renewal survey?
What is an occasional survey and who asks for it?
Which of your certificates would still be valid if the ship changed flag tomorrow?
Who issued your statutory certificates, and under what authority?

blocks.p: Four families, three numbers, one date. The families are SOLAS, MARPOL, other conventions, and insurance. The three numbers are 5 months / 3 months / 1 month of relief under regulation I/14. The one date is 3 February 2000, when the harmonized system took effect. Then the tanker overlay: Form B, ESP, CLC.

ul: SOLAS I/12 - issue and endorsement of certificates.
SOLAS I/14 - duration and validity; the five-month endorsement, the three-month voyage extension, the one-month period of grace.
SOLAS XI-1/2 and the ESP Code - the Enhanced Survey Programme for oil tankers and bulk carriers.
SOLAS chapter IX - the ISM Code, DOC and SMC. Chapter XI-2 - ISPS and the ISSC.
1988 Protocols to SOLAS and to the Load Line Convention - the harmonized system, in force 3 February 2000.
MARPOL Annex I regulations 6 to 10 - IOPP certificate, Form B supplement, surveys. Annex VI regulation 24 - the IEEC.
Tonnage Convention 1969 - the International Tonnage Certificate, which does not expire.
MLC 2006 Title 5 - the Maritime Labour Certificate and DMLC Parts I and II.
CLC 1992 and Bunkers 2001 - compulsory insurance certificates.

blocks.p: The MIW corpus holds the SOLAS Consolidated Edition 2024, which by its own cover incorporates amendments in effect on 1 July 2024. This examination sat in June 2024, so the operative consolidated edition at the sitting was the previous one. Regulations I/12 and I/14 are relied on here as unchanged across that boundary - they have stood in their harmonized form since the 1988 Protocol took effect in 2000 - but the earlier edition has not been read, and the reliance is recorded as an accepted limitation rather than presented as verified.

SOLAS Chapter I is not among the provisions verified against primary text in the corpus SOLAS log, so the regulation numbering and the extension periods are carried as authoritative secondary. No SOLAS wording is quoted anywhere. The model-certificate form letters are flagged for verification in the corpus's own construction record and are named subject to that flag.

The domestic statute at this sitting is the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958, under which the Directorate General of Shipping issues or delegates these certificates for Indian ships. The Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 is not law at this sitting and appears nowhere in this answer.

notes: THE SOLAS EDITION BOUNDARY IS ENGAGED AND IS THE REASON THIS QUESTION IS RATED MEDIUM RATHER THAN LOW. The corpus holds the Consolidated Edition 2024, in effect 1 July 2024. This sitting is June 2024. The operative consolidated edition at the sitting is the earlier one. The answer does not cite the 2024 edition as the applicable text; it states the effect of regulations I/12 and I/14, which have stood unchanged since the 1988 Protocol took effect on 3 February 2000, and records the reliance as an accepted limitation.

THE HONG KONG CONVENTION IS EXCLUDED AND THE EXCLUSION IS STATED. The corpus records it in force 26 June 2025 - a year after this sitting - so no IHM or Ready-for-Recycling certificate appears in the statutory list. The EU Ship Recycling Regulation is mentioned in the study guide only to explain why a candidate might wrongly reach for an IHM, and is correctly described as regional rather than a convention certificate.

THE HARMONIZED SYSTEM ITSELF CARRIES NO LIVE BOUNDARY. The 1988 Protocols entered into force on 3 February 2000, more than twenty-four years before this sitting, and the survey windows and validity periods have not moved since.

MSC 108 IS CHECKED AND NOT ENGAGED. It sat 15 to 24 May 2024, one month before this examination, and its resolutions - MSC.550(108), MSC.554(108), MSC.555(108), MSC.557(108), MSC.560(108) - were ADOPTED but not in force, with entry into force 1 January 2026. None of them touches SOLAS Chapter I certification in any event, and none is relied on here. Adopted is not in force, and that distinction is the standing rule on this paper.

THE INDIAN STATUTE BOUNDARY IS RESOLVED. The Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 governs. The Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 commenced 15 March 2026, twenty-one months after this sitting, and appears nowhere in this object.

MARPOL ANNEX VI IS NAMED FOR CERTIFICATE IDENTITY ONLY. The IAPP certificate, the IEEC at regulation 24 and the DCS Statement of Compliance are named as certificates with their hooks; no Annex VI provision is quoted, consistent with the corpus holding that Annex as citation-ready only.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: Two tasks of equal weight. Limb (a) is an enumeration marked on coverage and on correct attribution to the issuing convention - the stem asks twice for the convention reference, so an unattributed list cannot score. Limb (b) is itself two questions: define harmonization under the 1988 Protocol, and then apply regulation I/14 to a certificate that has just expired in a port with no survey capability. The scenario is the discriminator; it separates candidates who know the certification system from candidates who have memorised a certificate list.
decomposition_gate.mark_allocation: 16, set as 8 + 8. Printed marks are unambiguous. Within limb (b) the split is roughly even between the definition of harmonization and the expired-certificate procedure, because the stem gives each its own sentence.
decomposition_gate.examiner_expectation: A grouped, convention-attributed certificate list with the tanker-specific items visible - Form B on the IOPP supplement, the Enhanced Survey Programme, the CLC insurance certificate - and validity periods that show the exceptions rather than reciting five years throughout. Then the four elements of the harmonized system, and a procedure for the expired certificate that reaches the Administration for an extension under regulation I/14, names the three-month ceiling, and does not sail before it is granted.

questions.understand_first: There are two different things in this question and candidates run them together. A certificate is a piece of paper that says a survey was passed. A survey is the event that makes the paper true. Harmonization is not about the paper at all - it is about making all the surveys happen at the same time, so that one surveyor attendance discharges SOLAS, Load Lines and MARPOL together, on one anniversary date, in one three-month window, on one five-year clock. Once that is clear, the second half of limb (b) stops being a memory test. A certificate has expired; the survey that would renew it cannot be done here; the ship is therefore uncertificated and undetainably so. The regulation's answer is not to repair anything - it is to ask the flag State for a short, purpose-limited extension that gets the ship to a port where the survey can happen, and nothing more. Three months, one voyage, and the replacement certificate still runs from the old expiry date. The system is deliberately unforgiving about time, because the alternative is a fleet that renews its certificates whenever convenient.

steps.title: What an oil tanker carries, and under which convention
points: Four families - SOLAS, MARPOL, other conventions, insurance - not one undifferentiated list
The stem asks twice for the convention reference, so attribute every certificate

steps.title: SOLAS 1974/1988 certificates
points: Cargo Ship Safety Construction, Safety Equipment with Record of Equipment Form E, Safety Radio - or the combined Cargo Ship Safety Certificate, Form C
Safety Management Certificate and the Company's Document of Compliance - chapter IX and the ISM Code

Continuous Synopsis Record XI-1/5 and Minimum Safe Manning Document V/14 - neither expires
Enhanced Survey Programme under XI-1/2 and the ESP Code - a survey regime, not a certificate, but tanker-specific
Five years for all the certificates in this group

steps.title: MARPOL certificates - where the tanker differs most
points: IOPP certificate with the Form B supplement - Form B is the oil-tanker form, Form A is not
NLS certificate or IBC Certificate of Fitness where so certified - Annex II
ISPP - Annex IV; IAPP with supplement and EIAPP with the NOx Technical File - Annex VI
International Energy Efficiency Certificate - Annex VI regulation 24, valid for the ship's life
DCS Statement of Compliance - issued annually
Annex V garbage attracts no certificate - say so, because candidates invent one

steps.title: Other conventions
points: International Load Line Certificate - LL 1966/88, five years
International Tonnage Certificate 1969 - no expiry
Maritime Labour Certificate and DMLC Parts I and II - MLC 2006, 500 GT and above, five years with an intermediate inspection
AFS certificate - life of the system; BWM certificate - five years
CLC 1992 insurance certificate above 2,000 tonnes of persistent oil in bulk; Bunkers certificate above 1,000 GT - validity is the insurance period
Ship Sanitation Control (Exemption) Certificate - IHR 2005, six months, not IMO
Certificate of Class is NOT statutory - but the same society is usually the Recognized Organization

steps.title: Harmonization under SOLAS 74/88 - what it actually changed
points: The 1988 Protocols to SOLAS and Load Lines, in force 3 February 2000; MARPOL amended to match
One anniversary date for the ship, governing every harmonized certificate
A common five-year maximum validity, so they expire together
A common survey pattern - initial, annual, intermediate, renewal, additional - with a three-month window either side of the anniversary date
The intermediate survey REPLACES the second or third annual survey; it is not additional
Flexibility on issue and extension, so operational difficulty does not force uncertificated trading
The purpose is economic as well as regulatory - one attendance, less off-hire, no drift between certificates

steps.title: A certificate that has just expired, in a port that cannot survey
points: Start with the hard point: an expired statutory certificate is a detainable deficiency
Survey COMPLETE but certificate not issued or on board - endorsement of the existing certificate, up to five months from expiry
Certificate expired and the ship NOT in a port where she is to be surveyed - Administration may extend, three months maximum, to complete the voyage to the survey port
Short-voyage ships otherwise uncovered - a one-month period of grace
Condition one: on arrival at the survey port she may not leave on the extension - she needs the new certificate first
Condition two: the new certificate runs five years from the original expiry date, not from the survey

steps.title: The actions to take, in the order you would take them
points: Establish which certificate, the exact expiry, and whether the renewal survey has been completed - that determines which relief applies
Report to the Company and the DPA as an ISM non-conformity
Apply through the Recognized Organization to the flag Administration for endorsement, extension or grace - the RO cannot grant the three-month extension itself
Request an occasional or additional survey where a surveyor can attend, or arrange attendance at the next port
Notify the port State rather than let a PSCO find it
Notify P&I, hull underwriters and charterers - cover may be prejudiced and the ship will usually be off-hire
Test and record the equipment the certificate covers, to make the application credible
Do not sail until the extension is in hand, and then only to the nominated survey port

If a certificate has just expired and the port cannot survey, apply to the Administration under regulation I/14 for an extension of not more than three months, to complete the voyage to the survey port only - and the new certificate still runs five years from the original expiry date.

quick_revision.critical_regulation: SOLAS regulation I/14 for duration, validity and every form of relief - the five-month endorsement, the three-month voyage extension and the one-month period of grace - read with regulation I/12 for issue and endorsement. The harmonized system itself comes from the 1988 Protocols to SOLAS and to the Load Line Convention, in force 3 February 2000.
quick_revision.major_trap: Giving every certificate a five-year validity. The International Tonnage Certificate does not expire, the IEEC runs for the ship's life, the AFS certificate for the life of the system, the insurance certificates for the insurance period and the sanitation certificate for six months. Second trap: sailing on the three-month extension past the survey port - the regulation expressly forbids it, and the replacement certificate still runs from the original expiry date, so the extension buys a voyage, not time. Third trap, specific to this sitting: listing an IHM or Ready-for-Recycling certificate. The Hong Kong Convention entered into force on 26 June 2025, a year after this examination.

retrieval_cards.answer: International Tonnage Certificate 1969 - no expiry. IEEC - the ship's life, unless she changes flag or is majorly converted. AFS certificate - the life of the system. CLC and Bunkers insurance certificates - the insurance period, usually one year. DCS Statement of Compliance - annual. Ship Sanitation Control (Exemption) Certificate - six months. retrieval_cards.prompt: What did harmonization under the 1988 Protocols actually do?
retrieval_cards.answer: Four things: one anniversary date for the ship governing every harmonized certificate; a common five-year maximum validity so they expire together; a common survey pattern - initial, annual, intermediate, renewal, additional - with a window of three months either side of the anniversary date; and flexibility on issue and extension. In force 3 February 2000, with MARPOL amended to match. The intermediate survey replaces the second or third annual survey.
retrieval_cards.why: Candidates say 'all certificates expire together' and stop. The survey window and the common survey pattern are the operative parts.

retrieval_cards.prompt: A statutory certificate has just expired and the port cannot survey. What do you do?
retrieval_cards.answer: Establish whether the renewal survey has been completed. If it has, the Administration or RO may endorse the existing certificate for up to five months from expiry. If it has not, apply to the Administration - not the RO - to extend validity for no more than three months, solely to reach the survey port. Report it as an ISM non-conformity, notify the port State, P&I and charterers, and do not sail until the extension is on board.
retrieval_cards.why: The relief you can ask for depends entirely on whether the survey is done. Candidates reach for the three-month extension in every case.

retrieval_cards.prompt: After a three-month extension, when does the new certificate expire?
retrieval_cards.answer: Five years from the original expiry date of the old certificate, not five years from the renewal survey. And on arrival at the survey port the ship may not leave again on the strength of the extension - she must first hold the new certificate.
retrieval_cards.why: Both conditions are in the regulation and both are routinely missed. The extension buys a voyage, not time.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which certificate must NOT appear on a June 2024 statutory list?
retrieval_cards.answer: The International Certificate on Inventory of Hazardous Materials or a Ready-for-Recycling Certificate. The Hong Kong Convention entered into force on 26 June 2025, a year after this sitting. The EU Ship Recycling Regulation required an IHM earlier, but it is a regional instrument, not a convention certificate.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the paper's date-sensitive certificate. A later MIW answer that lists it belongs to a later sitting.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Is the Certificate of Class a statutory certificate?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. It is issued under the classification society's own rules and is a commercial and contractual document. But the same society, acting as a Recognized Organization authorised by the flag State, will normally have issued most of the statutory certificates on the flag's behalf - which is why the two are confused.
retrieval_cards.why: Naming the distinction AND the overlap is what shows understanding rather than a memorised exclusion.

blocks.h: 1. The single difference from which the rest follows

blocks.p: Both families answer the same question - where does a judge find the law? - and they answer it in opposite directions. A civil law system starts from a comprehensive written code enacted by the legislature; the judge's task is to find the applicable article and apply it to the facts. A common law system starts from the accumulated body of decided cases; the judge's task is to find the principle those cases establish and apply it, and in doing so may make new law. Everything else in limb (a) - precedent, the role of the judge, the role of the lawyer, the shape of the trial - follows from that one difference and should be presented as following from it.

rows: Primary source
Decided cases, supplemented by statute
Codified statute - civil, commercial, penal and procedural codes
Origin
England, spread through the Commonwealth and the United States
Roman law through the Napoleonic and German codifications; most of continental Europe, Latin America, much of Asia and Africa
Precedent
Binding - stare decisis; a higher court's ratio binds lower courts
Persuasive only - a consistent line of decisions carries weight but does not bind
Judicial law-making
Expressly part of the function - the common law develops through judgments
Not the function - the judge applies the code; law-making belongs to the legislature
Procedure
Adversarial
Inquisitorial
Statutory interpretation
Narrow and literal, because statute is read against a background of case law
Purposive, because the code is meant to be comprehensive and gaps are filled by reasoning from principle

blocks.p: In a common law court the judge is a neutral umpire. He or she does not investigate, does not call witnesses of the court's own motion, and does not decide what evidence should be sought. The judge rules on admissibility, controls the procedure, decides questions of law, directs the jury where there is one, and then decides the case on the material the parties have chosen to put forward. The judgment is reasoned at length, because it must be, since it will bind later courts - the judgment is itself a source of law. Judges are typically appointed late in a career, from among senior practising advocates.

In a civil law court the judge is an active investigator. The judge directs the inquiry, decides what evidence is needed, questions witnesses directly, and may appoint the court's own expert - who is the court's expert, not either party's. The judgment applies the code and is characteristically shorter and more formal, because it is not intended to create law for the future. Judges are usually career judges, trained and appointed as judges from the start rather than drawn from the bar.
The roles are the mirror image of the judicial ones.

rows: Control of the case
Drives it. Chooses the claims, the evidence, the witnesses and the strategy
Assists the court. The judge directs the inquiry; the advocate frames submissions within it
Evidence
Investigates, gathers, discloses on discovery, and presents
Proposes evidence to the judge, who decides what will be taken
Witnesses
Examines in chief and cross-examines the opponent's witnesses
Rarely cross-examines; questions are usually put through the judge
Skill valued
Oral advocacy and forensic technique
Written pleading and doctrinal reasoning from the code
Use of authority
Cites cases as binding authority
Cites the code, with academic commentary (la doctrine) and prior decisions as persuasive support

blocks.p: The practical consequence for a shipowner is real rather than academic. The same collision, litigated in a common law forum, produces long disclosure, witness statements and days of cross-examination; in a civil law forum it produces a court-appointed expert whose report will largely determine the outcome. That is why forum and jurisdiction clauses are negotiated as hard as they are.

blocks.h: 4. Adversarial and inquisitorial - the models these roles create

blocks.p: It is worth naming the two procedural models expressly, because the examiner's phrase "the roles of the lawyer and Judge" is really asking for them. Adversarial: two parties contest before a passive tribunal, and the truth is expected to emerge from the contest. Inquisitorial: the court investigates, and the truth is expected to emerge from the inquiry. Neither model exists in a pure form anywhere - English civil procedure has become markedly more judge-managed, and civil law systems have widened the parties' role - and saying so is the mark of an answer that has understood the distinction rather than memorised it.

blocks.h: 5. How a State becomes bound in the first place

blocks.p: Limb (b) needs one step before the common law / civil law contrast can be applied. A convention binds a State internationally when that State has consented to be bound - by ratification, acceptance, approval or accession - and the convention has entered into force. That is a question of international law and the same for every State. Whether the convention then has any effect inside that State, on its citizens and in its courts, is an entirely separate question answered by that State's own constitution. A State that has ratified but not implemented is in breach internationally and can be held to account for it - it may not plead its own internal law as an excuse - but a shipowner still cannot sue on the convention in its courts.

rows: The theory
International and domestic law are one legal order
They are two separate legal orders
On ratification
The treaty becomes part of domestic law automatically, usually on publication in the official journal
The treaty binds the State internationally but has no domestic effect until legislation is passed
What a court applies
The treaty itself, often ranking above ordinary statute
The implementing statute - and if the statute and the treaty diverge, the statute governs
Typical examples
France, the Netherlands, Japan, and most of Latin America
The United Kingdom, India, Australia, Canada, and the United States for non-self-executing treaties

blocks.p: Here is the point most answers get wrong, and stating it correctly is worth a mark on its own: monism and dualism do not map onto civil law and common law. They are two independent axes. The common law world is largely dualist because it inherited the British constitutional rule that the executive makes treaties and only Parliament makes law - a separation-of-powers point, not a sources-of-law point. Many civil law States are monist. But the Scandinavian civil law States are firmly dualist, and the United States - a common law system - treats some treaties as self-executing and others not. The correlation is a historical tendency, not a rule.
India is a common law system and a dualist one, which makes it the natural example for an Indian examination.

ul: The executive negotiates, signs and ratifies. There is no requirement of parliamentary approval to bind India internationally.

Article 253 of the Constitution empowers Parliament to make law for the whole or any part of the territory of India for implementing any treaty, agreement or convention with another country - and notably to do so even on subjects in the State List, so the federal division of powers is not an obstacle to implementation.

Until Parliament acts, the convention has no force in Indian courts. A ratified but unimplemented convention creates an international obligation and nothing more domestically, although Indian courts will use it as an aid to construing ambiguous legislation and will lean against a reading that puts India in breach.

For shipping, the implementing vehicle at this examination is the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958, whose Parts give domestic effect to SOLAS, MARPOL, the Load Line Convention, STCW and the collision regulations, supported by rules made under the Act and by DG Shipping circulars and merchant shipping notices that carry the detail. The Directorate General of Shipping administers it and authorises Recognized Organizations to survey and certify on India's behalf.

Where a convention is given effect by a dedicated statute rather than by the Merchant Shipping Act, that statute does the work - the Admiralty (Jurisdiction and Settlement of Maritime Claims) Act, 2017 for arrest and maritime claims, and the Marine Insurance Act, 1963 for marine insurance, are the two a Chief Engineer meets most often.

blocks.p: The practical consequence, and the one worth stating because it is the engineer's experience of the whole subject: the ship does not comply with SOLAS - she complies with the flag State's rules made under its implementing Act. Where the two differ, it is the national rule the surveyor enforces and the national rule the master must follow, and the divergence is India's problem at the IMO, not the ship's problem in port.

blocks.h: 8. The contrasting mechanism in a monist State

blocks.p: Take the same convention into France. On ratification and publication in the Journal Officiel the convention becomes part of French law directly, and under the French constitution a duly ratified treaty ranks above ordinary statute. No implementing Act is needed to make it enforceable, and a French court will apply the convention text itself. Two practical consequences follow. Implementation is faster, because no legislative slot is required. But it is also less adapted: penalties, enforcement machinery and administrative detail are not supplied by the convention, so a monist State still legislates for those, and a convention drafted for uniformity can sit awkwardly in a domestic legal order that has not been reshaped to receive it.

blocks.h: 9. Why the difference matters at sea

blocks.p: Uniformity is the entire point of maritime conventions, and both routes leak. The dualist route leaks through delay and divergence - years between ratification and implementation, and implementing statutes that shade the convention's meaning. The monist route leaks through interpretation - the same Article read differently by courts in different States, with no supranational tribunal to reconcile them. IMO's response to both is not legal but institutional: the III Code and the mandatory IMO Member State Audit Scheme, which audit whether a State has in fact given effect to the instruments it has ratified, and the flag State implementation machinery that sits alongside it. That is the honest closing point - the difference between the two systems is managed, not eliminated.

8 and 8. Limb (a) has three named sub-tasks - the main difference, the role of the lawyer, the role of the judge - so it needs three visible answers, and the safest way to make them visible is a comparison table for each. Limb (b) says "State and describe with examples", which is an instruction, not decoration: an answer with no named country cannot score full marks. Give India in detail because it is an Indian paper, and one monist State by way of contrast.

blocks.h: The mark-winning sentence in the whole question

blocks.p: Monism and dualism are not the same distinction as civil law and common law. Most candidates draw a single line down the page - common law on one side, civil law and monism on the other - and it is wrong. They are two independent axes: the Scandinavian States are civil law and dualist; the United States is common law and treats some treaties as self-executing. Write the correlation as a historical tendency and then say why: the common law world is largely dualist because it inherited the British rule that the executive makes treaties and only Parliament makes law, which is a separation-of-powers point rather than a sources-of-law point.

blocks.h: The two-step that limb (b) is really testing

ol: Becoming bound internationally - ratification, acceptance, approval or accession, plus entry into force. Identical for every State, and governed by the law of treaties.
Becoming enforceable domestically - automatic in a monist State on publication; requiring an implementing Act in a dualist one.

blocks.p: A State that has completed step one and not step two is in breach internationally and cannot plead its own internal law as an excuse - but a shipowner still has nothing to sue on in its courts. Getting that gap right is the substance of the limb.

blocks.h: India, in five lines you can write from memory

ul: Common law system, dualist State.
The executive ratifies; Article 253 empowers Parliament to legislate to implement - even on State List subjects.
Until it legislates, the convention has no domestic force, though courts use it to construe ambiguous statutes.
For shipping the vehicle is the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958, with rules and DG Shipping circulars supplying detail.
Also the Admiralty Act 2017 for arrest and maritime claims and the Marine Insurance Act, 1963 for marine insurance.

blocks.h: The statute trap on this sitting

blocks.p: The governing statute at a June 2024 examination is the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958. The Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 commenced on 15 March 2026 - twenty-one months after this paper - and must not appear in the answer. If you have read a later MIW answer that cites the 2025 Act, it belongs to a later sitting. This is the single most likely temporal error on this question, precisely because the 2025 Act is the natural thing for a candidate revising in a later year to reach for.

The doctrine of precedent and the Indian dualist position are both classically illustrated by decided cases, and it is tempting to name one. Do not, unless you are certain. A misattributed authority is worse than no authority in a law answer, and the principle scores the mark without it. This answer names none, for exactly that reason.

ul: Answering only the first sentence of limb (a) - the sources-of-law difference - and never reaching the judge and the lawyer, which are two-thirds of what is asked.
Saying the civil law judge "is like a prosecutor". He is not; he is an investigator for the court, and in a civil case there is no prosecution at all.
Presenting the adversarial and inquisitorial models as pure. Neither is, and modern English civil procedure is heavily judge-managed.
Writing limb (b) with no country named, when the stem says "with examples".
Equating dualism with common law, which is the error the whole limb is built to catch.
Saying a ratified convention automatically binds Indian citizens. It does not - Parliament must legislate first.
Reaching for the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 at a June 2024 sitting.
"Is precedent binding in a civil law system?" No - persuasive only. A consistent line of decisions carries real weight, but it does not bind.
"Who appoints the expert?" In a civil law court, the court does, and that expert's report will usually decide the case. In a common law court each party brings its own.
"India has ratified convention X. Can I rely on it in an Indian court tomorrow?" No, not until it is implemented - though the court may use it to construe an ambiguous Act.
"Give a common law State that is not dualist." The United States, for treaties its courts hold to be self-executing.
"Give a civil law State that is not monist." The Scandinavian States.
"Which Article of the Constitution?" 253. And its significance is that it reaches State List subjects, so federalism is not a defence to non-implementation.
"Does SOLAS bind your ship?" Strictly, the flag State's rules made under its implementing Act bind her. That is the answer that shows you understood limb (b).
Your flag State's rule is stricter than the convention. Which do you follow, and why?
How does an IMO convention amendment reach your ship? Take tacit acceptance through to the DG Shipping circular.
Which Indian Act implements MARPOL, and who enforces it?
What is the III Code and the Member State Audit Scheme for?
You are arrested in a civil law port. How will the proceedings differ from what you would expect at home?

blocks.p: CODE versus CASES; JUDGE versus LAWYER; then TWO STEPS and TWO AXES. Code against cases is the source. Whoever is passive in one system is active in the other - civil law judge active, common law lawyer active. Then limb (b): two steps (bound internationally, then enforceable domestically) and two axes (monist / dualist is not common law / civil law). Finish with India: Article 253, Merchant Shipping Act 1958.

ul: Article 253, Constitution of India - Parliament's power to legislate to implement treaties, including on State List subjects.
Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 - the implementing vehicle for the IMO conventions in India at this sitting.
Admiralty (Jurisdiction and Settlement of Maritime Claims) Act, 2017 - arrest and maritime claims.
Marine Insurance Act, 1963 - marine insurance, including general average at section 66.
Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties 1969 - signature, ratification, accession, entry into force, and the rule that internal law is no excuse for non-performance.
IMO Instruments Implementation Code (III Code) and the mandatory IMO Member State Audit Scheme - the institutional answer to divergent implementation.
MLC 2006 Article XIII - amendment by the ILO Special Tripartite Committee, an example of a convention whose amendment route is not IMO tacit acceptance at all.

blocks.p: This is the one question on the paper that rests mainly on legal theory rather than on a held instrument. The comparative material is carried as authoritative secondary and no textbook, author or case is named. MIW holds no law reports, and no case is cited anywhere in this answer.

The Constitution of India is not held by the MIW corpus. Article 253 is cited by number and effect only, and no constitutional wording is quoted. The Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 is likewise not held; its Parts are described by function rather than by section number.

The classification of named States as monist or dualist is given as the general position. A State's practice can differ between treaty types and can change over time, so the countries are offered as examples rather than as a fixed table.

notes: THE LEGAL THEORY CARRIES NO DATE. The common law / civil law contrast, the doctrine of precedent, the adversarial and inquisitorial models, and the monism / dualism distinction are structural features of legal systems, not dated law. The answer would be identical at any sitting in the last fifty years.

THE ONE LIVE BOUNDARY IS THE INDIAN STATUTE, AND IT IS RESOLVED. The Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 is named as the implementing vehicle. The Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 commenced 15 March 2026, twenty-one months after this sitting, and appears nowhere in this object. The study guide states the exclusion expressly rather than leaving it to be inferred, because on a question about how conventions are implemented in India the 2025 Act is exactly what a candidate revising in a later year would reach for.

THE OTHER INDIAN STATUTES NAMED ARE CHECKED AND OPERATIVE AT THE SITTING. The Admiralty (Jurisdiction and Settlement of Maritime Claims) Act, 2017 and the Marine Insurance Act, 1963 were both long in force in June 2024.
THE COASTAL SHIPPING ACT, 2025 AND THE BILLS OF LADING ACT, 2025 ARE CHECKED AND EXCLUDED. Both are held or flagged in the corpus India folder and both post-date this sitting. Neither is named.
ARTICLE 253 HAS NOT BEEN AMENDED IN ANY RELEVANT RESPECT AND CARRIES NO SITTING-SENSITIVE CONTENT.

THE III CODE AND THE MEMBER STATE AUDIT SCHEME WERE BOTH OPERATIVE WELL BEFORE THIS SITTING. The audit scheme became mandatory on 1 January 2016. No 34th Assembly resolution is relied on - those were adopted 3 December 2025, after this sitting.

Limb (b) is the harder limb and is where candidates fail: it asks how conventions are given effect in countries following 'the above system of laws' - meaning both - and it expressly demands examples. The discriminator is whether the candidate knows that monism and dualism are a SEPARATE axis from common law and civil law.

questions.understand_first: Strip the jargon and this is two questions about who decides. Limb (a): who decides what the law is? In a civil law country the legislature decided in advance and wrote it in a code, so the judge looks it up and the lawyer argues about how it applies. In a common law country the judges have been deciding it case by case for centuries, so the judge's own judgment becomes law and the lawyer's job is to find the cases and fight. Whoever is passive in one system is active in the other, and every other difference - precedent, cross-examination, the length of judgments, whose expert the court believes - falls out of that. Limb (b): who decides whether an international convention reaches you, the seafarer, on a ship in Mumbai? Two separate acts. First the State agrees to be bound internationally, which every State does the same way. Then the convention has to get inside that State's legal system, and that is where the systems part company. A monist State lets it in automatically on publication. A dualist State makes Parliament pass an Act first, and until it does, the convention is a promise between governments that no court will enforce. India is dualist, so the answer to "does SOLAS bind my ship?" is strictly no - the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 does.

steps.title: The single difference from which the rest follows
points: Fix the sense: 'civil law' here means the Romano-Germanic family, not civil versus criminal
Civil law starts from a comprehensive enacted code; common law from accumulated decided cases
Precedent is binding at common law (stare decisis), persuasive only in civil law
Judicial law-making is part of the common law function and no part of the civil law one
Statutory interpretation is narrow and literal at common law, purposive in civil law
Present everything that follows as flowing from this one difference

steps.title: The judge
points: Common law judge - neutral umpire; rules on admissibility and law; does not investigate
Long reasoned judgments, because they will bind later courts and are themselves a source of law
Appointed late, from senior advocates
Civil law judge - active investigator; directs the inquiry, questions witnesses, appoints the court's own expert
Shorter formal judgments applying the code, not intended to create law
A career judiciary, trained as judges from the start

steps.title: The lawyer
points: Common law advocate drives the case - claims, evidence, witnesses, strategy, discovery
Examination in chief and cross-examination; oral forensic skill is the valued competence
Cites cases as binding authority
Civil law advocate assists the court within an inquiry the judge directs
Proposes evidence rather than presenting it; questions usually put through the judge
Written pleading and doctrinal reasoning; cites the code, with commentary and prior decisions as persuasive
The practical consequence: the same collision is litigated completely differently, which is why forum clauses are negotiated hard

steps.title: Adversarial and inquisitorial - the models these roles create
points: Name both models expressly - this is what 'the roles of the lawyer and Judge' is really asking for
Adversarial: two parties contest before a passive tribunal; truth from the contest
Inquisitorial: the court investigates; truth from the inquiry
Neither exists in pure form - say so, because that is the mark of understanding rather than memorising

steps.title: How a State becomes bound in the first place
points: Consent to be bound - ratification, acceptance, approval or accession - plus entry into force
Identical for every State; a question of the law of treaties, not of the domestic system
Whether it then has effect INSIDE the State is a separate question answered by that State's constitution
A State that has ratified but not implemented is in breach and may not plead its internal law - but no shipowner can sue on the convention in its courts

steps.title: Monism and dualism
points: Monist - one legal order; the treaty becomes domestic law automatically on publication and often outranks ordinary statute
Dualist - two legal orders; no domestic effect until an implementing Act is passed, and the statute governs if it diverges
Examples: France, the Netherlands, Japan monist; the United Kingdom, India, Australia, Canada dualist
THE KEY POINT: monism and dualism do NOT map onto civil law and common law - two independent axes
The Scandinavian States are civil law and dualist; the United States is common law with self-executing and non-self-executing treaties
The correlation exists because the common law world inherited a separation-of-powers rule, not a sources-of-law rule

steps.title: India as the worked example
points: Common law system, dualist State
The executive negotiates, signs and ratifies without parliamentary approval
Article 253 empowers Parliament to legislate to implement - even on State List subjects, so federalism is no obstacle
Until then no domestic force, though courts use the convention to construe ambiguous legislation
The vehicle for shipping is the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958, with rules and DG Shipping circulars supplying detail; DG Shipping authorises ROs
Dedicated statutes elsewhere - Admiralty Act 2017, Marine Insurance Act 1963
The consequence to state plainly: the ship complies with the flag State's rules, not with SOLAS directly

steps.title: The contrasting mechanism in a monist State
points: France: on ratification and publication the convention is part of French law and outranks ordinary statute
No implementing Act needed; the court applies the convention text itself
Faster - no legislative slot required
But less adapted - penalties, enforcement and administrative detail still need domestic legislation

steps.title: Why the difference matters at sea
points: Uniformity is the point of maritime conventions and both routes leak
Dualist leak: delay between ratification and implementation, and implementing statutes that shade the meaning
Monist leak: the same Article read differently in different States, with no supranational tribunal
IMO's answer is institutional, not legal - the III Code and the mandatory Member State Audit Scheme
Close honestly: the difference is managed, not eliminated

questions.memory_cue: CODE v CASES, then TWO STEPS and TWO AXES. Code against cases is the whole of limb (a) (1) - and whoever is passive in one system is active in the other: civil judge active (2), common lawyer active (3). Limb (b): two steps - bound internationally (5), then enforceable domestically (6); and two axes - monist/dualist is NOT common/civil (6). Land it on India: Article 253, MS Act 1958 (7).

quick_revision.recall_15s: Civil law = codified statute, judge finds the article, precedent persuasive only, judge investigates, lawyer assists the court, inquisitorial. Common law = decided cases, precedent binding (stare decisis), judge a neutral umpire whose judgment is itself law, lawyer drives the case and cross-examines, adversarial. For limb (b), two steps: a State becomes bound internationally by ratification or accession plus entry into force; it becomes enforceable domestically automatically in a monist State on publication, but only by an implementing Act in a dualist one. Monism and dualism are a separate axis from civil and common law - Scandinavia is civil law and dualist, the USA is common law with self-executing treaties. India is common law and dualist: the executive ratifies, Article 253 lets Parliament legislate even on State List subjects, and shipping conventions arrive through the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958, its rules and DG Shipping circulars.
critical_numbers: Article 253 of the Constitution of India - the treaty-implementation power
Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 - the implementing statute at this sitting
Admiralty (Jurisdiction and Settlement of Maritime Claims) Act, 2017; Marine Insurance Act, 1963
The IMO Member State Audit Scheme became mandatory on 1 January 2016
Two axes, not one: civil/common law and monist/dualist are independent
quick_revision.critical_regulation: Article 253 of the Constitution of India is the provision that makes limb (b) an Indian answer rather than a general one: Parliament may legislate for the whole or any part of India to implement a treaty, and may do so even on State List subjects. The Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 is what it has produced for the IMO conventions at this sitting.
quick_revision.major_trap: Equating dualism with common law and monism with civil law. They are independent axes - the Scandinavian civil law States are dualist and the United States is a common law State with self-executing treaties. Second trap: writing limb (b) with no country named, when the stem expressly says "with examples". Third trap, specific to this sitting: citing the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025. It commenced on 15 March 2026, twenty-one months after this examination - the governing statute here is the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958. Fourth: naming a case you are not certain of. A misattributed authority is worse than none, and the principle scores without it.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the common law / civil law question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 The structural difference (code v cases). 2 The judge. 3 The lawyer. 4 Adversarial and inquisitorial. 5 Becoming bound internationally. 6 Monism and dualism. 7 India worked through. 8 A monist contrast. 9 Why it matters at sea. Sections 1-4 are limb (a); 5-9 are limb (b).
retrieval_cards.why: Limb (a) names three sub-tasks and limb (b) demands examples. Separate sections are what make all of them visible to the examiner.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Contrast the judge's role in the two systems.
retrieval_cards.answer: Common law: a neutral umpire. Rules on admissibility and questions of law, decides on the material the parties choose to put forward, and writes a long reasoned judgment that binds later courts. Appointed late from senior advocates. Civil law: an active investigator. Directs the inquiry, decides what evidence is needed, questions witnesses, appoints the court's own expert, and writes a shorter formal judgment applying the code. A career judiciary.
retrieval_cards.why: The role of the judge is one of three explicitly named sub-tasks in limb (a) and cannot be left implicit.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Contrast the lawyer's role in the two systems.
retrieval_cards.answer: Common law: drives the case - chooses claims, evidence, witnesses and strategy; gives discovery; examines in chief and cross-examines; cites cases as binding authority. Oral advocacy is the valued skill. Civil law: assists a court-directed inquiry - proposes evidence for the judge to take, rarely cross-examines, and puts questions through the judge; cites the code with commentary and prior decisions as persuasive. Written pleading is the valued skill.
retrieval_cards.why: Whoever is passive in one system is active in the other. That symmetry is the cleanest way to remember both roles at once.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Define monism and dualism.
retrieval_cards.answer: Monist: international and domestic law are one legal order, so a ratified and published treaty becomes part of domestic law automatically and often ranks above ordinary statute - France, the Netherlands, Japan. Dualist: two separate legal orders, so the treaty binds the State internationally but has no domestic effect until an implementing Act is passed, and if statute and treaty diverge the statute governs - the United Kingdom, India, Australia, Canada.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the core of limb (b). Without it the limb becomes a vague essay about international cooperation.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Are all common law States dualist and all civil law States monist?
retrieval_cards.answer: No - they are two independent axes. The Scandinavian States are civil law and firmly dualist. The United States is common law and treats some treaties as self-executing. The correlation exists only because the common law world inherited the British constitutional rule that the executive makes treaties and only Parliament makes law - a separation-of-powers point, not a sources-of-law point.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the single mark-winning sentence in the question, and the error the limb is built to catch.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How does an IMO convention reach a ship under the Indian flag?
retrieval_cards.answer: The executive ratifies or accedes, binding India internationally. Article 253 of the Constitution then empowers Parliament to legislate to implement it, including on State List subjects. Parliament does so through the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958, under which rules are made and DG Shipping circulars and merchant shipping notices supply the operational detail. DG Shipping administers it and authorises Recognized Organizations to survey and certify. Until Parliament acts, the convention has no force in an Indian court - though a court will use it to construe an ambiguous statute.
retrieval_cards.why: Limb (b) says 'with examples'. This is the example an Indian examiner is waiting for.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which Indian merchant shipping statute governs at a June 2024 sitting?
retrieval_cards.answer: The Merchant Shipping Act, 1958. The Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 commenced on 15 March 2026 - twenty-one months after this examination - and must not be cited on this paper. The Coastal Shipping Act, 2025 and the Bills of Lading Act, 2025 are likewise after this sitting.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the paper's standing statute trap, and this question walks straight into it because limb (b) invites the Indian example.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Strictly, does SOLAS bind your ship?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. India is dualist, so what binds an Indian ship is the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 and the rules made under it, which give effect to SOLAS. Where the national rule and the convention differ, the surveyor enforces the national rule and the master follows it; the divergence is India's problem at the IMO, not the ship's problem in port.
retrieval_cards.why: Saying this converts limb (b) from theory into the answer of someone who has actually sailed, and it is the natural oral follow-up.
