blocks.h: 1. The governing instrument at this sitting

blocks.p: Port State control is exercised under the enabling provisions of the conventions themselves - SOLAS I/19, MARPOL article 5 and regulation 11, Load Lines article 21, STCW X, MLC 2006 regulation 5.2.1 - and the procedure is set out in the IMO Assembly's Procedures for Port State Control. The edition in force at this examination is resolution A.1185(33), adopted on 6 December 2023, six months before this sitting. Naming the current resolution rather than an older one, or rather than a regional memorandum of understanding, is worth doing in the first line.

The initial inspection is limited: the PSCO checks the certificates and documents, and forms a general impression of the ship's condition. Clear grounds are what entitle the officer to go further, into a more detailed inspection. They exist where there is evidence that the ship, her equipment or her crew does not correspond substantially with the requirements of the relevant conventions, or that the master or crew is not familiar with essential shipboard procedures relating to the safety of ships or the prevention of pollution.

Two words in that definition carry the weight. Substantially - a trivial discrepancy is not clear grounds. And evidence - the officer needs something observed or documented, not a suspicion. Clear grounds are the threshold that protects the ship from an unlimited inspection, and a Chief Engineer who understands that will argue about the threshold rather than about the finding.

blocks.h: 3. The circumstances that create clear grounds

ul: Documents. Certificates absent, expired, invalid, incomplete or apparently falsified; required documents or records not on board; the Oil Record Book with unexplained gaps or entries inconsistent with the machinery fitted.
Equipment. Absence of principal equipment or arrangements required by the conventions - or equipment present but visibly not maintained.
Condition. The officer's own observations of serious hull, machinery or equipment deterioration, heavy corrosion, poor housekeeping, or conditions that are plainly unsafe.

People. The master or crew unable to demonstrate familiarity with essential shipboard operations - an engineer who cannot describe the operation of the oily-water separator or start the emergency generator is himself a clear ground.
Operations. Unsafe operations observed, or procedures required by the SMS not being followed.
Third-party information. A report from a pilot, a port authority, another Administration, a previous port State, a crew complaint or an incident report.
Manning. Evidence that the ship is not manned in accordance with her Minimum Safe Manning Document, or that hours of rest are not being observed.

blocks.p: These are a distinct class, and their significance is that they do not point at a piece of equipment - they point at the management system that should have kept the equipment right. A single failed pump is a deficiency; a failed pump plus no record that it was ever tested is an ISM deficiency, and it is far more serious because it implies every other item is equally unmanaged. Clear grounds for an ISM-related more detailed inspection include:

ul: The Safety Management Certificate or the Company's Document of Compliance absent, invalid, expired, or not matching the ship or the ship type.
No SMS documentation on board, or documentation that is uncontrolled, superseded, or in a language the crew cannot read.
The master unable to demonstrate his authority and responsibility under the SMS, or unaware of his obligation to conduct the master's review.
The Designated Person Ashore unidentified, or no contact details available to the crew.
No evidence of internal audits, or audits carried out with no non-conformities ever raised - which is itself evidence the audits are not real.
Drills and emergency exercises not carried out or not recorded at the intervals the SMS requires.
Maintenance not carried out in accordance with the SMS, or critical equipment not identified as critical.
Non-conformities, accidents or hazardous occurrences not reported, investigated or closed out.

A major non-conformity found - which is defined by the Code as a deviation posing a serious threat to personnel or the ship, or a serious risk to the environment, requiring immediate corrective action, and includes the lack of effective and systematic implementation of a requirement of the Code.

blocks.p: Where the evidence indicates that the SMS is not effectively implemented, the port State may detain the ship and, in a serious case, report the matter to the flag Administration and the Company - and the consequence can reach the Document of Compliance itself, not merely this ship.

blocks.h: 5. Five detainable deficiencies, their causes and their prevention

blocks.p: A deficiency is detainable where it is sufficiently serious to warrant the ship being detained until it is rectified - broadly, where the ship is unsafe to proceed to sea, presents an unreasonable threat of harm to the marine environment, or the deficiencies are so numerous that they show the system has failed. The five below are chosen from the engine room, because the question addresses the Chief Engineer.

rows: Emergency source of electrical power inoperative or unable to take its load - SOLAS II-1/42

Batteries never load-tested, only float-charged; the emergency generator started monthly on no load and never on the emergency switchboard; automatic starting and changeover untested; fuel stale or the day tank drained for use elsewhere

Test on load and record it; test the automatic start and the blackout changeover, not just the engine; treat the emergency generator as critical equipment in the SMS with its own PMS job and its own spares; log every test with the load carried
Steering gear failure, or the emergency steering arrangements unproven - SOLAS II-1/29

Steering gear tests treated as a paper exercise before departure; the alternative power supply and the changeover from bridge to local control never exercised; communications and the compass repeater in the steering flat not checked; no steering gear drill with the crew who would actually be there

Carry out and record the pre-departure tests properly, and hold the emergency steering drill at the interval required; post the changeover instructions in the steering flat; verify the alternative power supply actually starts and takes over; train the ratings who will operate it in the dark
Oily-water separator or 15 ppm alarm inoperative, bypassed or its records inconsistent - MARPOL Annex I

Coalescer elements exhausted and not replaced; the 15 ppm monitor uncalibrated or its cell fouled; the automatic stopping device disabled because it kept stopping; bilges accumulating faster than the equipment can process; Oil Record Book entries that do not reconcile with tank soundings - the classic finding that turns a deficiency into a prosecution

Never permit a bypass, in any circumstance, and say so to the whole department; maintain the coalescer and monitor on the PMS with genuine spares; prove the automatic stopping device and record the proof; reconcile the Oil Record Book against soundings yourself before arrival; attack the source of the bilge water rather than the volume - leaking glands and coolers
Fire pumps, fire main or fixed fire-extinguishing system not operational - SOLAS II-2/10

The emergency fire pump unprimed, its suction valve seized or its self-priming defective; the fire main corroded or isolated with valves shut for other work; the fixed system's bottle pressures out of date, its release arrangements untested, or its distribution valves inaccessible

Run the emergency fire pump under load and prove two jets at the required points; walk the fire main and lock the isolating valves open; keep the fixed-system survey current and the release station clear, labelled and drilled; include the fire pumps in the pre-arrival self-inspection
Bilge pumping arrangements defective, or the machinery space in an unsafe condition - excessive oil, fuel leaks, defective quick-closing valves or remote stops

Bilge wells full and their alarms disabled to stop the nuisance; quick-closing valves for the tanks wired open or their air reservoir empty; remote stops for pumps and fans never tested because testing means stopping machinery; oil-soaked lagging and unrepaired fuel leaks accepted as normal

Test the quick-closing valves and remote stops on a scheduled basis, in port, and record them; never disable an alarm - repair the cause; renew oil-soaked lagging and fit spray shields on high-pressure fuel lines; keep the bilges dry and clean as a standing departmental discipline, because a clean engine room ends more inspections than any document

blocks.p: One theme runs through the whole table and it is what the examiner is looking for behind the five examples: almost every detainable engine-room deficiency is a testing and recording failure before it is a mechanical failure. The equipment is usually capable of working. What is missing is the proof, at the moment the officer asks for it, that anyone had confirmed it recently.

blocks.h: 6. PR17 - what it is, and the scenarios that lead to it

blocks.p: A Procedural Requirement is an IACS instrument that binds IACS member societies in how they carry out their work; it is not an IMO instrument and it does not carry the force of a convention. Its authority is class practice and the IACS framework, and a candidate should describe it in those terms rather than saying that SOLAS requires it. PR 17 is the Procedural Requirement engaged when a ship classed by, or statutorily certified by, an IACS member society acting as a Recognized Organization is detained by a port State. It puts the society under an obligation to look into what happened, because a detention on an item the society certified is prima facie evidence that the society's own survey was inadequate. The scenarios that lead to it are therefore all variations on one theme:

ul: A detention where the detainable deficiency lies in an item the RO surveyed and certified on the flag State's behalf - structure, machinery, LSA, FFA, load line or a MARPOL item - so the certificate and the ship's actual condition are in conflict.

A detention on a statutory certificate the RO issued that turns out to have been issued when the ship did not meet the requirement, or issued outside the survey window, or issued without the survey having been properly carried out.
A detention shortly after a survey by the society - the closer in time, the stronger the implication that the survey missed what the port State found within weeks.

A detention arising from a major non-conformity in the SMS where the society is also the body that issued the Document of Compliance or Safety Management Certificate, so the audit as well as the survey is called into question.

A detention that reveals a systemic failure rather than a single defect - several deficiencies of a kind that the last survey should have found - which is what turns an individual report into a review of the surveyor, the office or the society's procedures.
A detention where the ship's class status was itself wrong - overdue surveys not recorded, conditions of class not imposed or not followed up, or class continued when it should have been suspended.

blocks.p: What follows is an investigation by the society into whether its survey or audit was deficient, a report to the flag Administration and to the Company, corrective action where the society's own procedures or personnel are at fault, and the recording of the detention against the society - which matters commercially, because port State control regimes publish detention performance by Recognized Organization and a flag State chooses its ROs partly on that record.

State the limit of the source honestly. MIW holds no IACS Procedural Requirement text, so the identity of the number 17 is carried as class-practice reference rather than from a read document, and no IACS wording is reproduced. The scenarios above do not depend on that: they are the circumstances in which a Recognized Organization must respond to a port State detention touching what it certified, and that is what the question is asking for.

6 + 6 + 4, and the shape of the answer should follow the marks exactly. Limb (a) has two defined terms and both must be defined, not just the famous one - a candidate who writes brilliantly on clear grounds and adds one line on ISM deficiencies loses half of six marks. Limb (b) asks for three things about five items - the deficiency, its cause, and the preventive action - which is fifteen pieces of information for six marks, so a table is not a stylistic preference here, it is the only way to fit them. Limb (c) is four marks and asks for scenarios, plural: a list of circumstances, not an essay.

Open with A.1185(33), Procedures for Port State Control, 2023, adopted 6 December 2023. Most candidates write "as per PSC procedures" or name a regional MOU. Naming the Assembly resolution, and the right edition of it, takes one line and immediately separates the answer. Do not name a 34th Assembly resolution on this paper - the 34th Assembly sat in December 2025, eighteen months after this examination.

blocks.h: The definition, in the words that matter

blocks.p: Clear grounds = evidence that the ship, her equipment or her crew does not correspond substantially with the requirements of the conventions, or that the master or crew is not familiar with essential shipboard procedures relating to safety or pollution prevention. Learn those three phrases. "Substantially" is what keeps a trivial finding from opening the ship up; "evidence" is what distinguishes clear grounds from suspicion; and the familiarity limb is the one candidates forget, even though an engineer who cannot operate his own separator is the commonest clear ground of all.

blocks.h: Initial, more detailed, expanded - keep the three apart

rows: Initial
Certificates and documents; the officer's general impression of condition
Any visit - no grounds needed
More detailed
An in-depth examination of the areas where the concern lies
Clear grounds
Expanded
A wider prescribed scope, typically on older or higher-risk ships including tankers
The ship's type, age and risk profile, not necessarily any deficiency

blocks.p: The question asks only about the second, but knowing that the third exists and is triggered differently is a common oral follow-up on a tanker paper.

blocks.h: Why the ISM half of limb (a) is the harder half

blocks.p: An equipment deficiency says one thing is wrong. An ISM deficiency says the system that should find things being wrong is itself not working - so nothing else on board can be relied on either. That is why a major non-conformity can detain a ship whose machinery is in reasonable order, and why the consequence can reach the Company's Document of Compliance and the rest of the fleet, not just this ship. Say that explicitly; it is the difference between listing ISM findings and understanding them.

Almost every detainable engine-room deficiency is a testing and recording failure before it is a mechanical failure. The emergency generator usually runs; what is missing is proof that anyone ran it on load. The quick-closing valves usually work; what is missing is a record of the last test. Write that sentence into the answer, because it converts five separate examples into one argument, and it is what a Chief Engineer is supposed to understand that a junior officer does not.

blocks.h: The one deficiency that is different

blocks.p: The oily-water separator is not like the other four. A bypass is not a maintenance failure - it is a deliberate act, it is a criminal offence in most jurisdictions, the Oil Record Book becomes a falsified document, and the consequences fall personally on the Chief Engineer, not on the company. Say so. An answer that lists "OWS not working" alongside "fire pump not working" as though they were the same kind of problem has missed the most important distinction in the limb.

blocks.h: PR17 - how to write four marks safely

blocks.p: Three moves. First, say what kind of thing it is: an IACS Procedural Requirement, binding on member societies, class practice and not an IMO instrument - so never write "SOLAS requires PR17". Second, give the trigger: a port State detention of a ship the society classed or statutorily certified as a Recognized Organization. Third, list the scenarios, which are all variants of the same conflict - the certificate said one thing and the port State found another, on an item the society was responsible for. Then note what follows: investigation, report to flag and Company, corrective action, and the detention recorded against the society's published performance.

ul: Defining clear grounds and never defining ISM-related deficiencies. Half of limb (a).
Listing five deficiencies without causes or preventive actions, when the stem asks for all three.
Giving deck deficiencies. The stem says "as Chief Engineer" - answer from the engine room.
Treating the OWS bypass as an ordinary maintenance deficiency.
Writing PR17 as though it were an IMO or SOLAS requirement.
Naming a regional memorandum of understanding as the source of the definition instead of the Assembly resolution.
Confusing a more detailed inspection with an expanded inspection.
"Which resolution?" A.1185(33) at this sitting. Not a 34th Assembly resolution - that Assembly sat in December 2025.
"Are clear grounds needed for the initial inspection?" No. They are needed to go beyond it.
"Is an unfamiliar crew a clear ground?" Yes - expressly, and it is the limb candidates omit.

"What makes a deficiency detainable?" That the ship is unsafe to proceed to sea, or presents an unreasonable threat of harm to the environment - or that the deficiencies are so numerous they show a systemic failure.
"Can a ship be detained on ISM alone?" Yes, on a major non-conformity, even with the machinery in fair order.
"Who issues PR17 and to whom?" The Recognized Organization, following a detention, reporting to the flag Administration and the Company - not the port State, and not the flag.
"Why does the society care?" Because detention performance by RO is published, and flag States choose their ROs on that record.
A PSCO asks you to start the emergency generator and put it on load. Talk me through it.
Show me your Oil Record Book and explain the last three entries.
You disagree with the detention. What can you do about it?
What is a Condition of Class and who imposes it?
Your ship is detained on an item your class surveyor passed last month. What happens next, and to whom?
How would your internal ISM audit have caught this before the port State did?

blocks.p: Two definitions, five failures, one conflict. Limb (a) is two definitions - clear grounds (evidence, substantially, familiarity) and ISM deficiencies (the system, not the item). Limb (b) is five failures and one sentence: tested and recorded, or it is a deficiency. Limb (c) is one conflict: the certificate says compliant, the port State found otherwise, and the RO issued the certificate. Every PR17 scenario is that sentence with a different item in it.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: Three limbs of decreasing size testing three different things. Limb (a) is definitional and tests whether the candidate knows the threshold that governs how far a PSCO may go - and it names TWO terms, so it is really two definitions. Limb (b) is the Chief Engineer's own limb: it wants five detainable deficiencies with causes and preventive action, which is a management answer, not a list. Limb (c) is small and specialised and tests whether the candidate knows what a Recognized Organization is and what happens to it when a ship it certified is detained.
decomposition_gate.mark_allocation: 16, set as 6 + 6 + 4. Printed marks are unambiguous. Limb (b)'s six marks cover fifteen pieces of information - five deficiencies times deficiency, cause and prevention - which is what forces a tabular answer. Limb (c)'s four marks call for a list of scenarios, not an essay.

questions.understand_first: Port State control is built on a single idea: the certificate is a claim, and the port State is entitled to test the claim - but only so far. The officer starts by reading the papers and looking around. That is all he is entitled to do, until something he sees contradicts what the papers say. That contradiction is what "clear grounds" means, and it is a protection for the ship as much as a power for the officer - without it, every inspection could become an unlimited one. So limb (a) is really asking: what is the evidence that unlocks the deeper inspection? And the second half adds the sharpest version of it: when the contradiction is not in a machine but in the management system, everything else on board becomes doubtful at once, which is why a major non-conformity can detain a ship whose machinery is fine. Limb (b) then turns the question round to your side of it. Every one of those five deficiencies is a machine that probably works but cannot be proved to work at the moment the officer asks - so the preventive action is never "repair it", it is "test it and record it". And limb (c) closes the loop: if the port State found what the certificate denied, somebody certified wrongly, and the society that did it has to answer for that.

steps.title: The governing instrument at this sitting
points: A.1185(33), Procedures for Port State Control, 2023, adopted 6 December 2023 - operative at this sitting
The enabling provisions: SOLAS I/19, MARPOL art 5 and reg 11, Load Lines art 21, STCW X, MLC reg 5.2.1
Do not name a 34th Assembly resolution - that Assembly sat December 2025

steps.title: "Clear grounds" - the definition
points: The initial inspection is limited to certificates, documents and a general impression of condition
Clear grounds = evidence that ship, equipment or crew does not correspond substantially with convention requirements
OR that master or crew are not familiar with essential shipboard procedures for safety or pollution prevention
'Substantially' excludes the trivial; 'evidence' excludes suspicion
They unlock the more detailed inspection - and they are a limit on the officer as much as a power

steps.title: The circumstances that create clear grounds
points: Documents - certificates absent, expired, invalid or apparently falsified; Oil Record Book gaps
Equipment - principal equipment or arrangements absent, or present but visibly unmaintained
Condition - observed serious deterioration, heavy corrosion, plainly unsafe conditions
People - crew unable to demonstrate familiarity with essential operations
Operations - unsafe operations observed, SMS procedures not followed
Third-party information - pilot, port authority, previous port State, crew complaint, incident report
Manning - not manned per the Safe Manning Document, or hours of rest not observed

steps.title: ISM-related deficiencies
points: The distinguishing feature: they point at the system, not at an item - so nothing on board can be relied on
SMC or DOC absent, invalid, expired or not matching the ship
No SMS documentation, or uncontrolled or superseded documentation, or in a language the crew cannot read
Master unable to demonstrate his authority under the SMS, or unaware of the master's review
DPA unidentified or no contact details available
No evidence of internal audits - or audits that never raise a non-conformity
Drills not carried out or not recorded; maintenance not per the SMS; critical equipment not identified
Non-conformities, accidents and hazardous occurrences not reported, investigated or closed
A major non-conformity - serious threat to personnel, ship or environment, requiring immediate corrective action, including systemic failure to implement the Code
Consequence can reach the Company's DOC and the rest of the fleet, not just this ship

steps.title: Five detainable deficiencies, their causes and their prevention
points: State the test first: unsafe to proceed to sea, unreasonable threat to the environment, or deficiencies so numerous they show systemic failure
Emergency source of power - never load-tested, changeover untested; prevent by testing ON LOAD and recording it
Steering gear and emergency steering - tests done on paper, changeover never exercised; prevent by real drills and posted instructions
OWS / 15 ppm equipment - coalescer exhausted, monitor uncalibrated, stopping device disabled, ORB not reconciling; prevent by never permitting a bypass and reconciling the ORB yourself
Fire pumps and fixed systems - emergency pump unprimed, main isolated, bottle survey lapsed; prevent by proving two jets and locking isolating valves open

Bilge arrangements and machinery space condition - alarms disabled, quick-closing valves wired open, remote stops untested, oil-soaked lagging; prevent by scheduled in-port testing and a standing cleanliness discipline
Close with the unifying sentence: these are testing and recording failures before they are mechanical failures

steps.title: PR17 - what it is, and the scenarios that lead to it
points: Say what it is: an IACS Procedural Requirement, binding on member societies - class practice, not an IMO instrument
The trigger: a port State detention of a ship the society classed or statutorily certified as a Recognized Organization
Scenario - detainable deficiency in an item the RO surveyed and certified, so certificate and condition conflict
Scenario - a certificate issued when the ship did not meet the requirement, outside the window, or without proper survey
Scenario - detention shortly after a survey by the society
Scenario - a major SMS non-conformity where the society also issued the DOC or SMC
Scenario - several deficiencies showing systemic failure the last survey should have found
Scenario - class status itself wrong: overdue surveys, conditions of class not imposed or not followed up
What follows: investigation, report to flag and Company, corrective action, and the detention recorded against the society's published RO performance
State the evidence limit openly - MIW holds no IACS text; no wording is quoted

questions.memory_cue: Two definitions, five failures, one conflict. Definitions: clear grounds = EVIDENCE + SUBSTANTIALLY + FAMILIARITY (2); ISM deficiencies = the SYSTEM, not the item (4). Five failures: power, steering, oil, fire, bilge - and one sentence for all of them, tested and recorded or it is a deficiency (5). One conflict: the certificate said compliant, the port State found otherwise, and the RO signed it (6).

quick_revision.recall_15s: A.1185(33), Procedures for Port State Control, 2023, adopted 6 December 2023, is the operative edition. Clear grounds = evidence that ship, equipment or crew does not correspond substantially with the conventions, or that master or crew are not familiar with essential shipboard procedures for safety or pollution prevention - they unlock the more detailed inspection. ISM-related deficiencies point at the management system, not at equipment: no SMS documentation, DOC or SMC invalid, master unable to demonstrate his authority, DPA unknown, no internal audits, drills not recorded, maintenance not per the SMS, non-conformities not closed - and a major non-conformity can detain the ship alone and reach the Company's DOC. Five detainable engine-room deficiencies: emergency generator not proven on load, steering gear / emergency steering untested, OWS or 15 ppm inoperative or bypassed with the ORB not reconciling, fire pumps or fixed system not operational, bilge arrangements, quick-closing valves and remote stops defective - all of them testing and recording failures before they are mechanical ones. PR17 is an IACS Procedural Requirement - class practice, not IMO - engaged when a port State detains a ship the society classed or certified as an RO, on an item the society was responsible for.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the port State control question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 Name A.1185(33). 2 Define clear grounds. 3 The circumstances that create them. 4 ISM-related deficiencies as a distinct class. 5 Five detainable deficiencies with cause and prevention, as a table. 6 PR17 - what it is, the scenarios, and the evidence limit. Sections 1-4 are limb (a), 5 is limb (b), 6 is limb (c).
retrieval_cards.why: Limb (a) names two terms and limb (b) asks three things about five items. Only a sectioned and tabulated answer makes all of it visible in the marks available.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Define "clear grounds".
retrieval_cards.answer: Evidence that the ship, her equipment or her crew does not correspond substantially with the requirements of the relevant conventions, or that the master or crew is not familiar with essential shipboard procedures relating to the safety of ships or the prevention of pollution. They are what entitles the PSCO to move from the initial inspection to a more detailed inspection.
retrieval_cards.why: 'Substantially' excludes the trivial and 'evidence' excludes suspicion. The crew-familiarity limb is the one candidates omit, and it is the commonest clear ground in practice.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why is an ISM-related deficiency more serious than an equipment deficiency?
retrieval_cards.answer: An equipment deficiency says one thing is wrong. An ISM deficiency says the system that should find things being wrong is not working - so nothing else on board can be relied on either. That is why a major non-conformity can detain a ship whose machinery is in reasonable order, and why the consequence can reach the Company's Document of Compliance and the rest of the fleet rather than just this ship.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the sentence that turns a list of ISM findings into an understanding of why the class exists.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What makes a deficiency detainable?
retrieval_cards.answer: That it is sufficiently serious to warrant detention until rectified - broadly, the ship is unsafe to proceed to sea, she presents an unreasonable threat of harm to the marine environment, or the deficiencies are so numerous that they demonstrate the management system has failed. The last of the three is the one candidates forget, and it is how a ship is detained on an accumulation of individually minor findings.
retrieval_cards.why: Stating the test before the five examples is what makes the examples look chosen rather than recalled.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name five detainable engine-room deficiencies and the single preventive theme.
retrieval_cards.answer: Emergency source of electrical power inoperative or never proven on load; steering gear or emergency steering defective or untested; oily-water separator or 15 ppm equipment inoperative, bypassed, or with an Oil Record Book that does not reconcile; fire pumps, fire main or fixed fire-extinguishing system not operational; bilge pumping arrangements, quick-closing valves or remote stops defective, with an unsafe machinery-space condition. The theme: every one is a testing and recording failure before it is a mechanical failure.
retrieval_cards.why: The unifying sentence is what a Chief Engineer is expected to supply and a junior officer is not.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why is the OWS deficiency different from the other four?
retrieval_cards.answer: A bypass is not a maintenance failure - it is a deliberate act. It is a criminal offence in most jurisdictions, it makes the Oil Record Book a falsified document, and the consequences fall personally on the Chief Engineer rather than on the company. Never permit one, in any circumstance.
retrieval_cards.why: An answer that lists 'OWS not working' beside 'fire pump not working' as the same kind of problem has missed the most important distinction in the limb.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is PR17 and what triggers it?
retrieval_cards.answer: An IACS Procedural Requirement - an instrument binding on IACS member societies in how they carry out their work. It is class practice and the IACS framework, not an IMO instrument, so never say SOLAS requires it. It is engaged when a port State detains a ship that an IACS member society has classed or statutorily certified as a Recognized Organization, because a detention on an item the society certified is evidence that the society's own survey was inadequate.
retrieval_cards.why: Saying what kind of instrument it is comes before saying what it does, and it is where most of the four marks are lost.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the scenarios that lead to PR17, and what follows.
retrieval_cards.answer: All variants of one conflict - the certificate said compliant and the port State found otherwise, on something the society was responsible for: a detainable deficiency in an item the RO surveyed and certified; a certificate issued when the ship did not comply; a detention shortly after a survey; a major SMS non-conformity where the society issued the DOC or SMC; or the class status itself wrong. What follows: investigation, report to flag and Company, corrective action, and the detention recorded against the society's published RO performance.
retrieval_cards.why: The scenarios are the four marks. Grouping them round one conflict makes them reconstructable rather than memorised.

questions.short_title: Cold Corrosion of Cylinder Liners in Super-Long-Stroke Engines
questions.text_verbatim: With the introduction of the new generation of super-long stroke engines and changed process parameters triggered by environmental compliance rules, “Cold Corrosion” of cylinder liners has grown to become a major issue for the latest generation of two-stroke engines. Discuss the causes and mitigation measures, stressing on the following: (16) A. Increased Jacket Cooling Water Temperatures Systems B. New Cylinder Liner designs C. New Cylinder Lubricators.

New Cylinder Liner designs

questions.verification_status: This is a pure marine-engineering question with no statutory content, and it is sourced on that footing. The chemistry - sulphur in the fuel oxidising to sulphur dioxide and trioxide in combustion, combining with water vapour to form sulphuric acid, and condensing on any surface below the acid dew point - is standard combustion and corrosion science and is carried as engineering and analytical-chemistry reference. The design responses are the published two-stroke practice of the low-speed engine designers, carried as authoritative secondary. NO ENGINE BUILDER, LICENSEE, PROPRIETARY SYSTEM, TRADE NAME, OIL COMPANY OR CYLINDER OIL PRODUCT IS NAMED ANYWHERE, and no jacket water temperature, liner wall temperature, feed rate in grammes per kilowatt-hour, base number, sulphur percentage other than the MARPOL limit, or wear rate in millimetres per thousand hours is asserted as a general value. Every one of those is engine, oil, fuel and service specific, and a figure carried from one installation to another is a genuine hazard as well as an evidential defect - the same discipline this paper applies at Q9. The single dated fact used is the 0.50 per cent m/m global sulphur limit outside emission control areas, in force since 1 January 2020, four and a half years before this sitting; it is used only to explain why base number selection changed, and no MARPOL Annex VI provision is quoted or numbered, consistent with the corpus holding that Annex as citation-ready only.
sources: ENGINEERING AND ANALYTICAL-CHEMISTRY REFERENCE - the cold corrosion mechanism: sulphur in the fuel oxidises during combustion to sulphur dioxide and, in part, to sulphur trioxide; sulphur trioxide combines with water vapour from combustion to form sulphuric acid vapour; the acid condenses on any surface whose temperature is below the acid dew point, which is far above the water dew point and rises with both the sulphur content and the cylinder pressure. Standard combustion and corrosion science, stated by mechanism and not attributed to any publication.

ENGINEERING REFERENCE - the effect of cylinder pressure on the acid dew point: raising the partial pressure of water vapour and sulphur trioxide raises the temperature at which the acid condenses, so the higher firing pressures of modern de-rated long-stroke engines increase the dew point at the same time as lower specific output reduces liner wall temperature. The two effects act in the same direction and that is the core of the answer.

P2 AUTHORITATIVE SECONDARY - published low-speed two-stroke design practice on jacket cooling water temperature control: raising the jacket outlet temperature, load-dependent cylinder liner temperature control, insulating tubes in the cooling bores, and separate or staged liner cooling circuits. Described by principle and function; no builder, series, system name or temperature value is asserted.

P2 AUTHORITATIVE SECONDARY - published two-stroke liner design practice: reduced and re-profiled bore cooling in the upper liner, insulating inserts, the anti-polishing ring or flame ring at the top of the liner to remove carbon deposits from the piston crown land, controlled surface finish and honing patterns for oil retention, and higher-alloy grey cast irons and surface treatments. Described by function; no proprietary name is used.

P2 AUTHORITATIVE SECONDARY - published cylinder lubrication practice: electronically controlled, timed, pulse injection of cylinder oil synchronised to the position of the piston ring pack; feed rate proportional to engine load and to the sulphur content of the fuel actually burned; load-change dependent dosage; and higher base number cylinder oils for cold-corrosion-prone service. Described by principle and function; no lubricator system, oil, base number or feed rate is named or numbered.

P2 AUTHORITATIVE SECONDARY - the 0.50 per cent m/m global sulphur limit for fuel oil used outside emission control areas, in force since 1 January 2020, under MARPOL Annex VI. Used solely to explain why cylinder oil base number is now selected against the fuel actually burned rather than against a worst case. No Annex VI provision is quoted or numbered; the corpus holds Annex VI as citation-ready only.

ENGINEERING JUDGEMENT - the analysis that the three mitigation routes are one control problem approached from three directions (raise the surface temperature, change the surface, neutralise what lands on it), that over-treatment is a failure mode symmetrical with under-treatment, and the sequencing and monitoring advice in the closing section. Reasoned from the mechanisms rather than taken from a recommendation.

The relative contribution of cold corrosion as against abrasive and adhesive wear in any given case of high liner wear cannot be settled from the wear rate alone; the answer states the diagnostic signatures rather than asserting a proportion.

QP2406 Q5 - the ISM maintenance and critical-equipment regime under which liner monitoring is planned and recorded

blocks.p: Cold corrosion is sulphuric acid attack on the cylinder liner running surface, and it happens for one reason: part of the liner is colder than the acid can stay a vapour. Sulphur in the fuel burns to sulphur dioxide and, in part, oxidises further to sulphur trioxide. The sulphur trioxide combines with the water vapour that combustion also produces, and forms sulphuric acid. Acid vapour condenses on any surface below its dew point - and the sulphuric acid dew point is far above the water dew point, high enough to sit within the normal range of liner wall temperatures. Where the liquid acid lands and is not neutralised by the alkaline reserve in the cylinder oil, it attacks the iron.

The name is a slight misnomer and it is worth saying so: the liner is not cold in any absolute sense. It is below the acid dew point at that point on the stroke, which is a different and much higher threshold.

blocks.h: 2. Why the new generation of engines made it worse

blocks.p: The stem asserts a causal chain and the answer should trace it rather than assume it. Two things happened at once, and they push in the same direction.

rows: Longer stroke, lower speed, larger bore-to-stroke ratio
Propulsive efficiency - a larger, slower propeller. Driven by EEDI and fuel cost
A longer, larger liner has more surface area to cool and a greater temperature spread along the stroke, so the upper liner can sit below the dew point over more of the cycle
De-rating and habitual part-load running
Slow steaming for fuel economy and emissions
Less heat into the liner, so lower wall temperature - directly below the dew point
Higher maximum combustion pressure
Thermal efficiency and specific fuel consumption
Raises the partial pressures of water vapour and sulphur trioxide, and so raises the acid dew point itself
Exhaust gas recirculation and other NOx measures
MARPOL Annex VI Tier III compliance
Recirculated gas carries water vapour and acid species back into the charge, increasing the acid available to condense
More effective cooling systems
Component life and thermal loading
Removes heat efficiently from exactly the region that most needs to stay hot

blocks.p: So the wall temperature came down while the dew point went up. The margin between them - which is all that ever protected the liner - was squeezed from both ends. That is the whole explanation, and stating it in one sentence is what distinguishes an answer that understands the problem from one that lists remedies.

blocks.h: 3. How it presents, and how to tell it from other wear

ul: Location. Attack concentrated in the upper part of the liner, in the region swept by the piston rings near top dead centre, where the wall is coolest relative to the acid dew point and the oil film is most stressed.

Pattern. The classic clover-leafing - lobed zones of heavy wear between the lubricator quills, where oil distribution is thinnest and the acid is therefore least neutralised. Clover-leafing is the signature of a neutralisation failure, not of a mechanical one.

Surface appearance. A dull, matt, etched or micro-pitted surface rather than the polished or scored appearance of adhesive or abrasive wear. In severe cases the graphite flakes stand proud as the iron matrix is dissolved around them.
Rate. Wear rates rising sharply and out of proportion to running hours, often after a change of service pattern rather than after any mechanical event.

Corroborating evidence. Rising iron in the scrape-down oil with the residual base number falling to little or nothing - the direct measurement that the alkaline reserve is being consumed faster than it is being supplied. That is the link to used-oil analysis.

blocks.p: The distinction matters because the remedies are opposite. Abrasive wear is answered by better filtration and cleaner air and fuel; adhesive wear or scuffing by more oil and a better film; cold corrosion by a hotter surface and more alkalinity. Treating corrosion as scuffing by simply increasing the feed rate of an unsuitable oil wastes oil and fixes nothing.

blocks.h: 4. Limb A - increased jacket cooling water temperature

blocks.p: The most direct measure: if the liner is below the dew point, raise the liner. Jacket cooling water outlet temperatures on modern low-speed engines are held significantly higher than was once normal, and the measures used to achieve and control that are:

ul: A raised jacket water outlet temperature set point, so the whole liner runs hotter and more of the stroke sits above the acid dew point.

Load-dependent liner temperature control - the crucial refinement. A fixed high temperature is wrong at full load, where thermal loading and the risk of local boiling in the cooling passages become the limit. So the control system raises the jacket temperature as load falls, holding the liner wall in its target band across the whole operating range. This is what makes habitual slow steaming survivable.

Separate or staged cooling circuits, so the upper liner - the part that matters - can be controlled independently of the cylinder cover and the rest of the jacket, rather than all of it being cooled to suit the hottest component.
Reduced cooling of the upper liner by design, achieved through the bore-cooling geometry discussed under limb B; temperature control and liner design are the same measure approached from two ends.
Liner wall temperature monitoring by embedded sensors, so the control acts on the temperature that matters rather than on the coolant temperature that is merely convenient to measure.

blocks.p: The limits must be stated, because an examiner is testing whether the candidate knows that this measure has a ceiling. Raising jacket water temperature reduces the margin to boiling and steam pocket formation in the cooling passages, which would cause local overheating and thermal cracking; it increases thermal stress in the liner and cover; it demands attention to system pressure and to venting; and it shifts load onto the freshwater cooler and the central cooling system. The higher-temperature circuit also makes water treatment and inhibitor control less forgiving. It is a controlled measure, not a free one - and none of it works without correct venting, correct treatment and a control system that is actually in service rather than in manual.

blocks.h: 5. Limb B - new cylinder liner designs

blocks.p: The liner itself was redesigned to hold heat where it is needed and to keep the oil film where it is put.

rows: Insulating tubes or inserts in the cooling bores
Reduce heat transfer from the upper liner locally, raising wall temperature in the top region without changing the coolant temperature - and without altering the liner's structural design
Re-profiled bore cooling - fewer, shallower or shorter bores in the upper region
The same result by geometry: cooling is concentrated where thermal load demands it and withdrawn from where corrosion demands heat
Insulating collar or jacket at the top of the liner
Raises the temperature of the very top of the stroke, the region most exposed to condensation
Anti-polishing ring (flame ring) at the top of the liner

A slightly reduced-bore ring that scrapes carbon deposits from the piston crown top land. Those deposits otherwise polish the honed surface, destroy oil retention and wipe the oil film off the upper liner - which turns a lubrication problem into a corrosion problem. It also confines combustion gas above the ring pack
Controlled surface finish - honing pattern, wave-cut or profiled grooves

Retains oil in the surface so a film survives at top dead centre where hydrodynamic support has collapsed, and helps distribute oil circumferentially between the quills, which is the direct attack on clover-leafing
Higher-alloy grey cast irons and surface treatments
Improve resistance to acid attack and to scuffing; the graphite structure is chosen for oil retention as well as for strength
Liner wall temperature sensor pockets
Make the controlling variable measurable, which is what allows load-dependent temperature control to be closed-loop rather than open-loop
Repositioned and increased lubricator quills, and improved quill design
Deliver oil into the top of the stroke and distribute it circumferentially, directly addressing the between-quill zones where clover-leafing forms

blocks.p: The unifying idea is worth stating: these are not eight separate inventions. They are all attempts to keep the top of the liner hot and keep the oil on it, and each of them fails if the others are neglected.
The third route accepts that some acid will condense and concentrates on neutralising it where and when it lands. This is where the largest change has occurred, and it has three parts.

ul: Electronic, timed, pulse injection. The mechanical lubricator driven from the engine and delivering a continuous or crank-angle-fixed dose has been replaced by an electronically controlled system that injects a measured pulse at a chosen crank angle, so the oil arrives on the liner immediately before the ring pack sweeps it upward and is distributed by the rings themselves. Timing and quantity become independent variables, controllable per cylinder.

Feed rate proportional to load AND to fuel sulphur. The governing principle is that the alkalinity delivered must match the acid produced. Acid production is proportional to fuel burned and to the sulphur content of the fuel actually being burned, so the feed rate is set against the sulphur of the fuel in service and adjusted whenever the fuel changes - which now happens routinely on entering and leaving an emission control area. A minimum feed rate is always respected for film maintenance, because below it the oil stops lubricating however alkaline it is.

Load-change dependent dosage. A temporary increase in feed rate during and after load changes, manoeuvring, and running in, when the ring pack and liner temperatures are unsettled and the film is most at risk.

Higher base number cylinder oils. Where the service is cold-corrosion prone, an oil with a greater alkaline reserve delivers more neutralising capacity per unit of oil, so acid can be neutralised without flooding the cylinder with oil. Oils are now selected for the combination of fuel sulphur and engine duty, not for the fuel alone.

blocks.p: The relationship between fuel sulphur and cylinder oil changed direction after the global sulphur limit of 0.50 per cent m/m outside emission control areas took effect on 1 January 2020. Lower sulphur means less acid, and so in principle a lower base number - but on a cold-corrosion-prone engine the acid that does form still condenses, and an oil chosen only for the low sulphur can leave the liner with too little reserve. That is why the modern rule is that base number is selected against fuel sulphur and engine duty together, and why scrape-down analysis rather than a table decides it.

blocks.h: 7. The other failure mode - too much treatment

blocks.p: This is where a good answer separates itself, because the examiner's word is "mitigation" and every mitigation here has a cost. Over-lubricating, or using an oil more alkaline than the service needs, is not a safe error:

ul: The calcium-based detergent additives that carry the alkalinity form hard ash and deposits when their reserve is not consumed by acid. Those deposits build on the piston crown, the top land and the ring grooves.

Those deposits are themselves abrasive, and they polish the honed liner surface, destroying the oil retention the surface finish was designed to give - so an over-alkaline oil can produce bore polishing and scuffing while trying to prevent corrosion.
Deposits cause ring sticking and blow-by, which raises liner temperature unevenly and damages the film.
And the oil is wasted, at significant cost, on an engine whose cylinder oil consumption is a major operating expense.

blocks.p: So cold corrosion control is a balance, not a maximum: enough alkalinity to neutralise the acid actually formed, delivered where it is needed, and no more. Under-treatment corrodes the liner; over-treatment polishes it. Both end as excessive wear, which is why the wear rate alone does not tell you which mistake you are making.
None of the three measures can be set correctly without measurement, and this is the part that belongs to the Chief Engineer rather than to the designer:

ul: Scrape-down oil analysis - iron content, which measures the wear actually occurring, together with the residual base number, which measures whether the alkaline reserve is being over-supplied or exhausted. Iron high and residual BN near zero means corrosion and under-dosing; iron high with residual BN high means the problem is not corrosion at all and more oil will make it worse. This single pair of numbers, trended, is the most useful diagnostic on the subject.
Liner wall temperature monitoring, where fitted - the direct measure of whether the temperature-control strategy is achieving its target.
Scavenge port inspections - liner surface condition, the presence and evenness of the oil film, ring condition and free movement, and the deposit condition of the piston crown and top land.
Periodic liner wear measurement at the same reference positions, trended over time rather than judged against any absolute figure.
Cylinder oil feed rate records read alongside fuel sulphur, load history and the analysis results, so the feed rate is a controlled variable and not a setting somebody adjusted once.

blocks.p: The engine builder's own service letters and the oil supplier's recommendation for the specific installation govern every actual number. No feed rate, base number, jacket temperature or wear limit should be carried between installations, and none is quoted here for exactly that reason.

Sixteen marks, undivided, with three named sub-headings. That structure is generous and dangerous at the same time: generous because the examiner has told you three of the sections to write, dangerous because a candidate who writes only those three has not answered the stem, which asks for the causes and mitigation measures, stressing on the following. "Stressing on" means those three carry the weight - not that they are the whole answer. So the shape is: cause first, then the three named sections in the printed order, then the balance and the monitoring that make them work. Roughly a fifth on cause, half across the three named limbs, and the rest on the closing analysis.

blocks.h: The sentence the whole question turns on

blocks.p: The wall temperature came down while the acid dew point went up. Everything in the question is contained in that. Longer stroke and part-load running cool the liner; higher firing pressure raises the pressure of water vapour and sulphur trioxide and so raises the temperature at which the acid condenses. The margin that protected the liner was squeezed from both ends. Write that early and every mitigation afterwards reads as a deliberate response rather than a memorised list.

blocks.h: Get the chemistry right in one line

blocks.p: Sulphur burns to SO2; part oxidises to SO3; SO3 plus water vapour gives H2SO4; it condenses below the acid dew point, which is much higher than the water dew point and rises with both sulphur content and cylinder pressure. Candidates who write "water condenses and causes corrosion" have described a different and far less aggressive mechanism, and lose the foundation of the answer.

blocks.h: The name is misleading - say so

blocks.p: The liner is not cold. It is below the acid dew point at that point on the stroke, which is a much higher threshold than "cold" suggests. A single sentence making that point signals that you understand the mechanism rather than the label.

ul: Upper liner, in the ring-swept region near top dead centre.
Clover-leafing - lobed heavy wear between the lubricator quills, where the oil is thinnest and least neutralising. This is a neutralisation signature, not a mechanical one.
Matt, etched or micro-pitted surface - not the polish of bore polishing and not the scoring of scuffing. In severe cases graphite flakes stand proud as the iron dissolves around them.

blocks.p: And the corroborating measurement: iron up in the scrape-down oil with residual base number near zero.

blocks.h: The three limbs are one control problem

rows: A - jacket water temperature
Raise the surface above the dew point
Boiling and steam pockets in the cooling passages; thermal stress; less forgiving water treatment
B - liner design
Change the surface - hold heat locally, keep the oil on it
Fixed at build or at renewal; not adjustable in service
C - lubrication
Neutralise what lands, where and when it lands
Over-treatment causes ash deposits, bore polishing and ring sticking

blocks.p: Presenting them as three attacks on one problem - hotter surface, better surface, neutralised surface - is worth more than treating them as three unrelated topics, and it is exactly what "discuss the causes and mitigation measures" invites.

blocks.h: The part most candidates miss: over-treatment

blocks.p: More cylinder oil and higher base number are not free. The calcium detergent that carries the alkalinity forms hard ash deposits if its reserve is not consumed by acid; those deposits are abrasive, they polish the honed surface and destroy oil retention, and they cause ring sticking and blow-by. So an over-alkaline oil can produce the very wear it was chosen to prevent. Under-treatment corrodes, over-treatment polishes, and both show up as high wear - which is why the wear rate alone cannot tell you which mistake you have made. Writing this paragraph is what turns a good answer into a Class I answer.

blocks.h: The one pair of numbers that diagnoses it

blocks.p: Iron and residual base number in the scrape-down oil, trended together. Iron high with residual BN near zero: corrosion, under-dosed - raise the feed rate or the base number. Iron high with residual BN still high: it is not corrosion, and more oil will make it worse - look for abrasive ingress, scuffing or a mechanical cause. That single diagnostic is the practical link between this question and Q9 on the same paper.

Jacket water temperatures, liner wall temperatures, acid dew points, feed rates in grammes per kilowatt-hour, base numbers and wear rates in millimetres per thousand hours are all engine, oil, fuel and service specific. The engine builder's service letters and the oil supplier's recommendation for the specific installation govern them. In an examination, describing the control principle and saying that the value comes from the builder scores better than a remembered figure that may belong to a different engine - and in service, a figure carried between installations is a hazard.

ul: Describing water condensation rather than sulphuric acid condensation. Different mechanism, far less aggressive.
Saying the liner is "too cold" without saying below what. The acid dew point is the reference, and it moves.
Missing that higher firing pressure raises the dew point, and so treating the problem as purely a cooling issue.
Writing only the three lettered sections and never answering "discuss the causes".
Treating cold corrosion as a lubrication problem alone, and answering the whole question under limb C.
Recommending maximum feed rate and maximum base number as though over-treatment had no cost.
Naming engine builders, systems, oils and figures - which invites a follow-up you cannot support.
Ignoring monitoring, and so leaving no way to know whether any of the measures worked.
"Why is it called cold corrosion when the liner is at a few hundred degrees?" Because it is below the acid dew point locally, not cold absolutely.

"Does the 0.50 per cent sulphur cap solve it?" No. Less sulphur means less acid, but the acid that forms still condenses on a cool surface - and an oil chosen only for low sulphur can leave too little reserve.
"What is clover-leafing and why between the quills?" Lobed heavy wear where oil distribution is thinnest, so acid is least neutralised. It is a lubrication-distribution signature.
"What does the anti-polishing ring actually do?" Scrapes carbon deposits off the piston crown top land, so they cannot polish the liner and wipe the oil film.

"Why raise jacket water temperature as load falls rather than keeping it high always?" Because at full load the limit is thermal loading and boiling in the cooling passages. It is load-dependent control, not a fixed high setting.
"You have high wear and high iron in the scrape-down. Increase the feed rate?" Only if the residual base number is low. If it is high, the cause is not corrosion and more oil will make it worse.
"Can over-lubrication damage the engine?" Yes - ash deposits, bore polishing, ring sticking and blow-by.
Take me through a scavenge port inspection and tell me what you would look for.
What is in your scrape-down oil analysis report and how do you act on it?
You are entering an emission control area and changing to low-sulphur fuel. What happens to your cylinder lubrication?
Your jacket water outlet temperature control has failed to manual. What are the risks and what do you do?
How would you measure liner wear, and what would you compare it against?
Where would you expect the wear to be worst, and why there?

blocks.p: The margin closed from both ends - then three ways to reopen it. Cause: wall temperature down (long stroke, part load, better cooling), dew point up (high firing pressure, EGR). Mitigation: HOTTER surface (limb A - jacket water, load-dependent), BETTER surface (limb B - insulation, bore cooling, anti-polishing ring, honing), NEUTRALISED surface (limb C - timed injection, feed rate against sulphur, higher BN). Then the balance: too much treatment polishes what too little corrodes. And the diagnostic: iron and residual BN, together.

ul: NO IMO OR STATUTORY INSTRUMENT PRESCRIBES A CYLINDER LUBRICATION REGIME. This is engine builder practice and no instrument has been named to give the answer false authority.

MARPOL Annex VI - the 0.50 per cent m/m global sulphur limit for fuel oil used outside emission control areas, in force since 1 January 2020, and the Tier III NOx requirements that drove EGR. Used only to explain the change in base number selection and in charge composition; no provision is quoted or numbered.

Engine builder service letters and the oil supplier's recommendation for the specific installation - the only correct sources for feed rates, base numbers, jacket water temperatures and wear limits. Not held by MIW and not reproduced.
ISM Code chapter 10 - maintenance of the ship and equipment, and the identification of critical equipment, under which liner monitoring and scrape-down sampling are planned and recorded.

blocks.p: This question carries no statutory content and the answer says so rather than borrowing authority from an unrelated instrument. The chemistry is standard combustion and corrosion science; the design responses are published low-speed two-stroke practice, carried as authoritative secondary and described by function.

No numeric value is asserted anywhere as a general rule - no jacket cooling water temperature, no liner wall temperature, no acid dew point, no feed rate, no base number and no wear rate. Every one is engine, oil, fuel and service specific, and a figure carried between installations is a hazard as well as an evidential defect. This is the same discipline MIW applies to condemning limits at Q9 on this paper.
No engine builder, licensee, engine series, proprietary lubricator system, trade name, oil company or cylinder oil product is named. The systems are described by what they do.

The only dated fact used is the 0.50 per cent m/m global sulphur limit outside emission control areas, in force since 1 January 2020 - four and a half years before this sitting. No MARPOL Annex VI provision is quoted or numbered; the MIW corpus holds Annex VI as citation-ready only.

notes: ALMOST NO TEMPORAL CONTENT. Sulphuric acid condensation on a surface below its dew point is chemistry, not dated law. The design responses - raised and load-dependent jacket water temperature, insulated and re-profiled bore cooling, the anti-polishing ring, controlled honing, timed electronic cylinder lubrication and higher base number oils - were all established two-stroke practice well before this sitting. The answer would be materially identical at any sitting from about 2015 onwards.

THE ONLY DATED FACT USED IS THE GLOBAL SULPHUR LIMIT, AND IT IS COMFORTABLY OPERATIVE. The 0.50 per cent m/m limit for fuel oil used outside emission control areas took effect on 1 January 2020, four and a half years before this sitting. It is used solely to explain why cylinder oil base number is now selected against the fuel actually burned. No MARPOL Annex VI provision is quoted or numbered.
MARPOL ANNEX VI TIER III IS NAMED ONLY AS THE DRIVER FOR EGR, NOT AS A DATED REQUIREMENT. No Tier III application date, emission control area boundary or NOx limit value is asserted.

MEPC 81 IS PAST AND MEPC 82 IS FUTURE, AND NEITHER IS RELIED ON. MEPC 81 met 18 to 22 March 2024, three months before this sitting; MEPC 82 met 30 September to 4 October 2024, after it. No resolution from either is cited, because none bears on cylinder lubrication.

THE SEEMP INVERSION TRAP IS CHECKED AND NOT ENGAGED. MEPC.346(78) is the operative SEEMP guideline at this sitting and MEPC.395(82) is future, but this question does not touch SEEMP, energy efficiency planning or carbon intensity at all. The trap is recorded as checked so that a later reader knows it was considered rather than missed.
THE IMO NET-ZERO FRAMEWORK AND THE GREENHOUSE GAS FUEL INTENSITY MECHANISM ARE EXCLUDED ENTIRELY. Both belong to October 2025 and neither appears in this object.
NO DONOR WAS ACCEPTED, SO THERE IS NO DONOR CONTAMINATION ROUTE. Nothing in the built set covers cold corrosion, cylinder lubrication or liner wear.
NO ENGINE BUILDER FIGURE IS CARRIED, SO NOTHING IN THIS ANSWER CAN GO STALE THROUGH A REVISED SERVICE LETTER. That is a deliberate consequence of the no-numbers discipline, not an accident of it.

The intent is to test whether the candidate understands a mechanism well enough to explain why a set of design changes were made, rather than whether he can list them. The discriminator is the causal chain: that lower wall temperature and higher acid dew point are two separate effects acting in the same direction.

The three lettered items are weighting instructions rather than a mark split, so the answer allocates roughly a fifth to cause and recognition, about half across the three named limbs in printed order, and the remainder to the over-treatment balance and the monitoring that closes the loop.
decomposition_gate.examiner_expectation: The sulphuric acid mechanism correctly stated with the acid dew point named; the causal chain from long stroke, de-rating, part load, higher firing pressure and EGR to a squeezed margin; the three named mitigation routes described by principle with their limits; recognition that over-treatment causes ash deposits, bore polishing and ring sticking; and scrape-down analysis of iron with residual base number as the diagnostic.
primary_source_plan: State the chemistry by mechanism - sulphur to SO2 to SO3 to H2SO4, condensing below the acid dew point - without attributing it to any publication.
Establish the two-directional squeeze on the temperature margin BEFORE listing any mitigation, so the mitigations read as responses.
Describe every design feature by function. Name no builder, licensee, engine series, proprietary system, oil company or product.
Assert no numeric value of any kind as a general rule, applying the discipline established at QP2411-Q9 and used again at this paper's Q9.

The only dated element is the sulphur limit, in force four and a half years earlier. The deliberate absence of builder figures means nothing here can go stale through a revised service letter.
decomposition_gate.jurisdiction_risk: NONE - There is no statutory content, no Indian statute is engaged, and the answer says expressly that no instrument prescribes a cylinder lubrication regime rather than borrowing authority from an unrelated one.
technical_ambiguities: 'Cold corrosion' is a misleading term - the liner is at a high absolute temperature and is merely below the ACID dew point locally. The answer fixes the sense expressly rather than adopting the label uncritically.

Limb A is printed as 'Increased Jacket Cooling Water Temperatures Systems', which is awkward. It is read as the jacket cooling water temperature and its control system, including load-dependent control, and the reading is stated.

High liner wear can be corrosive, abrasive or adhesive, and the wear rate alone does not discriminate. The answer gives the diagnostic signatures - location, clover-leafing, surface appearance, and iron against residual base number - rather than asserting a proportion.
The acid dew point rises with both sulphur content and cylinder pressure. The functional relationship is stated; no correlation, chart or equation is reproduced, because MIW holds none.
