questions.understand_first: There is a temperature above which sulphuric acid stays a vapour and passes harmlessly out of the cylinder, and below which it condenses as liquid acid on the liner. That temperature is the acid dew point, and the entire question is about the margin between it and the liner wall. For most of the history of the low-speed engine that margin was comfortable and nobody thought about it. Then two things happened at once, for good reasons that had nothing to do with corrosion. Engines got longer in the stroke, slower, de-rated, and were run at part load for weeks - all of which puts less heat into the liner, so the wall got cooler. And firing pressures went up for efficiency, which raises the partial pressures of water vapour and sulphur trioxide in the cylinder and so raises the dew point itself. The margin was squeezed from both ends and it closed. Once you see it as a margin, the three lettered sections stop being a list of remedies and become the only three things you can possibly do: make the wall hotter (A), change the wall so it holds its heat and holds its oil (B), or accept that acid will land and neutralise it (C). And the last insight, which most candidates never reach: the neutralising is a balance, not a maximum, because the calcium that carries the alkalinity turns into abrasive ash if there is no acid for it to react with.

steps.title: What cold corrosion is
points: Sulphur in the fuel burns to SO2, part oxidises to SO3
SO3 plus combustion water vapour gives sulphuric acid vapour
It condenses on any surface below the acid dew point - far above the water dew point
Liquid acid attacks the iron wherever the oil's alkaline reserve does not neutralise it
Say the name is a misnomer - the liner is below the dew point, not cold

steps.title: Why the new generation of engines made it worse
points: Longer stroke, lower speed, bigger bore-to-stroke - more surface to cool, greater spread along the stroke
De-rating and habitual part load - less heat in, so lower wall temperature
Higher maximum combustion pressure - raises partial pressures and so raises the dew point
EGR and other NOx measures - recirculate water vapour and acid species into the charge
More effective cooling - removes heat from exactly the region that needs to stay hot
The one-sentence answer: wall temperature down, dew point up, margin squeezed from both ends

steps.title: How it presents, and how to tell it from other wear
points: Location - upper liner, ring-swept region near top dead centre
Clover-leafing between the lubricator quills - a neutralisation signature, not a mechanical one
Matt, etched, micro-pitted surface; graphite standing proud in severe cases
Wear rate rising out of proportion to hours, often after a change of service pattern
Scrape-down: iron up, residual base number down
Contrast: abrasive wear wants filtration, scuffing wants film, corrosion wants heat and alkalinity

steps.title: Limb A - increased jacket cooling water temperature
points: Raised jacket water outlet set point - more of the stroke above the dew point
Load-dependent control - raise temperature as load FALLS; a fixed high setting is wrong at full load
Separate or staged circuits so the upper liner is controlled independently of the cover
Reduced upper-liner cooling by design - the same measure from the other end (see limb B)
Liner wall temperature sensors so control acts on the variable that matters
State the limits: boiling and steam pockets, thermal stress, system pressure and venting, cooler duty, less forgiving water treatment

steps.title: Limb B - new cylinder liner designs
points: Insulating tubes or inserts in the cooling bores - raise upper wall temperature locally
Re-profiled bore cooling - fewer, shallower or shorter bores in the upper region
Insulating collar at the top of the liner
Anti-polishing ring (flame ring) - scrapes carbon off the piston crown top land, which would otherwise polish the liner and wipe the film
Controlled surface finish - honing pattern, wave-cut or profiled grooves for oil retention and circumferential distribution
Higher-alloy grey cast irons and surface treatments
Sensor pockets for liner wall temperature; repositioned and improved lubricator quills
Unify them: keep the top of the liner hot and keep the oil on it

steps.title: Limb C - new cylinder lubricators
points: Electronic timed pulse injection at a chosen crank angle - timing and quantity become independent variables, per cylinder
Oil delivered just before the ring pack sweeps up, and distributed by the rings
Feed rate proportional to load and to the sulphur of the fuel actually burned, adjusted at every fuel change
A minimum feed rate always respected for film maintenance
Load-change dependent dosage during manoeuvring, load changes and running in
Higher base number oils where the service is corrosion prone - more reserve per unit of oil
Since the 0.50 per cent limit of 1 January 2020, BN is chosen against fuel sulphur AND engine duty together, decided by scrape-down analysis rather than a table

steps.title: The other failure mode - too much treatment
points: Unconsumed calcium detergent forms hard ash deposits on crown, top land and ring grooves
Those deposits are abrasive and polish the honed surface, destroying oil retention
Ring sticking and blow-by follow, raising liner temperature unevenly
And the oil is wasted, at real cost
Under-treatment corrodes, over-treatment polishes - both end as high wear, which is why wear rate alone cannot diagnose

steps.title: Monitoring - what closes the loop
points: Scrape-down analysis: iron AND residual base number, trended together - the key diagnostic
Iron high, BN near zero - corrosion, under-dosed. Iron high, BN high - not corrosion, and more oil will worsen it
Liner wall temperature monitoring where fitted
Scavenge port inspections - surface condition, film, ring condition, crown and top land deposits
Periodic wear measurement at fixed reference positions, trended not absolute
Feed rate records read against fuel sulphur, load history and analysis results
Every actual number comes from the builder's service letters and the oil supplier for that installation - carry none between ships

questions.memory_cue: The margin closed from both ends; three ways to reopen it. CAUSE: wall temperature DOWN while the acid dew point goes UP (2). MITIGATION: HOTTER surface (4), BETTER surface (5), NEUTRALISED surface (6). BALANCE: too much treatment polishes what too little corrodes (7). DIAGNOSTIC: iron and residual BN, together (8).

quick_revision.recall_15s: Sulphur burns to SO2, part oxidises to SO3, which combines with combustion water vapour to form sulphuric acid. It condenses wherever the liner is below the acid dew point - much higher than the water dew point - and attacks the iron unless the cylinder oil's alkaline reserve neutralises it. The new generation made it worse from both directions: long stroke, de-rating and part load put less heat into the liner, while higher firing pressure and EGR raise the dew point. Signature: upper liner, clover-leafing between the quills, matt etched surface, iron up and residual BN down in the scrape-down. Mitigation: A raise jacket water temperature with load-dependent control - limited by boiling in the cooling passages and thermal stress; B liner design - insulating tubes and re-profiled bore cooling, insulating collar, anti-polishing ring, controlled honing for oil retention, higher-alloy irons; C lubrication - electronic timed pulse injection, feed rate against load and the sulphur actually burned, load-change dosage, higher base number oils. But over-treatment forms calcium ash, polishes the bore and sticks the rings - so it is a balance, and iron with residual BN is what tells you which way to move.
critical_numbers: 0.50 per cent m/m global sulphur limit for fuel oil outside emission control areas, in force 1 January 2020 - the only figure quoted in this answer
NO jacket water temperature, liner wall temperature, acid dew point, feed rate, base number or wear rate is quoted as a general value - every one is engine, oil, fuel and service specific
The governing sources for those values are the engine builder's service letters and the oil supplier's recommendation for the specific installation
quick_revision.critical_regulation: None. No IMO or statutory instrument prescribes a cylinder lubrication regime or a liner temperature, and the answer says so rather than borrowing authority from an unrelated instrument. MARPOL Annex VI is named only for the 0.50 per cent sulphur limit that changed base number selection, and for the Tier III requirements that drove exhaust gas recirculation.
quick_revision.major_trap: Describing water condensation instead of sulphuric acid condensation. Different mechanism, far less aggressive, and it removes the foundation of the whole answer. Second trap: treating the problem as purely a cooling issue and missing that higher firing pressure raises the dew point - the margin closes from both ends, not one. Third: recommending maximum feed rate and maximum base number as if over-treatment were free. Unconsumed calcium detergent forms abrasive ash, polishes the honed bore and causes ring sticking - so an over-alkaline oil can cause the wear it was chosen to prevent. Fourth: writing only the three lettered sections and never answering "discuss the causes". Fifth: quoting a remembered temperature, feed rate or base number - they are installation specific, and a figure carried between engines is a hazard as well as an examination risk.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the cold corrosion question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 The mechanism. 2 Why the new generation made it worse. 3 Recognition and differential diagnosis. 4 Limb A - jacket cooling water temperature. 5 Limb B - liner design. 6 Limb C - cylinder lubricators. 7 The over-treatment balance. 8 Monitoring. The three lettered items are weighting instructions, not the whole answer - the stem also asks for the causes.
retrieval_cards.why: A candidate who writes only sections 4, 5 and 6 has answered the sub-headings and not the question.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is cold corrosion, chemically?
retrieval_cards.answer: Sulphur in the fuel burns to SO2 and part oxidises to SO3; the SO3 combines with combustion water vapour to form sulphuric acid, which condenses on any liner surface below the acid dew point and attacks the iron where the cylinder oil's alkaline reserve does not neutralise it. The acid dew point is far above the water dew point, which is why the liner can be at several hundred degrees and still be "cold".
retrieval_cards.why: Candidates who describe water condensation have described a different and far less aggressive mechanism.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why did the new generation of engines make cold corrosion worse?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because the temperature margin closed from both ends. Long stroke, de-rating and habitual part-load running put less heat into the liner, lowering the wall temperature. Higher maximum combustion pressure raises the partial pressures of water vapour and sulphur trioxide and so raises the acid dew point itself. EGR returns water vapour and acid species to the charge, and more effective cooling removes heat from precisely the region that needs to stay hot.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the sentence the whole question turns on, and treating it as purely a cooling problem loses half the causal analysis.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How do you recognise cold corrosion rather than abrasive or adhesive wear?
retrieval_cards.answer: Upper liner, in the ring-swept region near top dead centre. Clover-leafing - lobed heavy wear between the lubricator quills, where oil distribution is thinnest and acid is least neutralised. A matt, etched or micro-pitted surface rather than a polished or scored one, with graphite standing proud in severe cases. And in the scrape-down oil, iron rising with residual base number falling.
retrieval_cards.why: The remedies are opposite - abrasive wear wants filtration, scuffing wants film, corrosion wants heat and alkalinity - so the diagnosis has to come first.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Limb A - how is jacket cooling water temperature used, and what limits it?
retrieval_cards.answer: A raised outlet set point so more of the stroke sits above the dew point, and crucially load-dependent control: raise the temperature as load falls, because a fixed high setting is wrong at full load. Separate or staged circuits control the upper liner independently of the cover. Limits: reduced margin to boiling and steam pockets in the cooling passages, higher thermal stress, and less forgiving water treatment.
retrieval_cards.why: Load-dependent control is what makes slow steaming survivable, and stating the limits is what shows the measure is understood rather than recited.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Limb B - name the liner design responses and the idea behind them.
retrieval_cards.answer: Insulating tubes or inserts in the cooling bores and re-profiled bore cooling - fewer, shallower or shorter bores in the upper region; an insulating collar at the top; the anti-polishing ring (flame ring) scraping carbon from the piston crown top land; controlled honing, wave-cut or profiled grooves for oil retention and circumferential distribution; higher-alloy grey cast irons and surface treatments; sensor pockets; and repositioned, improved lubricator quills. The single idea: keep the top of the liner hot and keep the oil on it.
retrieval_cards.why: Presenting eight features as one idea is worth more than listing them, and it is what the word "discuss" is asking for.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Limb C - what changed in cylinder lubrication?
retrieval_cards.answer: Electronic, timed, pulse injection at a chosen crank angle, so oil arrives just before the ring pack sweeps upward and timing and quantity become independent, per-cylinder variables. Feed rate proportional to load and to the sulphur of the fuel actually burned, adjusted at every fuel change, with a minimum rate always respected for film maintenance. Load-change dependent dosage during manoeuvring, load changes and running in. And higher base number oils where the service is corrosion prone, delivering more alkalinity per unit of oil.
retrieval_cards.why: The governing principle is that the alkalinity delivered must match the acid produced - which is why the fuel's sulphur, not a fixed setting, drives the feed rate.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why is more cylinder oil and higher base number not always the answer?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because the calcium detergent carrying the alkalinity forms hard ash deposits when its reserve is not consumed by acid. Those deposits build on the crown, top land and ring grooves; they are abrasive; they polish the honed liner and destroy the oil retention the surface finish was designed to give; and they cause ring sticking and blow-by. Under-treatment corrodes and over-treatment polishes - both end as high wear, which is why the wear rate alone cannot tell you which mistake you are making.
retrieval_cards.why: This paragraph is what separates a Class I answer from a competent one, and it is the commonest oral follow-up on the topic.

retrieval_cards.prompt: You have high liner wear and high iron in the scrape-down oil. Do you increase the feed rate?
retrieval_cards.answer: Only if the residual base number is low. Iron high with residual BN near zero means the alkaline reserve is being exhausted - corrosion, under-dosed, so raise the feed rate or the base number. Iron high with residual BN still high means the acid is not the problem, and more oil will make it worse - look for abrasive ingress, scuffing or a mechanical cause. The two numbers are only diagnostic together.
retrieval_cards.why: This single pair, trended, is the most useful diagnostic on the subject and is the direct link to the used-oil analysis question on this same paper.

blocks.h: 1. The functional requirements - ISM Code paragraph 1.4

blocks.p: The Code does not describe a safety management system; it states what one must be able to do. Paragraph 1.4 requires every Company to develop, implement and maintain an SMS that includes six functional requirements. Four marks, six items - so they are listed, correctly and completely, and not discussed:

ol: A safety and environmental protection policy.
Instructions and procedures to ensure safe operation of ships and protection of the environment, in compliance with relevant international and flag State legislation.
Defined levels of authority and lines of communication between, and among, shore and shipboard personnel.
Procedures for reporting accidents and non-conformities with the provisions of the Code.
Procedures to prepare for and respond to emergency situations.
Procedures for internal audits and management reviews.

blocks.p: Two observations are worth one line each. The list is closed and numbered in the Code, so a candidate who offers five items or eight has demonstrably not read paragraph 1.4. And requirement six is the one this question then examines at length in limb (B) - the Code builds its own audit obligation into its definition of a safety management system, so a system without internal audit is not a deficient SMS but not an SMS at all.

For context in a single sentence: the ISM Code was adopted by resolution A.741(18) and made mandatory through SOLAS chapter IX, and its objectives under paragraph 1.2 are to ensure safety at sea, prevention of human injury or loss of life, and avoidance of damage to the environment and to property. The functional requirements are the machinery by which those objectives are pursued.

blocks.h: 2. The objectives of an ISM internal audit

blocks.p: An internal audit is the Company auditing itself - its own ships and its own shore organisation - against its own SMS and against the Code. Its objectives are:

ul: To verify that safety and pollution-prevention activities comply with the SMS - that what is written down is what is being done.
To verify the effectiveness of the SMS, which is a separate and harder question: a procedure can be followed exactly and still not be achieving anything.
To confirm continued compliance with the ISM Code and with applicable statutory and flag State requirements.
To identify non-conformities, and the conditions that could give rise to them, before they become accidents - the audit looks for latent weakness, not only for breaches.
To confirm that corrective actions from previous audits, incidents and inspections have been implemented and are effective, rather than merely closed on paper.
To provide the Company's management with objective evidence on which the management review can be based.
To drive continual improvement of the system, and to reinforce safety awareness among the crew by involving them in it.

blocks.p: The distinction that separates a good answer here: an internal audit audits the system, it does not inspect the ship. A superintendent's inspection asks whether the pump works. An audit asks whether there is a procedure that would have found out, whether it was followed, whether it was recorded, and whether the record was reviewed. Both are necessary and they are not the same activity.

blocks.h: 3. How the internal audit helps the external audit

blocks.p: The external audit is carried out by the flag Administration or by a Recognized Organization acting for it, and leads to the Document of Compliance for the Company and the Safety Management Certificate for the ship. The internal audit supports it in five distinct ways, and listing them as five is what earns the marks:

rows: Finds and closes non-conformities first
What would have been an external finding is already a closed internal one with evidence of corrective action - the strongest possible demonstration that the system works
Produces the objective evidence the external auditor asks for
Audit reports, non-conformity records, corrective actions and their verification are exactly the documents an external auditor will call for, and they exist because the internal audit created them
Familiarises the crew with being audited
Crew who have been asked to explain their responsibilities under the SMS by an internal auditor answer the external auditor confidently. Hesitation, not the answer, is what an auditor records
Verifies that the documentation is controlled and current
Superseded manuals, uncontrolled copies and missing records are among the commonest external findings and are trivially avoidable internally
Feeds the management review
Which is itself a functional requirement, and demonstrates to the external auditor that the loop from finding to management decision actually closes

blocks.p: The negative case makes the point sharply and is worth stating: a Company whose internal audits never raise a non-conformity has not proved its ships are perfect. It has proved that its internal audits are not real - and an external auditor who sees a run of clean internal reports will look harder, not less hard.

blocks.h: 4. The salient issues addressed in an internal audit

ul: The safety and environmental protection policy - is it implemented and understood at all levels, ashore and on board?
Company responsibility and authority, and the identity, role and accessibility of the Designated Person Ashore.
The master's responsibility and authority, including his overriding authority to take whatever action he considers necessary, and the conduct and content of the master's review of the SMS.
Resources and personnel - manning, qualification, familiarisation of newly joined seafarers, and training identified and delivered.
Shipboard operations - that plans and instructions for key operations exist, are used, and reflect what the ship actually does.
Emergency preparedness - drills and exercises carried out, recorded, and reviewed for lessons rather than merely ticked.
Reports and analysis of non-conformities, accidents and hazardous occurrences - are they raised, investigated, analysed for cause and closed out?
Maintenance of the ship and equipment, and in particular the identification and testing of critical equipment - the point at which many audits actually bite.
Documentation - control, currency, availability at the point of use, and the removal of superseded documents.
Certification - DOC and SMC valid, endorsed and matching the ship and ship type.

blocks.h: 5. Frequency, and the arithmetic over the SMC cycle

blocks.p: Paragraph 12.1 requires the Company to carry out internal safety audits on board and ashore at intervals not exceeding twelve months. The Code allows that interval to be exceeded in exceptional circumstances, and then by not more than three months.

So over the five-year validity of the Safety Management Certificate the minimum is at least five internal audits - one in each twelve-month period. It is worth putting the internal cycle beside the external one, because the question invites the comparison:

rows: Who
The Company, using auditors independent of the area audited
The flag Administration or a Recognized Organization
Interval
Not exceeding 12 months; in exceptional circumstances not more than 15
Initial; at least one intermediate verification between the second and third anniversary date; renewal within five years
Number over the SMC's five years
At least five
Initial, one intermediate, renewal
Output
Internal audit report and non-conformities, feeding the management review
The Safety Management Certificate; and for the Company, the Document of Compliance, subject to annual verification

blocks.p: Two further requirements of paragraph 12 belong here because examiners ask for them: personnel carrying out the audit should be independent of the areas being audited unless the size and nature of the Company make that impracticable; and the results must be brought to the attention of all personnel having responsibility in the area involved, whose management must take timely corrective action.
These two are defined in the Code and the definitions should be given as such.

rows: Non-conformity (1.1.9)
An observed situation where objective evidence indicates the non-fulfilment of a specified requirement
Corrective action within an agreed time; the certificate stands
Major non-conformity (1.1.10)

An identifiable deviation posing a serious threat to the safety of personnel or the ship, or a serious risk to the environment, that requires immediate corrective action; and it includes the lack of effective and systematic implementation of a requirement of the Code
Immediate action required; may lead to suspension or withdrawal of the SMC or DOC, and is a detainable finding for a port State

blocks.p: Three points about these definitions repay attention. Objective evidence is what distinguishes a non-conformity from an opinion - an auditor must be able to point at something. A specified requirement means the SMS, the Code, or a statutory requirement, so a Company that writes a demanding procedure creates the possibility of a non-conformity against itself, which is why procedures should say what the ship will actually do. And the second half of the major non-conformity definition is the one most often forgotten: systemic failure to implement the Code is itself major, even where no single deviation is dangerous. A ship on which nothing in particular is wrong, but on which the SMS is plainly not being used, is a major non-conformity.

First, a point of accuracy the examiner will not penalise but will notice: the printed stem says "non-conformities, Accident and Hazardous occurrences", while paragraph 9.1 of the Code requires the SMS to include procedures ensuring that non-conformities, accidents and hazardous situations are reported to the Company, investigated and analysed with the object of improving safety and pollution prevention. The terms are used interchangeably in practice; the answer treats them together and cites the Code's own wording.
The Code does not define "accident", and it is worth saying so rather than inventing a definition. In practice:

ul: An accident is an unintended event that has caused harm - injury or death, damage to the ship, cargo or equipment, or damage to the environment.

A hazardous occurrence - or hazardous situation - is an event or condition that could have caused such harm but did not. It is the near miss, and it is the more valuable of the two, because it carries the same information about the system at none of the cost.
A non-conformity is different in kind from both: it is not an event at all, but a state of non-compliance with a specified requirement, and it may exist for months without anything happening.

blocks.p: Worked examples make the distinction visible, and an examiner asking for "examples" is asking for exactly this:

rows: The fire drill record shows the last drill was eight weeks ago; the SMS requires monthly
Non-conformity
Objective evidence of non-fulfilment of a specified requirement. Nothing has happened
A fitter suffers a lost-time hand injury while replacing a fuel pump
Accident
An unintended event that has caused harm
A high-pressure fuel line sprays onto a hot surface; there is no fire because the shielding held
Hazardous occurrence
Could have caused serious harm and did not. Report and investigate exactly as if it had
A spanner is dropped from a grating into an empty walkway
Hazardous occurrence
No harm, but the same failure with someone below is a fatality
The oily-water separator's 15 ppm alarm is found disconnected
Major non-conformity
Serious risk to the environment requiring immediate corrective action - and it implies deliberate defeat of the system
Bunkering overflows and oil reaches the water
Accident, and a reportable pollution incident
Harm has occurred; separate statutory reporting is engaged beyond the SMS
The SMS is on board but no one uses it; records are written up retrospectively
Major non-conformity
Lack of effective and systematic implementation of the Code, which the definition expressly includes

blocks.p: The reporting duty under paragraph 9.1 runs to all three, and the object stated in the Code is not punishment but improvement. That is the closing point worth making: a reporting culture that produces few hazardous occurrence reports is not a safe ship - it is a ship where near misses are not being reported, and the system has been denied the information it exists to process.

4 + 6 + 6, and the mark split tells you the writing style for each limb. Limb (A) is four marks for six listed items - so list them, numbered, and move on. Any candidate who writes three paragraphs of discussion on the functional requirements has spent six marks' worth of time earning four. Limb (B) contains four separate questions - objectives, help to external audit, salient issues, frequency - and each needs a visible answer. Limb (C) asks for three terms with examples, and the examples are not optional decoration; they are how the distinctions are demonstrated.

blocks.h: Paragraph 1.4 - learn it as a closed list of six

blocks.p: Policy - Procedures - Authority - Reporting - Emergency - Audit. Six items, in the Code's own order. The list is closed, so offering five or eight shows you have not read it. A useful mnemonic is that the first two say what the system contains, the third says who does what, and the last three are the three loops that keep it alive: reporting things that went wrong, preparing for things that might, and checking the system itself.

blocks.h: The self-referential point worth one sentence

blocks.p: The sixth functional requirement is internal audits and management reviews - so the Code builds its own audit obligation into its definition of a safety management system. A system without internal audit is not a deficient SMS; it is not an SMS at all. Saying that links limb (A) directly into limb (B) and shows the two are one subject.

An audit audits the system; an inspection inspects the ship. A superintendent's inspection asks whether the pump works. An audit asks whether there is a procedure that would have found out, whether it was followed, whether it was recorded, and whether anyone reviewed the record. Candidates who describe an internal audit as "a thorough inspection by the Company" have missed the whole point of the Code.

A Company whose internal audits never raise a non-conformity has not proved that its ships are perfect; it has proved that its audits are not real. An external auditor who sees a run of clean internal reports looks harder. This is also, from the other side, the ISM-related clear ground a PSCO uses - see Q3 on this paper.

ul: Internal audits on board and ashore, at intervals not exceeding twelve months (paragraph 12.1).
In exceptional circumstances that interval may be exceeded by not more than three months - so fifteen months absolute maximum.
Over the SMC's five-year validity: at least five internal audits.
Auditors should be independent of the area audited, unless the size and nature of the Company make that impracticable.
External: initial, at least one intermediate verification between the second and third anniversary date, and renewal within five years. The DOC is subject to annual verification.

blocks.p: The question expressly asks for the minimum frequency "during the five-year validity of the ship's Safety Management Certificate", so give the twelve-month rule and do the arithmetic - five audits. Candidates give the rule and never answer the question actually asked.

blocks.h: The half of the major non-conformity definition everyone forgets

blocks.p: Most candidates give the first half - a serious threat to personnel or the ship, or a serious risk to the environment, requiring immediate corrective action. The definition also expressly includes the lack of effective and systematic implementation of a requirement of the Code. That is how a ship with nothing in particular wrong, but on which the SMS is plainly not used, is a major non-conformity. Write both halves.

blocks.h: Non-conformity, accident, hazardous occurrence - the clean test

rows: Non-conformity
No - a state
Not necessarily
Objective evidence of non-fulfilment of a specified requirement
Accident
Yes
Yes
Unintended event that has caused injury, damage or pollution
Hazardous occurrence
Yes
No - but could have
The near miss; same information, none of the cost

blocks.p: The one-line version: a non-conformity is a state, an accident is an event with harm, a hazardous occurrence is an event without harm.

blocks.h: A wording point the examiner will notice

blocks.p: The stem says "Hazardous occurrences"; the Code at paragraph 9.1 says hazardous situations. They are used interchangeably in practice. Noting the variation in half a sentence and then citing paragraph 9.1 correctly shows you have read the Code rather than a summary of it - and it costs nothing.

ul: Discussing the functional requirements at length for four marks, and then rushing the twelve-mark half of the paper.
Giving five functional requirements, or inventing a seventh. The list at 1.4 is closed and numbered.
Describing an internal audit as an inspection.
Giving the twelve-month rule but never answering "how many during the five-year SMC validity".
Omitting the three-month exceptional-circumstances allowance.
Giving only the first half of the major non-conformity definition.
Attributing a definition of "accident" to the ISM Code. It does not define one - say so.
Answering limb (C) with definitions and no examples, when the stem says "with example".
"How many functional requirements?" Six, at paragraph 1.4.
"What is the maximum internal audit interval?" Twelve months - fifteen in exceptional circumstances, and the exception must be exceptional.
"Who can carry out an internal audit?" Personnel independent of the area audited, unless the Company's size makes that impracticable. The Chief Engineer cannot audit his own department.
"Give a major non-conformity with nothing broken." An SMS that is on board but not used - systemic failure to implement, which the definition expressly covers.
"Does the ISM Code define an accident?" No.
"Which is more useful, an accident report or a near-miss report?" The near miss - same information about the system, none of the cost.
"What happens to the certificate on a major non-conformity?" Immediate corrective action; the SMC or DOC may be suspended or withdrawn, and a port State can detain on it.
"How often is the DOC verified?" Annually. The SMC has an intermediate verification between the second and third anniversary.
Who is your DPA and how would you contact him tonight?
Show me the last internal audit report and the non-conformities raised on your department.
What is the master's overriding authority and where is it written?
Which equipment on your ship is identified as critical, and how do you know?
You find a hazardous occurrence that would embarrass a junior engineer. What do you do?
Your internal audit is due next month and you are on a long voyage. What are your options?

blocks.p: This is the most securely sourced question on the paper. The MIW corpus holds the official IMO resolution chain for the ISM Code and records its storage classification as full official text legally available. The corpus also fixes the amendment cutoff: MSC.353(92), in force 1 January 2015, is the most recent amendment to the Code itself. That places this June 2024 sitting nine and a half years inside a stable period - so, uniquely on this paper, there is no amendment boundary to manage at all.

Notwithstanding that verbatim use is legally permitted for this instrument, no paragraph of the Code is reproduced word for word here. Paragraphs are cited by number and their effect stated, as a matter of MIW house discipline.

One open corpus verification is carried forward: that no ISM amendment was adopted after MSC.353(92). Nothing in this answer depends on a later amendment. The intermediate amendment entry-into-force dates for MSC.179(79), MSC.195(80) and MSC.273(85) are flagged unverified in the corpus and are not asserted anywhere - only the adopting resolution, the mandatory application through SOLAS chapter IX, and MSC.353(92) are dated.

SOLAS chapter IX is held in the corpus base but is not among the provisions verified against primary text, so the DOC and SMC validity and verification periods are authoritative secondary. The domestic statute at this sitting is the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958, under which the Directorate General of Shipping issues DOCs and SMCs or authorises Recognized Organizations to do so; the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 is not law at this sitting and appears nowhere in this answer.

notes: THIS IS THE ONLY QUESTION ON THE PAPER WITH NO AMENDMENT BOUNDARY AT ALL, AND THAT IS ESTABLISHED FROM HELD EVIDENCE RATHER THAN ASSUMED. The corpus ISM instrument log records MSC.353(92), adopted 21 June 2013 and in force 1 January 2015, as the most recent amendment to the ISM Code, with no later amending resolution identified in the IMO resolution index. The Code therefore stood unchanged for nine and a half years before this sitting, and every paragraph relied on here - 1.2, 1.4, 1.1.9, 1.1.10, 5, 9.1, 10 and 12 - was in force in this form.

MSC 108 IS CHECKED AND NOT ENGAGED. It sat 15 to 24 May 2024, one month before this examination. Its resolutions were adopted but not in force, with entry into force 1 January 2026, and none of them amends the ISM Code. MSC.560(108) amends the STCW Code on bullying and harassment, which is a different instrument and is not relied on here. Adopted is not in force.

A.1184(33) IS OPERATIVE BUT IS CORRECTLY CLASSIFIED AS GUIDANCE. The Revised guidelines on implementation of the ISM Code by Administrations were adopted in December 2023, six months before this sitting, so they were operative. The corpus records them expressly as supporting guidance and NOT part of the Code text, and that classification is respected: they are used for the audit and verification framework and never as a source of Code obligations.
THE 34TH ASSEMBLY IS CHECKED AND EXCLUDED. Its resolutions were adopted 3 December 2025, eighteen months after this sitting. No A.12xx(34) resolution appears anywhere in this object.

THE SOLAS EDITION CAVEAT RECORDED AT Q1 APPLIES HERE IN WEAKER FORM AND IS RECORDED RATHER THAN IGNORED. The corpus holds the Consolidated Edition 2024, in effect 1 July 2024 - after this sitting. Chapter IX supplies the DOC and SMC regime relied on here and was not amended across that boundary on any reading of the amendment register, but the earlier edition has not been read.

CYBER RISK IS DELIBERATELY ABSENT AND THE ABSENCE IS REASONED. MSC-FAL.1/Circ.3 and resolution MSC.428(101) brought cyber risk into safety management systems from the first annual DOC verification after 1 January 2021, so cyber risk WAS a live SMS topic at this sitting. It is not written into this answer because the printed stem does not ask for it - limb (A) asks for the paragraph 1.4 list, which is unchanged, and limbs (B) and (C) ask about audit and definitions. The rejected donor QP2606-Q5 limb (b) is precisely a question about the Code's evolution including cyber risk; importing it would have answered a question this paper does not ask.

DONOR CONTAMINATION SWEEP: CLEAN, AND NO DONOR WAS ADOPTED. QP2606-Q5 is a June 2026 paper and QP2502-Q3 a February 2025 one, twenty-four and eight months after this sitting. Both were rejected as topical-only on task grounds before any text was read for reuse, which also removed the forward-contamination risk each carried.
THE INDIAN STATUTE BOUNDARY IS RESOLVED. The Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 governs. The Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 commenced 15 March 2026 and appears nowhere in this object.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: Three limbs testing three different depths of the same instrument. Limb (A) is pure recall of a closed, numbered list and is marked as recall. Limb (B) is the substantial limb and contains FOUR distinct questions inside one paragraph - the objectives of an internal audit, how it helps the external audit, the salient issues addressed, and the minimum frequency over the five-year SMC validity - each of which must be visibly answered. Limb (C) is definitional but expressly demands examples, so the examples are the evidence that the distinctions are understood rather than memorised.
decomposition_gate.mark_allocation: 16, set as 4 + 6 + 6. Printed marks are unambiguous. The 4-mark limb carries six listed items, which is a signal to list rather than discuss; each 6-mark limb carries multiple sub-questions and needs a sectioned or tabulated answer to make them all visible.
decomposition_gate.examiner_expectation: All six functional requirements at paragraph 1.4, complete and in order. For limb (B): audit objectives that show an audit tests the SYSTEM rather than the ship; a real account of how internal audit prepares the ground for external verification; the salient issues; and the twelve-month interval WITH the arithmetic of at least five audits over the SMC cycle. For limb (C): the Code's own definitions of non-conformity and major non-conformity including the systemic-failure half, an honest statement that the Code does not define 'accident', and worked examples that separate a state from an event with harm from an event without.
primary_source_plan: Take the paragraph numbering and the amendment cutoff from the corpus ISM instrument log BEFORE writing, and confirm that MSC.353(92) leaves the Code stable at this sitting.
Use the corpus log's own question-coverage map, which ties internal audit to paragraph 12 and the master's review to 5.1.5, rather than recalling paragraph numbers.
State effects and cite paragraph numbers; reproduce no paragraph verbatim, notwithstanding that the corpus records verbatim use as permitted.
Treat A.1184(33) strictly as guidance, because the corpus records it expressly as not part of the Code text.
Note the printed stem's 'hazardous occurrences' against the Code's 'hazardous situations' rather than silently substituting one for the other.
Do not import cyber risk. It was a live SMS topic at this sitting but the printed stem does not ask for it, and the rejected donor QP2606-Q5 is exactly the question that does.
decomposition_gate.freshness_risk: LOW - the lowest on the paper. The ISM Code has not been amended since MSC.353(92) entered into force on 1 January 2015, nine and a half years before this sitting, and every paragraph relied on stood in this form.
decomposition_gate.jurisdiction_risk: LOW - The Code applies uniformly through SOLAS chapter IX. In India the Directorate General of Shipping issues the DOC and SMC or authorises Recognized Organizations to do so, under the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 at this sitting; the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 is prohibited.
technical_ambiguities: The printed stem says 'Hazardous occurrences' where ISM paragraph 9.1 says hazardous SITUATIONS. The variation is noted expressly and both are treated; no claim is made that 'hazardous occurrence' is a defined term of the Code.
The ISM Code does not define 'accident'. The answer says so and takes the ordinary meaning rather than attributing a definition to the Code that it does not contain.
'The minimum frequency of such an audit ... during the five-year validity' asks for a count, not just the interval rule. The answer gives both the twelve-month rule and the resulting minimum of five.

Limb (B) asks what an internal audit helps the external audit to do, which invites the negative case as well - a Company with no internal findings looks worse, not better. That is stated because it is the sharpest form of the point.

Whether the exceptional-circumstances extension of three months is available is a matter of judgement for the Company and the Administration; it is stated as an exception, not as a routine entitlement.
decomposition_gate.target_answer_shape: Seven numbered sections. Section 1 is limb (A) as a numbered list of six with two short observations. Sections 2 to 5 are limb (B), one section per sub-question, with the internal-versus-external comparison as a table. Sections 6 and 7 are limb (C): the two defined terms as a table, then accidents and hazardous occurrences with a worked-examples table.

questions.understand_first: The ISM Code is short, and it is short on purpose. It does not tell you how to run a ship - it tells you that you must write down how you run your ship, do what you wrote, record that you did it, and check yourself. That is the whole architecture, and the six functional requirements in limb (A) are just that architecture itemised. Once that is clear, limb (B) stops being a separate topic: the internal audit is the check yourself step, and it is written into the definition of a safety management system rather than bolted on to it. And the crucial thing about an audit is what it is not - it is not an inspection. An inspection asks whether the pump works. An audit asks whether there was a procedure that would have found out, whether anyone followed it, whether anyone wrote it down, and whether anyone read what was written. Limb (C) then supplies the vocabulary the system uses to talk about its own failures, and the three words are genuinely different: a non-conformity is a state of affairs, an accident is an event where harm happened, and a hazardous occurrence is an event where it nearly did. The last is the most valuable, because it carries the same information at none of the cost - which is why a ship reporting no near misses is not a safe ship, it is a quiet one.

steps.title: The functional requirements - ISM Code paragraph 1.4
points: List them, do not discuss them - four marks for six items
1 A safety and environmental protection policy
2 Instructions and procedures for safe operation and environmental protection, in compliance with international and flag State legislation
3 Defined levels of authority and lines of communication, shore and shipboard
4 Procedures for reporting accidents and non-conformities with the Code
5 Procedures to prepare for and respond to emergency situations
6 Procedures for internal audits and management reviews
Note the list is closed and numbered - five or eight shows you have not read 1.4
Note requirement 6 is what limb (B) then examines: the Code builds audit into the definition of an SMS
One line of context: adopted by A.741(18), mandatory through SOLAS chapter IX; objectives at 1.2

steps.title: The objectives of an ISM internal audit
points: Verify that activities comply with the SMS - what is written is what is done
Verify the SMS is effective, which is a separate and harder question
Confirm continued compliance with the Code and with statutory and flag State requirements
Identify non-conformities and the conditions that could give rise to them
Confirm previous corrective actions were implemented and are effective, not merely closed on paper
Provide objective evidence for the management review
Drive continual improvement and reinforce crew safety awareness
The distinction to state: an audit audits the system; an inspection inspects the ship

steps.title: How the internal audit helps the external audit
points: Finds and closes non-conformities first - a closed internal finding with evidence beats an open external one
Produces exactly the objective evidence the external auditor will call for
Familiarises the crew with being audited - hesitation is what auditors record, not the answer
Verifies documentation is controlled and current - superseded manuals are a commonest external finding
Feeds the management review, showing the loop from finding to decision actually closes
The negative case: audits that never raise a non-conformity prove the audits are not real, and the external auditor looks harder

steps.title: The salient issues addressed in an internal audit
points: Policy - implemented and understood at all levels
Company responsibility and authority; the DPA's identity, role and accessibility
Master's responsibility and overriding authority; the master's review (5.1.5)
Resources and personnel - manning, qualification, familiarisation, training
Shipboard operations - plans and instructions exist, are used, and match what the ship does
Emergency preparedness - drills carried out, recorded and reviewed for lessons
Reports and analysis of non-conformities, accidents and hazardous occurrences - raised, investigated, closed
Maintenance and critical equipment identification and testing (paragraph 10)
Documentation control and currency; certification - DOC and SMC valid and matching

steps.title: Frequency, and the arithmetic over the SMC cycle
points: Paragraph 12.1 - internal safety audits on board and ashore, intervals not exceeding twelve months
In exceptional circumstances, exceeded by not more than three months - fifteen absolute
Answer the question asked: over the SMC's five years, at least five internal audits
Auditors independent of the area audited unless Company size makes it impracticable
Results brought to the attention of all personnel responsible, with timely corrective action
Contrast the external cycle: initial, intermediate between the second and third anniversary, renewal at five years; DOC verified annually

steps.title: Non-conformity and major non-conformity
points: 1.1.9 non-conformity - an observed situation where objective evidence indicates non-fulfilment of a specified requirement
1.1.10 major non-conformity - an identifiable deviation posing a serious threat to personnel or the ship, or a serious risk to the environment, requiring immediate corrective action
AND it includes the lack of effective and systematic implementation of a requirement of the Code - the half everyone forgets
'Objective evidence' distinguishes a finding from an opinion
'Specified requirement' includes the Company's own SMS - so write procedures the ship will actually follow
Consequence: corrective action for one; suspension or withdrawal of SMC or DOC, and detention, for the other

steps.title: Accidents and hazardous occurrences
points: Note the wording: the stem says 'occurrences', paragraph 9.1 says hazardous situations - treat both
The Code does not define 'accident' - say so rather than inventing one
Accident = unintended event that has caused harm - injury, death, damage or pollution
Hazardous occurrence = event that could have and did not - the near miss
Non-conformity = not an event at all, but a state of non-compliance
Give worked examples: drill overdue (NC); fitter's hand injury (accident); fuel spray with no fire (hazardous occurrence); 15 ppm alarm disconnected (major NC); SMS on board but unused (major NC)
Paragraph 9.1's object is improvement, not punishment - and few near-miss reports means under-reporting, not safety

questions.memory_cue: Six, then four, then three. SIX at 1.4: Policy, Procedures, Authority, Reporting, Emergency, Audit (1). FOUR questions hidden in limb (B): objectives (2), helps external how (3), salient issues (4), how often - twelve months, so five over the cycle (5). THREE in limb (C): a state, an event with harm, an event without (6-7) - and the forgotten half of major: systemic failure to implement is itself major (6).

quick_revision.recall_15s: Paragraph 1.4 - six functional requirements: safety and environmental protection policy; instructions and procedures for safe operation and environmental protection; defined levels of authority and lines of communication; procedures for reporting accidents and non-conformities; procedures to prepare for and respond to emergencies; procedures for internal audits and management reviews. Internal audit verifies the SMS is complied with AND effective, finds non-conformities and the conditions that breed them, checks previous corrective actions, and feeds the management review - it audits the system, it does not inspect the ship. It helps the external audit by closing findings first, producing the objective evidence, familiarising the crew and controlling the documentation. Paragraph 12.1: intervals not exceeding twelve months, exceeded in exceptional circumstances by not more than three - so at least five over the SMC's five years, by auditors independent of the area audited. 1.1.9 non-conformity = objective evidence of non-fulfilment of a specified requirement; 1.1.10 major = serious threat to personnel, ship or environment requiring immediate action, and includes the lack of effective and systematic implementation of the Code. An accident has caused harm; a hazardous occurrence could have; a non-conformity is a state, not an event. Reporting duty at 9.1.
critical_numbers: SIX functional requirements at paragraph 1.4 - a closed, numbered list
Internal audits at intervals not exceeding TWELVE months (paragraph 12.1); exceptional circumstances allow not more than THREE months more
At least FIVE internal audits over the five-year validity of the SMC
External: initial, at least one intermediate verification between the SECOND and THIRD anniversary date, renewal within five years; the DOC is verified ANNUALLY
A.741(18) adopted 4 November 1993; mandatory through SOLAS chapter IX from 1 July 1998
MSC.353(92) in force 1 January 2015 - the most recent amendment, so the Code is unchanged at this sitting
quick_revision.critical_regulation: ISM Code paragraph 1.4 for the six functional requirements and paragraph 12.1 for the twelve-month internal audit interval - those two carry ten of the sixteen marks between them. Read with paragraphs 1.1.9 and 1.1.10 for the definitions and 9.1 for the reporting duty.
quick_revision.major_trap: Giving only the first half of the major non-conformity definition. It is a serious threat requiring immediate corrective action and it expressly includes the lack of effective and systematic implementation of a requirement of the Code - which is how a ship with nothing broken can carry a major non-conformity. Second trap: giving the twelve-month interval but never answering the question actually asked, which is how many over the five-year SMC validity - the answer is at least five. Third: describing an internal audit as an inspection; it audits the system, not the ship. Fourth: attributing a definition of "accident" to the ISM Code - it does not define one. Fifth: writing three paragraphs on the functional requirements for four marks and then rushing the twelve marks that follow.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the ISM Code question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 The six functional requirements (limb A). 2 Objectives of the internal audit. 3 How it helps the external audit. 4 Salient issues addressed. 5 Frequency and the five-year arithmetic (2-5 are limb B). 6 Non-conformity and major non-conformity. 7 Accidents and hazardous occurrences with examples (6-7 are limb C).
retrieval_cards.why: Limb (B) hides four separate questions inside one printed paragraph. One section each is the only way to make all four visible.

retrieval_cards.prompt: List the six functional requirements of the ISM Code.
retrieval_cards.answer: Paragraph 1.4: (1) a safety and environmental protection policy; (2) instructions and procedures to ensure safe operation and protection of the environment in compliance with international and flag State legislation; (3) defined levels of authority and lines of communication between and among shore and shipboard personnel; (4) procedures for reporting accidents and non-conformities; (5) procedures to prepare for and respond to emergency situations; (6) procedures for internal audits and management reviews.
retrieval_cards.why: A closed, numbered list of six. Offering five or eight demonstrates you have not read paragraph 1.4.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the difference between an internal audit and an inspection?
retrieval_cards.answer: An inspection inspects the ship - it asks whether the pump works. An audit audits the system - it asks whether there was a procedure that would have found out, whether it was followed, whether it was recorded, and whether the record was reviewed. Both are necessary and they are not the same activity.
retrieval_cards.why: Candidates who describe an internal audit as 'a thorough Company inspection' have missed the architecture of the whole Code.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How often are internal ISM audits required, and how many over the SMC cycle?
retrieval_cards.answer: Paragraph 12.1: internal safety audits on board and ashore at intervals not exceeding twelve months. In exceptional circumstances the interval may be exceeded by not more than three months. Over the five-year validity of the Safety Management Certificate that means at least five internal audits. Auditors should be independent of the area audited unless the size and nature of the Company make that impracticable.
retrieval_cards.why: The stem asks for the number over the five-year cycle, not just the interval rule. Candidates give the rule and never do the arithmetic.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Define non-conformity and major non-conformity.
retrieval_cards.answer: Non-conformity (1.1.9): an observed situation where objective evidence indicates the non-fulfilment of a specified requirement. Major non-conformity (1.1.10): an identifiable deviation posing a serious threat to the safety of personnel or the ship, or a serious risk to the environment, requiring immediate corrective action - and it includes the lack of effective and systematic implementation of a requirement of the Code.
retrieval_cards.why: The second half of the major definition is the half candidates omit, and it is how a ship with nothing broken carries a major non-conformity.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Distinguish a non-conformity, an accident and a hazardous occurrence, with examples.
retrieval_cards.answer: A non-conformity is a state, not an event - the fire drill record shows eight weeks where the SMS requires monthly. An accident is an event where harm occurred - a fitter suffers a lost-time hand injury. A hazardous occurrence is an event where harm nearly occurred - a high-pressure fuel line sprays onto a hot surface and the shielding prevents a fire. Note the ISM Code does not define 'accident', and paragraph 9.1 uses hazardous situations where the stem says occurrences.
retrieval_cards.why: The stem says 'with example'. The examples are how the distinctions are demonstrated rather than asserted.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give a major non-conformity where nothing is broken.
retrieval_cards.answer: An SMS that is on board but is not being used - records written up retrospectively, procedures unknown to the crew, non-conformities never raised. That is the lack of effective and systematic implementation of a requirement of the Code, which paragraph 1.1.10 expressly includes in the definition of a major non-conformity.
retrieval_cards.why: It proves you know the second half of the definition, and it is the classic oral question on the topic.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Your Company's internal audits have never raised a non-conformity. Is that good?
retrieval_cards.answer: No - it is evidence that the audits are not real. An external auditor who sees a run of clean internal reports will look harder, not less hard. The purpose of the internal audit is to find non-conformities and the conditions that could give rise to them; an audit that finds nothing has not performed its function.
retrieval_cards.why: The negative case is the sharpest way to state what an internal audit is for, and it links directly to the ISM-related clear grounds a PSCO uses.

LIMB (a) <- QP2512-Q6 (December 2025). Its printed stem is 'With regards to Minimum requirements for seafarers to work on a ship, as per MLC 2006, write a short note on the following: (16) (a) Minimum age to work on a ship. (b) Medical certification for duties on board. (c) Training and Qualification. (d) Recruitment and Placement.' LIMBS (b) AND (c) <- QP2403-Q9 (March 2024). Its printed stem is 'a) Discuss the key provisions and requirements outlined in the MLC, including those related to seafarers' employment contracts, working hours, accommodation, health and safety, and access to medical care and welfare facilities. (8) b) Discuss the challenges and limitations associated with the effective implementation and enforcement of the MLC, including issues related to flag State jurisdictions, Port State Control, and non-compliance by shipowners and operators. (8)'. Limb (a) there maps onto conditions of employment here; limb (b) there maps onto compliance and enforcement here. THIS DONOR IS THE MOST VALUABLE OF THE THREE FOR A REASON THAT IS TEMPORAL RATHER THAN SUBSTANTIVE - see the next entry.

QP2403-Q9 IS THE ONLY DONOR ON THIS ENTIRE PAPER THAT PRE-DATES THE SITTING. March 2024 is three months BEFORE June 2024. Every other donor across all nine questions travels backward into this sitting and had to be reversed. This one travels forward, which means its MLC temporal frame is a floor rather than a hazard: anything QP2403-Q9 could correctly say about the MLC in March 2024 remains correct in June 2024, because no MLC amendment entered into force in that window. It is the lowest-risk donor relation on the paper and it was still re-derived rather than inherited.

What is cause of the ever-increasing number of seafarer's getting abandoned in various parts of the world?
