blocks.h: 1. What the Convention is, and which version applies here

blocks.p: The Maritime Labour Convention, 2006 is an International Labour Organization instrument - not an IMO one - adopted by the International Labour Conference at its 94th (Maritime) Session in 2006 and in force since 20 August 2013. It consolidated some sixty-eight earlier maritime labour instruments into one, and is widely called the fourth pillar of international maritime regulation alongside SOLAS, MARPOL and STCW.
Its structure must be understood before any limb can be answered properly, because the four limbs of this question are simply four parts of it:

ul: Articles - the general obligations and the machinery of the Convention.
Regulations - the substantive requirements, grouped into five Titles.
The Code, Part A - Standards, which are mandatory.
The Code, Part B - Guidelines, which are not mandatory, but which a Member must give due consideration to.

blocks.p: The five Titles are: Title 1 minimum requirements for seafarers to work on a ship; Title 2 conditions of employment; Title 3 accommodation, recreational facilities, food and catering; Title 4 health protection, medical care, welfare and social security protection; Title 5 compliance and enforcement. Limbs (a), (b) and (c) of this question are Titles 1, 2 and 5; limb (d) sits inside Title 2 at Regulation 2.5.

One further point of machinery, because it distinguishes this Convention from every IMO instrument on the paper: the Code is amended not by MSC or MEPC tacit acceptance but by the Special Tripartite Committee under Article XIII, using the Convention's own simplified amendment procedure. The amendment set operative at this examination is the 2018 set; the 2022 amendments enter into force on 23 December 2024, six months after this sitting, and are not law here.

blocks.h: 2. Limb (a) - Title 1: minimum requirements for seafarers to work on a ship

blocks.p: Title 1 asks a single question in four parts: is this person allowed to be on this ship at all?

rows: 1.1 Minimum age
No person below the minimum age may be employed or work on a ship

The minimum age is 16. Night work by seafarers under 18 is prohibited, subject to a limited exception where it would impair training. Work likely to jeopardise the health or safety of a seafarer under 18 is prohibited outright, and the types of such work are determined by national law after consultation
1.2 Medical certificate
No seafarer may work without a valid medical certificate attesting fitness for the duties to be performed

Valid for a maximum of two years, or one year if the seafarer is under 18. A colour vision certificate is valid for a maximum of six years. A certificate issued under STCW is accepted. Where a certificate expires at sea it continues in force until the next port where a qualified practitioner is available, not exceeding three months. In urgent cases a seafarer may be permitted to work without a valid certificate until the next port, for a limited period
1.3 Training and qualifications
Seafarers must be trained, certificated or otherwise qualified for their duties
Training and certification in accordance with STCW; and no seafarer may work unless successfully completed training in personal safety on board
1.4 Recruitment and placement
Seafarers must have access to an efficient and well-regulated recruitment and placement system, free of charge

No fees or other charges for recruitment or placement may be borne directly or indirectly by the seafarer, other than the cost of the statutory medical certificate, the national seafarer's book and a passport. Private services must be licensed or regulated, must maintain a register, must verify that employment agreements meet the Convention, and must operate a system of protection - insurance or equivalent - to compensate seafarers for monetary loss from the service's or the shipowner's failure to meet its obligations. Where a shipowner uses a service in a State that has not ratified, he must satisfy himself that it meets the same requirements

blocks.p: The no-fees rule in Regulation 1.4 is the one to write with emphasis. It is the Convention's answer to debt bondage in the manning market, it is routinely evaded, and it is the provision under which a port State inspection most often finds something a candidate would not have predicted.
If Title 1 is about admission, Title 2 is about the bargain - and everything in it hangs off one document.

ul: Regulation 2.1 - the Seafarers' Employment Agreement. Every seafarer must have a written agreement signed by both the seafarer and the shipowner, giving decent working and living conditions. The seafarer must be given an opportunity to examine and seek advice on it before signing. An original signed copy is held by each, and a copy and, where the agreement is not in English, an English-language summary of its terms must be available on board for inspection. Where a collective bargaining agreement forms part of it, that too must be on board. Standard A2.1 lists the required particulars, and the seafarer must be given a document containing a record of employment that contains no statement as to the quality of his work or his wages.

Regulation 2.2 - Wages. Paid at no greater than monthly intervals and in full, in accordance with the agreement and any applicable collective agreement. Seafarers must be given a monthly account showing payments and the exchange rate used. Seafarers must be able to allot all or part of their earnings to their families, and any charge for the service must be reasonable and the exchange rate fair.

Regulation 2.3 - Hours of work and hours of rest. This is the provision candidates get wrong, so state it in the Convention's own alternative form: a Member must fix either a maximum number of hours of work - not exceeding 14 in any 24-hour period and 72 in any seven-day period - or a minimum number of hours of rest - not less than 10 in any 24-hour period and 77 in any seven-day period. Where the rest option is used, rest may be divided into no more than two periods, one of which must be at least six hours, and the interval between consecutive rest periods must not exceed fourteen hours. Records must be kept and the schedule posted in an accessible place. Musters, drills and safety work may interrupt rest, with compensatory rest given.

Regulation 2.4 - Entitlement to leave. Paid annual leave calculated on the basis of a minimum of 2.5 calendar days per month of employment. Any agreement to forgo the minimum leave is prohibited, except in cases provided for by the competent authority.

Regulation 2.5 - Repatriation, with the financial security system dealt with at limb (d) below. Seafarers are entitled to repatriation at no cost to themselves in the defined circumstances, and the maximum duration of service on board before repatriation is less than twelve months.
Regulation 2.6 - Compensation for the ship's loss or foundering, including an indemnity against unemployment resulting from it.
Regulation 2.7 - Manning levels - sufficient, safe and efficient manning, having regard to the safe manning document and to fatigue.
Regulation 2.8 - Career and skill development and opportunities for employment.

blocks.p: It is worth adding, because the examiner is testing breadth, that Titles 3 and 4 complete the picture of conditions on board - accommodation, recreational facilities, food and catering under Title 3, and health protection, on-board and onshore medical care, shipowner liability, occupational safety and health, welfare facilities and social security under Title 4. Naming them in a sentence shows the whole Convention has been read even though limb (b) does not require them in detail.
Title 5 has three parts, one for each actor, and the strength of the Convention is that it does not rely on any one of them.

ul: The flag State must establish an effective system of inspection and certification of maritime labour conditions (5.1.1), and may authorise Recognized Organizations to carry it out (5.1.2).

5.1.3 - the Maritime Labour Certificate and the Declaration of Maritime Labour Compliance. Required for ships of 500 gross tonnage and above engaged on international voyages or operating from a port, or between ports, in another country. The certificate is valid for a maximum of five years, subject to an intermediate inspection between the second and third anniversary date. The DMLC Part I is drawn up by the flag State and identifies the national requirements; Part II is drawn up by the shipowner and sets out the measures adopted to ensure ongoing compliance. Both are attached to the certificate and carried on board.
5.1.4 - Inspection and enforcement, with a sufficient number of qualified inspectors, powers to require deficiencies to be remedied, and power to prohibit the ship from leaving port until they are.

5.1.5 - On-board complaint procedures. Every ship must have procedures allowing seafarers to complain about breaches of the Convention, with safeguards against victimisation. The seafarer has a right to complain directly to the master, and to the flag State and other authorities.
5.1.6 - Marine casualties, requiring official inquiry into serious casualties involving loss of life or injury.

blocks.h: 5. Limb (c) - port State and labour-supplying responsibilities

ul: 5.2.1 - Inspections in port. A valid Maritime Labour Certificate and DMLC are prima facie evidence of compliance, so the ordinary inspection is limited to checking them. Where there are clear grounds - the documents are not produced or are not valid, there are grounds to believe conditions do not conform, or a complaint has been received - a more detailed inspection may be carried out. Deficiencies must be rectified; where they are serious, or repeated, or the subject of a valid complaint, the ship may be detained until they are.

5.2.2 - Onshore seafarer complaint-handling procedures. A seafarer may complain ashore in any port, and the port State must have a procedure to handle it, seeking resolution at ship level first and reporting to the flag State where it cannot be resolved.

blocks.p: A Member is also responsible for the seafarer recruitment and placement services operating in its territory, and for the social security protection of seafarers ordinarily resident there. This is the limb of Title 5 that reaches the manning agent, and it is what makes the no-fees rule in Regulation 1.4 enforceable at source.

blocks.h: 6. Limb (c) - the two provisions that make the system work

ul: "No more favourable treatment" - Article V(7). A Member must ensure that ships flying the flag of a State that has not ratified the Convention receive no more favourable treatment than ships of a State that has. Without this, non-ratification would be a commercial advantage; with it, a ship cannot escape the Convention by choosing a flag.

Substantial equivalence - Article VI. A Member may implement Part A of the Code by measures substantially equivalent to it, provided it is satisfied they give full effect to the general purpose and objective of the provision. This is what made near-universal ratification achievable, and it is also the seam through which national divergence enters.

blocks.p: The honest closing observation on limb (c): the Convention's enforcement is strong on documents and weaker on conditions. A certificate and a DMLC are prima facie evidence, and an inspection that finds the papers in order will usually go no further. That is why the complaint procedures at 5.1.5 and 5.2.2, and the port State's power to act on a complaint, matter more in practice than the certificate does.

blocks.h: 7. Limb (d) - abandonment, and when it arises

blocks.p: Abandonment is dealt with under Regulation 2.5 and Standard A2.5.2, introduced by the 2014 amendments, which are in force at this sitting. Before them the Convention gave a right to repatriation with no guarantee that anyone solvent would pay for it - which is precisely the position that produced the problem.
A seafarer is regarded as abandoned where, in breach of the Convention or of the employment agreement, the shipowner does any of three things:

ol: Fails to cover the cost of the seafarer's repatriation;
Leaves the seafarer without the necessary maintenance and support - which in practice means food, water, fuel, power, medical care and accommodation;
Otherwise unilaterally severs ties with the seafarer, including failure to pay contractual wages for a period of at least two months.

blocks.p: Two features of that definition are worth pointing out. It does not require the shipowner to have disappeared - a shipowner who is present, contactable and simply not paying can abandon a crew. And the third limb makes two months of unpaid wages a sufficient trigger on its own, which converts a slow financial failure into a defined event with defined remedies.

ul: Every ship to which the Convention applies must carry financial security - typically provided by the P&I club - to assist seafarers in the event of abandonment.

A certificate or other documentary evidence of that security, issued by the provider, must be posted in a conspicuous place on board where seafarers can see it, and must state the provider's contact details.

The seafarer, or a nominated representative, has direct access to the provider - the claim does not go through the shipowner, which is the point, since the shipowner is by definition the party who has failed.

The security must cover outstanding wages and other entitlements up to a defined limit, the cost of repatriation, and the seafarer's essential needs - which the Convention itself enumerates as including adequate food, clothing where necessary, accommodation, drinking water, essential fuel for survival on board, necessary medical care, and any other reasonable costs.
Assistance must be provided promptly, and the security may not be cancelled without prior notice to the flag State.

blocks.h: 9. Limb (d) - why the numbers rise, and what the institutions do

ul: Single-ship companies and opaque ownership. The corporate owner of one ageing vessel can be allowed to fail at no cost to the beneficial owner, leaving nothing to pursue.
Ageing tonnage in marginal trades, where a modest fall in freight rates makes the ship uneconomic and the cheapest option is to stop paying.

Arrest and detention. A ship arrested for debt or detained for deficiencies stops earning immediately while her costs continue, and crews are frequently abandoned on board a vessel they may not lawfully leave.
Sanctions, war risk and trade disruption, which can strand a ship and her crew with no lawful means of trading or of being paid.
Registries and manning chains with weak oversight, together with recruitment through unlicensed agents in States with limited enforcement capacity.
Seafarers' weak bargaining position - fear of blacklisting, debts incurred to obtain the job, and reluctance to leave the ship because leaving may forfeit the wage claim.
And a reporting effect that should be acknowledged rather than ignored: part of the increase reflects better reporting through the joint database, not only more incidents.

rows: ILO

Owns the Convention and its amendment machinery through the Special Tripartite Committee; maintains, jointly with IMO, the database of reported abandonment incidents; provides the standards against which flag and port States act
IMO
Joint custodian of the database with ILO, and the forum through which the port State control machinery that detects abandonment operates
ITF

Not a regulator but the most effective practical actor - its inspectorate boards ships, identifies unpaid wages, negotiates with owners and charterers, funds food and repatriation in emergencies, and pursues wage claims, backed by industrial action and by ITF-approved collective agreements
Flag State
Must be notified before security is cancelled; must facilitate repatriation and, ultimately, bears responsibility where the shipowner does not act
Port State
Detects the situation, may detain, handles the onshore complaint under 5.2.2, and in practice provides the humanitarian response first
P&I club / financial security provider
Pays - wages up to the limit, repatriation and essential needs - on direct application by the seafarer

blocks.p: The structural point to close on: the 2014 amendments did not create a right; they created a payer. The right to repatriation existed long before them. What was missing was certainty that someone solvent stood behind it, and a certificate on the bulkhead with a telephone number the seafarer can use without the shipowner's permission is what supplies it.

Sixteen marks, four limbs, no printed sub-marks - so the examiner has left the allocation open and will mark on balance. Four roughly equal parts is the safe reading, and the discipline that matters is not overrunning limb (a). Title 1 is the easiest material in the question and candidates write half the paper on it, then run out of time at limb (d), which is the limb that actually distinguishes answers. Budget the time before you start writing.

blocks.h: Get the architecture down in three lines

blocks.p: Articles, Regulations, Code Part A Standards (mandatory), Code Part B Guidelines (not mandatory). Five Titles: 1 minimum requirements, 2 conditions of employment, 3 accommodation and food, 4 health and welfare, 5 compliance and enforcement. This question is Titles 1, 2, 5 plus Regulation 2.5. Writing that opening paragraph makes every subsequent limb look like a part of a system rather than a separate recollection - and it is three lines.

Not IMO. Adopted by the International Labour Conference in 2006, in force 20 August 2013, and amended by the Special Tripartite Committee under Article XIII - not by MSC or MEPC tacit acceptance. Candidates who describe MLC amendments arriving by tacit acceptance have confused it with SOLAS. One sentence on this is cheap and it is the kind of thing that is asked orally.

blocks.h: The temporal point that governs this whole question

blocks.p: At a June 2024 sitting the Convention stands as amended through the 2018 set. The 2022 amendments entered into force on 23 December 2024 - six months after this examination. So do not write, as current obligations, the things the 2022 set introduced: appropriately sized personal protective equipment, free drinking water, the strengthened food and catering provisions, social connectivity and internet access, the repatriation of the remains of a deceased seafarer, or the reporting duties added around the abandonment database. If you have revised from a later syllabus or read a later MIW answer, those will be sitting in your memory as law. Here they are not.

The good news, and the thing to be sure of: the 2014 amendments are in force and have been for years. Limb (d) - the whole abandonment financial security system - is operative law at this sitting, not future law. So limb (d) can be written in full and with confidence.

blocks.h: Hours of rest - state it as an alternative

blocks.p: This is where candidates lose marks by giving half the rule. The Member fixes either maximum hours of work - 14 in 24 and 72 in 7 - or minimum hours of rest - 10 in 24 and 77 in 7. Under the rest option: no more than two periods, one of at least six hours, and no more than fourteen hours between consecutive rest periods. Learn all six numbers as one block, because the examiner will ask for the one you left out.

blocks.h: The other numbers in Title 1 and 2

ul: Minimum age 16; night work under 18 restricted; hazardous work under 18 prohibited.
Medical certificate 2 years, or 1 year under 18; colour vision 6 years; expiry at sea continues to the next port, up to 3 months.
Wages at intervals no greater than monthly.
Leave at 2.5 calendar days per month of employment.
Maximum service on board before repatriation: less than 12 months.
MLC certification at 500 GT and above on international voyages; certificate 5 years with an intermediate inspection between the second and third anniversary.
Abandonment trigger: wages unpaid for at least 2 months.

blocks.h: The definition of abandonment - three limbs, and the two subtleties

blocks.p: Fails to pay for repatriation; leaves the seafarer without necessary maintenance and support; or otherwise unilaterally severs ties, including failure to pay contractual wages for at least two months. Then the two points that show understanding: the shipowner does not have to have disappeared - a present, contactable owner who simply stops paying has abandoned the crew; and two months of unpaid wages is a sufficient trigger on its own, which turns a slow financial failure into a defined event with defined remedies.

blocks.h: The sentence to end limb (d) with

blocks.p: The 2014 amendments did not create a right - they created a payer. The right to repatriation was always there. What was missing was a solvent party standing behind it and a way for the seafarer to reach that party without the shipowner's cooperation. A certificate posted on the bulkhead with a number the seafarer can call is the whole reform in one object.

blocks.h: Do not quote a ratification figure

blocks.p: The temptation is to write "over 100 States and more than 96 per cent of world tonnage". Those figures are from a later date than this sitting and cannot be carried back honestly. Say that ratification is very wide, covering the great majority of world tonnage, and move on. It costs nothing and it cannot be wrong. The same applies to abandonment statistics - name the joint ILO/IMO database as the mechanism and give no number.

ul: Spending half the answer on Title 1 and leaving limb (d) unwritten.
Calling the MLC an IMO convention.
Giving the hours-of-rest limits without the hours-of-work alternative, or giving four of the six numbers.
Treating Part B Guidelines as mandatory. Part A Standards are mandatory; Part B is not.
Saying the DMLC is one document. Part I is the flag State's; Part II is the shipowner's.
Omitting "no more favourable treatment", which is what stops flag-shopping out of the Convention.
Defining abandonment as the shipowner disappearing. He need not disappear.
Writing 2022-amendment content - PPE sizing, drinking water, connectivity - as law at a June 2024 sitting.
Quoting a ratification count or an abandonment statistic.
"Who signs the seafarers' employment agreement?" The seafarer and the shipowner - not the master, and not the manning agent.
"Who draws up DMLC Part II?" The shipowner. Part I is the flag State's.
"Can a seafarer be charged a placement fee?" No - other than the statutory medical certificate, the national seafarer's book and a passport.
"What is the maximum period of service before repatriation?" Less than twelve months.
"Is a valid Maritime Labour Certificate conclusive?" No - it is prima facie evidence. Clear grounds or a complaint reopen the inspection.
"What does 'no more favourable treatment' mean?" A non-ratifying flag gets no advantage - Article V(7).
"Who pays when a crew is abandoned?" The financial security provider, usually the P&I club, on direct application by the seafarer.
"Where is the abandonment certificate kept?" Posted in a conspicuous place on board, with the provider's contact details - go and look at yours.
"Is two months' unpaid wages abandonment?" Yes, on its own, under the third limb of the definition.
Show me your seafarers' employment agreement and the record of hours of rest for your department.
Where is the financial security certificate posted, and who would you telephone?
Your ship has not been paid for ten weeks and the owner is not answering. What are your options?
What is in DMLC Part II and who wrote it?
How does a port State inspector deal with an MLC complaint from a rating?
Which Title covers accommodation and food, and what would an inspector look at?

blocks.p: Four limbs, four Titles, four numbers. Limb (a) is Title 1 - AGE, MEDICAL, TRAINING, AGENCY. Limb (b) is Title 2 - the AGREEMENT and everything hanging off it (wages, hours, leave, repatriation). Limb (c) is Title 5 - FLAG certifies, PORT inspects, SUPPLY State regulates the agent. Limb (d) is Reg 2.5 / Standard A2.5.2 - a CERTIFICATE, a PHONE NUMBER, and a PAYER. The four numbers to carry in: 16 (age), 2 years (medical), 10 in 24 / 77 in 7 (rest), 2 months (abandonment).

ul: Articles - V(7) no more favourable treatment; VI substantial equivalence; XIII the Special Tripartite Committee.
Title 1 - Reg 1.1 minimum age; 1.2 medical certificate; 1.3 training and qualifications; 1.4 recruitment and placement.

Title 2 - Reg 2.1 seafarers' employment agreement and Standard A2.1; 2.2 wages; 2.3 hours of work and rest; 2.4 leave; 2.5 repatriation; 2.6 compensation for ship's loss; 2.7 manning; 2.8 career development.
Regulation 2.5 and Standard A2.5.2 - abandonment and financial security, introduced by the 2014 amendments, IN FORCE at this sitting.
Titles 3 and 4 - accommodation, food and catering; health protection, medical care, welfare and social security.
Title 5 - 5.1.1 to 5.1.6 flag State; 5.2.1 and 5.2.2 port State; 5.3 labour-supplying responsibilities.
Joint ILO/IMO database of reported abandonment incidents; the ITF inspectorate - industry actors, not law.

blocks.p: This question rests on the strongest single source in the MIW corpus. The official ILO Compendium of maritime labour instruments, Fourth revised edition, 2026 is held, and the corpus records the instrument text as public domain on the source's own statement - a materially more permissive position than the IMO publications. Even so, no provision is reproduced verbatim here; provisions are cited by number and their effect stated, as a matter of MIW house discipline.

The amendment position is the decisive fact and it is verified rather than assumed. The corpus amendment table, checked against the Compendium, records the 2014 amendments in force, the 2016 set in force 8 January 2019, the 2018 set in force 26 December 2020, the 2022 set in force 23 December 2024 and the 2025 set not yet in force. This examination sat in June 2024, so the operative Convention is the MLC as amended through the 2018 set, and nothing the 2022 amendments introduced appears here as law. That is the exact inversion of what the corpus register says for current law - the register is maintained for the present and records the 2022 set as the latest in force - and getting the direction right is the single most important temporal judgement on this paper.

No ratification count and no tonnage percentage is asserted. The corpus figure - 110 ratifications, more than 96 per cent of world gross tonnage - is stated 'as of September 2025', fifteen months after this sitting, and cannot honestly be carried backwards. This is the critical positive finding: Regulation 2.5 and Standard A2.5.2 - the definition of abandonment, the financial security system, the posted certificate, direct access, and the scope of assistance - were introduced by the 2014 set, which the corpus records as in force well before this sitting. THE 2016 AND 2018 SETS ARE ALSO IN FORCE. The 2016 harassment and bullying amendments took effect 8 January 2019 and the 2018 wages-while-held-captive amendments on 26 December 2020, both well before this sitting.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: One sixteen-mark question in four named limbs, each of which is a whole Title or a whole Regulation of the MLC. The intent is breadth with control: the examiner wants to know whether the candidate can navigate the Convention's structure rather than recite one part of it well. The discriminator is limb (d) - abandonment is the part most candidates have not revised, and it is also the part carrying the most recent substantive reform.
decomposition_gate.mark_allocation: 16, undivided, with no printed sub-marks against the four limbs. Four roughly equal parts is the safe reading. The practical risk is not misallocation by the examiner but by the candidate: Title 1 is the easiest material and overruns, leaving limb (d) unwritten.
decomposition_gate.examiner_expectation: The Convention's architecture named briefly - Articles, Regulations, mandatory Part A Standards, non-mandatory Part B Guidelines, five Titles. Then Title 1 in its four parts with the numbers; Title 2 built around the seafarers' employment agreement with the hours-of-rest alternative stated correctly; Title 5 split three ways between flag State, port State and labour-supplying responsibilities, with 'no more favourable treatment' named; and abandonment defined in its three limbs with the financial security system described.
primary_source_plan: Read the corpus MLC amendment table BEFORE writing anything, and fix which amendment set is in force at the sitting. This is the governing act for the whole question.
Confirm specifically that the 2014 amendments - the abandonment financial security system - are in force, because limb (d) stands or falls on that.
Confirm that the 2022 amendments post-date the sitting, and list what they introduced so that it can be positively excluded rather than passively omitted.
Take the issuing-organisation and amendment-machinery points from the corpus log, so the ILO / Article XIII distinction is sourced rather than recalled.
Do NOT carry the corpus ratification figure back to the sitting - it is dated September 2025.
Read all three limb-level donor stems on both sides before deciding how each may be used, and check each donor's position relative to the 23 December 2024 boundary.

The MLC Code is amended on a rolling basis by the Special Tripartite Committee and a set entered into force six months after this sitting. Any answer to this question is only correct for a stated window, and the window here closes on 23 December 2024.
decomposition_gate.jurisdiction_risk: LOW to MEDIUM. The Convention applies uniformly and India gives effect to it under the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 at this sitting, with DG Shipping issuing Maritime Labour Certificates or authorising ROs. Article VI substantial equivalence permits national divergence in implementation, which is noted rather than detailed.
technical_ambiguities: The four limbs carry no printed marks. Equal weighting is assumed and the assumption is stated, because unequal weighting would change the answer's shape.

Limb (a)'s phrase 'minimum requirements for seafarers to work on a ship' is the exact title of Title 1, so the limb is read as Title 1 in its four Regulations rather than as a general question about crew standards.
Hours of work and rest are expressed in the Convention as an ALTERNATIVE that the Member chooses between. Giving only one half is the commonest error, so both are stated.
The Convention does not use the word 'abandonment' as a defined term in Regulation 2.5 itself; the three-limb test comes from Standard A2.5.2. The answer attributes it correctly.

MLC certification thresholds are stated as the Convention's general rule at 500 gross tonnage on international voyages. Flag State practice on smaller ships and domestic trades varies and is not asserted.

questions.understand_first: The MLC is easiest to hold in your head if you stop thinking of it as a convention and start thinking of it as the life cycle of one seafarer's employment. Before he can join, is he old enough, medically fit, trained, and was he recruited without paying for the privilege? That is Title 1 and it is limb (a). Once he joins, what has he actually been promised, and what does the Convention insist is in that promise - a written agreement he had a chance to read, wages monthly, hours limited, leave accruing, and a ticket home? That is Title 2 and it is limb (b). Then: who makes any of this true? The flag State certifies, the port State checks, the State the manning agent sits in regulates the agent - and no flag can escape by not ratifying. That is Title 5 and it is limb (c). And limb (d) is what happens when the whole arrangement collapses - when the shipowner stops answering, the wages stop, and the crew are sitting on a ship in a foreign port with no food and no ticket. The Convention's answer, and this is the part worth understanding rather than memorising, is not another right. The right to go home already existed and was worth nothing against an insolvent owner. What the 2014 amendments added was a solvent payer and a telephone number on the bulkhead that the seafarer can call without asking the shipowner's permission.

steps.title: What the Convention is, and which version applies here
points: An ILO instrument, not IMO - International Labour Conference 2006, in force 20 August 2013; the 'fourth pillar'
Articles; Regulations; Code Part A Standards (mandatory); Code Part B Guidelines (not mandatory)
Five Titles: 1 minimum requirements, 2 conditions of employment, 3 accommodation and food, 4 health and welfare, 5 compliance and enforcement
Amended by the Special Tripartite Committee under Article XIII - not by IMO tacit acceptance
At this sitting the Convention stands as amended through the 2018 set; the 2022 amendments come into force 23 December 2024

steps.title: Limb (a) - Title 1: minimum requirements for seafarers to work on a ship
points: Reg 1.1 minimum age - 16; night work under 18 restricted; hazardous work under 18 prohibited
Reg 1.2 medical certificate - max 2 years, 1 year under 18, colour vision 6 years; STCW certificate accepted; expiry at sea runs to the next port, up to 3 months
Reg 1.3 training and qualifications - STCW certification, plus completed training in personal safety on board

Reg 1.4 recruitment and placement - no fees charged to the seafarer except the statutory medical, seafarer's book and passport; private services licensed and regulated, keeping a register, verifying agreements, and operating a system of protection to compensate monetary loss
Emphasise the no-fees rule - it is the Convention's answer to debt bondage and is routinely evaded

steps.title: Limb (b) - Title 2: conditions of employment
points: Reg 2.1 the Seafarers' Employment Agreement - written, signed by seafarer and shipowner, opportunity to examine and seek advice, original held by each, copy and English summary available on board for inspection; any collective agreement on board too
Reg 2.2 wages - at intervals no greater than monthly, monthly account, right of allotment to family
Reg 2.3 hours - EITHER max work 14 in 24 / 72 in 7 OR min rest 10 in 24 / 77 in 7; rest in no more than two periods, one of at least 6 hours, interval not exceeding 14 hours
Reg 2.4 leave - minimum 2.5 calendar days per month; forgoing it is prohibited save as the competent authority provides
Reg 2.5 repatriation - at no cost to the seafarer; maximum service before repatriation less than 12 months
Reg 2.6 compensation for the ship's loss; 2.7 manning levels; 2.8 career and skill development
Name Titles 3 and 4 in one sentence to show the whole Convention has been read

steps.title: Limb (c) - Title 5: flag State responsibilities
points: 5.1.1 an effective system of inspection and certification; 5.1.2 Recognized Organizations may be authorised
5.1.3 the Maritime Labour Certificate and DMLC at 500 GT on international voyages, 5 years with an intermediate inspection between the second and third anniversary
DMLC Part I is the flag State's; Part II is the SHIPOWNER'S - the classic trap
5.1.4 inspection and enforcement, including the power to prohibit departure
5.1.5 on-board complaint procedures with safeguards against victimisation; 5.1.6 casualty inquiry

steps.title: Limb (c) - port State and labour-supplying responsibilities
points: 5.2.1 the certificate and DMLC are prima facie evidence, so the ordinary inspection checks documents
Clear grounds - documents not produced or invalid, grounds to believe conditions do not conform, or a complaint received - open a more detailed inspection
Deficiencies must be rectified; serious, repeated or complaint-based deficiencies may bring detention
5.2.2 onshore seafarer complaint-handling, seeking resolution at ship level first and reporting to the flag State
5.3 labour-supplying - responsibility for recruitment services in the territory and social security for resident seafarers; this is what makes the Reg 1.4 no-fees rule enforceable at source

steps.title: Limb (c) - the two provisions that make the system work
points: Article V(7) no more favourable treatment - a non-ratifying flag gets no advantage, so a ship cannot escape the Convention by choosing a flag
Article VI substantial equivalence - Part A may be implemented by substantially equivalent measures; what made near-universal ratification possible, and the seam through which divergence enters
Close honestly: enforcement is strong on documents and weaker on conditions, which is why the complaint procedures matter most in practice

steps.title: Limb (d) - abandonment, and when it arises
points: Regulation 2.5 and Standard A2.5.2, introduced by the 2014 amendments - IN FORCE at this sitting
Before them the right to repatriation existed with no guarantee that anyone solvent would pay

Three limbs: fails to cover repatriation; leaves the seafarer without necessary maintenance and support; or otherwise unilaterally severs ties, including failure to pay contractual wages for at least two months
Subtlety one: the shipowner need not have disappeared
Subtlety two: two months of unpaid wages is sufficient on its own

steps.title: Limb (d) - the financial security system
points: Financial security, usually from the P&I club, carried by every ship to which the Convention applies
A certificate posted in a conspicuous place on board with the provider's contact details
Direct access by the seafarer or a nominated representative - the claim does not go through the shipowner, who is by definition the party who failed
Covers outstanding wages to a defined limit, repatriation, and essential needs - food, clothing, accommodation, drinking water, essential fuel, medical care
Provided promptly; the security may not be cancelled without prior notice to the flag State

steps.title: Limb (d) - why the numbers rise, and what the institutions do
points: Causes: single-ship companies and opaque ownership; ageing tonnage in marginal trades; arrest and detention stopping earnings while costs continue; sanctions and trade disruption; weak registries and unlicensed agents; seafarers' weak bargaining position; and better reporting inflating the trend
ILO owns the Convention and its amendment machinery, and co-hosts the abandonment database
IMO co-hosts the database and supplies the port State control machinery that detects abandonment
ITF - not a regulator but the most effective practical actor: its inspectorate boards ships, pursues wage claims and funds food and repatriation
Flag State notified before security is cancelled and ultimately responsible; port State detects, detains and handles the onshore complaint
The security provider pays
Close: the 2014 amendments did not create a right - they created a payer

questions.memory_cue: Four limbs, four Titles, four numbers. Title 1 - AGE, MEDICAL, TRAINING, AGENCY (2). Title 2 - the AGREEMENT and everything hanging off it (3). Title 5 - FLAG certifies (4), PORT inspects and the SUPPLY State regulates the agent (5), over NO MORE FAVOURABLE TREATMENT (6). Abandonment: a CERTIFICATE, a PHONE NUMBER, a PAYER (7-9). Numbers: 16 / 2 years / 10 in 24 / 2 months. And the date that governs everything: the 2022 amendments are NOT in force here (1).

quick_revision.recall_15s: ILO convention, in force 20 August 2013, amended by the Special Tripartite Committee under Article XIII. Structure: Articles, Regulations, Part A Standards mandatory, Part B Guidelines not; five Titles. (a) Title 1 - age 16, night work and hazardous work under 18 restricted; medical certificate 2 years (1 under 18, colour vision 6); STCW training plus personal safety training; recruitment free of charge to the seafarer, agencies licensed with a system of protection. (b) Title 2 - written SEA signed by seafarer and shipowner, copy on board; wages monthly with an account and allotments; hours EITHER 14 in 24 / 72 in 7 work OR 10 in 24 / 77 in 7 rest, rest in no more than two periods one of at least six hours; leave 2.5 days per month; repatriation, service under 12 months. (c) Title 5 - flag State certifies with the Maritime Labour Certificate and DMLC (Part I flag, Part II shipowner) at 500 GT, five years with an intermediate inspection; port State treats the certificate as prima facie evidence and may inspect further on clear grounds or a complaint, and detain; labour-supplying States regulate the agents; Article V(7) no more favourable treatment. (d) Abandonment under Standard A2.5.2 (2014 amendments, in force): the shipowner fails to pay repatriation, leaves the seafarer without maintenance and support, or unilaterally severs ties including two months' unpaid wages - answered by financial security, a certificate posted on board, direct access, and cover for wages, repatriation and essential needs.

2022 amendments in force 23 DECEMBER 2024 - six months AFTER this sitting, so not law here

Hours: EITHER 14 in 24 and 72 in 7 of work, OR 10 in 24 and 77 in 7 of rest; rest in no more than two periods, one of at least 6 hours, interval not exceeding 14 hours

quick_revision.critical_regulation: Standard A2.5.2, introduced by the 2014 amendments and in force at this sitting, is the provision that makes limb (d) answerable - it supplies the three-limb definition of abandonment and the financial security system behind it. Read with Regulation 2.5 on repatriation, and with Title 5 for the certification and inspection machinery that detects the failure.
quick_revision.major_trap: Writing 2022-amendment content as law at a June 2024 sitting - appropriately sized PPE, free drinking water, the strengthened food and catering provisions, social connectivity and internet access, repatriation of a deceased seafarer's remains. Those entered into force on 23 December 2024, six months after this examination, and a candidate revising from a later syllabus will have them in mind as current. Second trap: giving only one half of the hours rule - it is an alternative between maximum work and minimum rest, and the examiner will ask for the half you omitted. Third: saying DMLC is one document - Part I is the flag State's, Part II is the shipowner's. Fourth: defining abandonment as the shipowner disappearing - he need not; two months of unpaid wages is enough on its own. Fifth: quoting a ratification figure - the available number is dated fifteen months after this sitting and cannot be carried back. Sixth: calling the MLC an IMO convention.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the MLC 2006 four-limb question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 Architecture and which amendment set applies. 2 Limb (a) Title 1 - age, medical, training, recruitment. 3 Limb (b) Title 2 - the employment agreement and everything hanging off it. 4 Limb (c) Title 5 - flag State, port State, labour-supplying, plus no more favourable treatment. 5-6 Limb (d) - the three-limb definition of abandonment, then financial security, causes and institutions.
retrieval_cards.why: Four limbs with no printed sub-marks means equal weighting and strict time discipline. Title 1 is the easiest material and is what overruns, leaving limb (d) - the discriminating limb - unwritten.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Limb (a) - the four parts of Title 1 with their numbers.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1.1 minimum age - 16; night work and hazardous work restricted under 18. 1.2 medical certificate - maximum 2 years, 1 year under 18, colour vision 6 years; STCW certificates accepted. 1.3 training - STCW certification plus completed training in personal safety on board. 1.4 recruitment and placement - no fees charged to the seafarer except the statutory medical, seafarer's book and passport; services licensed and operating a system of protection against monetary loss.
retrieval_cards.why: Four Regulations, four numbers. The no-fees rule is the Convention's answer to debt bondage and is the one most often found breached.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State the MLC hours of work and rest rule in full.
retrieval_cards.answer: A Member fixes either maximum hours of work - not exceeding 14 in any 24-hour period and 72 in any seven-day period - or minimum hours of rest - not less than 10 in any 24-hour period and 77 in any seven-day period. Under the rest option, rest may be divided into no more than two periods, one of at least six hours, and the interval between consecutive rest periods must not exceed fourteen hours. Records are kept and the schedule posted; drills interrupting rest attract compensatory rest.
retrieval_cards.why: It is an alternative, not a single rule, and candidates give half of it. Learn all six numbers as one block.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Limb (c) - who does what under Title 5?
retrieval_cards.answer: Flag State (5.1) - inspection and certification, may authorise ROs; issues the Maritime Labour Certificate and DMLC at 500 GT, five years with an intermediate inspection; on-board complaint procedures. Port State (5.2) - the certificate is prima facie evidence, so the ordinary inspection checks documents; clear grounds or a complaint open a more detailed inspection, and detention may follow. Labour-supplying State (5.3) - regulates the agents. Over all of it, Article V(7) no more favourable treatment.
retrieval_cards.why: Three actors, and the Convention deliberately does not rely on any one. Missing the labour-supplying limb loses a third of the limb.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Who draws up DMLC Part I and Part II?
retrieval_cards.answer: Part I is drawn up by the flag State and identifies the national requirements implementing the Convention. Part II is drawn up by the shipowner and sets out the measures adopted to ensure ongoing compliance on that ship. Both are attached to the Maritime Labour Certificate and carried on board.
retrieval_cards.why: The classic trap. Candidates describe the DMLC as a single flag State document and lose the mark.

retrieval_cards.prompt: When is a seafarer regarded as abandoned?
retrieval_cards.answer: Under Standard A2.5.2 (2014 amendments), where in breach of the Convention or the employment agreement the shipowner: fails to cover the cost of repatriation; leaves the seafarer without the necessary maintenance and support; or otherwise unilaterally severs ties, including failure to pay contractual wages for at least two months. Note that the shipowner need not have disappeared, and that two months of unpaid wages is a sufficient trigger on its own.
retrieval_cards.why: The two subtleties are what turn a memorised definition into an understood one, and the second converts a slow financial failure into a defined event with defined remedies.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How does the abandonment financial security actually work?
retrieval_cards.answer: Every ship carries financial security, usually from the P&I club. A certificate is posted in a conspicuous place on board with contact details. The seafarer has direct access to the provider - the claim does not go through the shipowner, who is by definition the party that failed. It covers outstanding wages to a defined limit, repatriation and essential needs - food, accommodation, drinking water, essential fuel, medical care - and must be provided promptly.
retrieval_cards.why: The reform is procedural rather than substantive: the right to go home already existed, and what was added was a solvent payer the seafarer can reach unaided.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which MLC amendments must NOT be cited at a June 2024 sitting?
retrieval_cards.answer: The 2022 amendments. They entered into force on 23 December 2024, six months after this examination, and introduced appropriately sized PPE, free drinking water, strengthened food and catering, social connectivity, and repatriation of a deceased seafarer's remains. The 2025 amendments are excluded absolutely. What is in force: the 2014 set (abandonment financial security), the 2016 set and the 2018 set.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the paper's most consequential temporal boundary, and it runs the wrong way for anyone revising from a later syllabus.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What did the 2014 amendments actually change?
retrieval_cards.answer: They did not create a right - they created a payer. The right to repatriation existed long before them and was worth nothing against an insolvent single-ship owner. The 2014 amendments added compulsory financial security, a certificate posted on board, and direct access to the provider without the shipowner's cooperation. They also added financial security for death or long-term disability from occupational injury.
retrieval_cards.why: One sentence that reframes the whole limb, and the best possible close to the answer.

blocks.p: A Protection and Indemnity club is a mutual association of shipowners, charterers and operators, formed to cover the third-party liabilities arising from the operation of their ships. The word that governs everything else in the answer is mutual: the members are the club. There are no external shareholders, no profit is taken out, an underwriting surplus is retained for the members and a deficit is met by them.

So a club is not a company selling a product to a customer. It is a group of shipowners sharing each other's liabilities, governed by a board of directors drawn from the membership and administered day to day by professional managers. Twelve clubs participate in the International Group, through which the largest claims are shared - and that figure moves with mergers, so it is worth writing as "the twelve clubs of the International Group" rather than as a permanent fact.

blocks.h: 2. Why it is not ordinary marine insurance

blocks.p: The three differences the corpus itself identifies are mutuality, breadth of cover, and the absence of a fixed sum insured, and those are the three to write if only one line is available.

blocks.h: 3. How the club collects funds - the tiers

blocks.p: This is the second half of limb (a), and it is answered in tiers because that is what the funding structure is.

ol: Advance call. Levied on entry for the policy year and usually paid in instalments. This is the estimated cost of the year, collected up front.

Supplementary call. Levied if the year's claims and expenses exceed the advance calls plus investment income. It is not a penalty - it is the mutual mechanism operating exactly as designed, the members carrying the year between them.

Release call. Payable by a member leaving the club, buying out his exposure to future supplementary calls on the policy years still open. Policy years are kept open for several years because liability claims take years to mature - which is the whole reason a release call exists.

Deductible. The member bears an agreed first amount of every claim. Its purpose is not revenue but behaviour: it suppresses small-claim frequency and keeps the member's own claims-handling discipline engaged.

blocks.p: The advance call is assessed on the member's entered tonnage, and then rated for the ship type, the trade and area of operation, the crew's nationality and terms of employment, the standard of management - and, dominating all of them, the member's own claims record. A club is a mutual, but it is not a subsidy: a member with a poor record pays for it.

Indian law recognises this machinery expressly, and it is worth one line because it makes the answer an Indian one. The Admiralty (Jurisdiction and Settlement of Maritime Claims) Act, 2017 lists at section 4(1)(s) "insurance premium (including mutual insurance calls)" among the maritime claims for which a vessel may be arrested. An unpaid call is therefore not merely a debt - it is a claim that can put the ship under arrest.

blocks.h: 4. Above the club - the International Group

blocks.p: No single mutual could carry a very large casualty, so above the club sit three further layers:

ul: The club's own retention - the amount each club keeps for its own account.
The International Group Pooling Agreement - claims above that retention are shared among the participating clubs, so a single catastrophic claim is met by the whole group rather than by one club.
The Group's collective reinsurance, placed in the market for the whole Group, and above that a further overspill layer met by the members themselves through an overspill call.

blocks.p: This structure is the reason a shipowner can obtain liability cover of a magnitude no ordinary insurer would write, and the reason a coastal State facing a major pollution casualty has somebody solvent to claim against. No figures are given here for the retention, the pool layers, the reinsurance attachment or the overspill limit, because they are reset every policy year; quoting one is the surest way to be wrong in an oral.

blocks.h: 5. "Protection" - liabilities to people and to the world

blocks.p: The two halves of the club's name are two halves of the cover, and the division is genuinely useful: protection is everything except cargo, indemnity is cargo.

ul: Crew - personal injury, illness and death; medical, hospital and funeral expenses; repatriation; loss of personal effects; and wages in defined circumstances such as after a casualty.
Other persons - injury to or death of stevedores, pilots, visitors, passengers and other third parties.

Collision liability - the proportion of collision liability not covered by the hull and machinery policy, which classically covers only three-fourths of running-down liability, together with liabilities excluded from the hull cover.
Fixed and floating objects - damage to piers, jetties, berths, buoys, cables, pipelines and navigational aids.
Pollution - liability for oil and other pollution, clean-up costs and the cost of preventive measures, beyond what the hull policy reaches.
Wreck removal - the cost of raising, removing, destroying, lighting or marking the wreck where that is compulsory by law.
Stowaways, refugees and persons rescued at sea - maintenance, deviation and repatriation costs.
Quarantine and disinfection expenses arising from infectious disease on board.

Fines - for pollution, for cargo shortage or overlanding, for immigration, customs and smuggling breaches, and for breaches of safety or navigation rules, so far as the rules permit and subject to the board's discretion.
Towage and salvage liabilities under approved contracts, and liabilities under approved indemnities.
Legal costs of investigating, defending or settling any of the above.
Loss of, damage to, shortage of and contamination of cargo carried, arising from breach of the contract of carriage.
Cargo's proportion of general average where it cannot be recovered from cargo interests because of a breach of the contract of carriage by the owner - which is the direct link to Q8 on this paper.
Liabilities under approved bills of lading and charterparty terms, and under contracts approved by the club.
The cost of disposing of damaged or unclaimed cargo, and liabilities arising from through and transhipment carriage.

blocks.h: 7. The boundary - what P&I does not cover, and why

blocks.p: This paragraph is what raises an answer above a list, because it shows the logic of the cover rather than its contents.

ul: Damage to the member's own ship - that is the hull and machinery policy's subject, not the club's.

The member's own trading loss. Delay and loss of hire after a casualty are the owner's own economic loss, not a liability to anyone, and fall to a separate loss-of-hire cover if it has been bought. This is the commonest misconception on the topic: P&I covers liabilities, not the owner's own losses.
War risks, which are separately insured.
Liabilities arising from unapproved contracts, or from terms more onerous than the club permits - the club underwrites the member's liability, not the member's willingness to accept anyone's terms.
Liabilities arising from the ship trading in breach of her class, certification or the terms of entry.

blocks.p: And the corollary that is the club's real commercial function alongside paying claims: because the club stands behind the member's liabilities, it also underwrites the member's compulsory insurance certificates - the blue cards that produce the CLC 1992 and Bunkers Convention certificates, the MLC 2006 financial security for repatriation, abandonment and contractual claims, and the wreck-removal certificate under the Nairobi Convention. Without a club entry a ship cannot obtain those certificates, and without them she cannot trade. See Q1 and Q6 on this paper.

blocks.h: 8. How the club handles a claim

blocks.p: A club is not a passive payer. Its handling has three characteristics that distinguish it from an ordinary indemnity insurer:

ul: It takes control of the defence. The club appoints or approves lawyers, surveyors and experts, and the member must not admit liability or settle without the club's agreement. Doing so can prejudice the cover.

It works through a worldwide network of correspondents. The correspondent in the port of the incident attends the ship, takes statements while the crew are still on board and their memory is fresh, arranges surveys and joint surveys with cargo interests, and advises the master immediately - which is why the correspondent's contact details are on board and why the master should reach them before anyone else.

It provides security to prevent or lift an arrest. This is the club's single most valuable practical service. Rather than a cash deposit or a bank guarantee, the club issues a letter of undertaking to the claimant, promising to satisfy any judgment or award up to a stated sum. That releases the ship, or prevents her being detained at all - and under the Admiralty Act 2017, arrest in rem is a real and immediate risk in an Indian port.

blocks.p: Two governing principles sit behind all of it. Pay to be paid: the classic mutual principle is that the member must first discharge the liability and is then indemnified, although clubs exercise discretion and pay directly in practice, particularly where a seafarer or a coastal State is the claimant. And utmost good faith: the member must disclose fully and must not prejudice the club's position - which is what makes prompt and complete notification a condition of the cover rather than a courtesy.

blocks.h: 9. The procedure for filing a claim

ol: Notify immediately. The master or the Company notifies the club - directly and through the local correspondent - as soon as an incident occurs or a claim is threatened. Club rules impose notification time limits and late notification can prejudice or defeat the claim. Notify on suspicion; do not wait for certainty.

Preserve and gather the evidence, at once. Log entries, engine and bridge data, the Oil Record Book, statements from the crew involved, photographs, damaged items, cargo condition and stowage records, tank soundings, and the relevant SMS records. Evidence that is not taken while the ship is in port and the crew are on board is usually lost for good.

Arrange survey. The correspondent instructs a surveyor on the club's behalf; where cargo or a third party is involved, a joint survey with the other side's surveyor is arranged so the facts are agreed before the argument starts.
Do not admit liability and do not settle. Sign nothing beyond a factual receipt or protest; refer every demand to the club.
Note protest where the circumstances call for it, and issue the appropriate letters of protest or holding replies to third parties.

Submit the formal claim to the club with the supporting documentation - the incident report, survey reports, invoices, wage and medical records, the bill of lading and charterparty, and legal correspondence.
Request security where arrest is threatened or has occurred, so the club can issue its letter of undertaking and the ship can sail.
Cooperate through the defence. The club conducts negotiation, mediation, arbitration or litigation; the member provides witnesses and documents and follows the club's instructions.

Settlement and reimbursement. The club settles the third-party claim or reimburses the member, less the deductible; and where the loss was another party's fault the club pursues recovery by subrogation, stepping into the member's rights - a principle of the Marine Insurance Act, 1963 in Indian law.

blocks.p: The Chief Engineer's part in that sequence is narrow and decisive: report immediately, preserve the machinery evidence and the records before anything is disturbed, write down what happened while it is fresh, and admit nothing. Most claims that fail on the facts fail because the evidence was not taken in the first twenty-four hours.

5 + 5 + 6, and the marks tell you where the writing goes. Limb (a) is two questions - what is a club, and how does it collect money - so the funding tiers must be visible and not folded into a general description of mutuality. Limb (b) is a classification question: the marks are in placing risks correctly on either side of the protection / indemnity line, not in the length of the list. Limb (c) carries the most marks and is the limb most often written thinnest, because candidates know what a club is and have never thought about what happens after an incident. Give limb (c) the most space.

Mutual. The members are the club - no shareholders, no profit extracted, surplus retained and deficit met by the members. Every other feature follows: calls not premiums, because a call is what a member of an association contributes and can be adjusted after the event; no fixed sum insured, because the club covers the liability incurred rather than a stated value; and very wide cover, extensible by the board's omnibus discretion, because the members decide what the association covers.

blocks.h: The Indian point that costs one line and earns more

blocks.p: The Admiralty (Jurisdiction and Settlement of Maritime Claims) Act, 2017 lists at section 4(1)(s) "insurance premium (including mutual insurance calls)" as a maritime claim. So an unpaid call can support the arrest of the vessel. In an Indian examination, one sentence naming an Indian statute that recognises the exact mechanism you have just described is worth more than another paragraph on mutuality.

Protection is people and the world; indemnity is cargo. Learn it that way and every risk sorts itself. Crew, passengers, stevedores, pilots, collision liability beyond the hull cover, fixed and floating objects, pollution, wreck removal, stowaways, quarantine, fines and legal costs are all protection. Loss, damage, shortage and contamination of cargo, cargo's proportion of general average unrecoverable through the owner's breach, and liabilities under approved bills of lading are indemnity.

blocks.h: The exclusion that is nearly always got wrong

blocks.p: P&I covers liabilities, not the owner's own losses. Damage to your own ship is hull and machinery. Delay and loss of hire after a casualty is your own trading loss, not a liability to anybody, and falls to a separate loss-of-hire cover if it was bought. War risks are separately insured. Writing this paragraph converts a memorised list into a demonstrated understanding of what the cover is for.

Hull and machinery classically covers only three-fourths of running-down (collision) liability. The remaining one-fourth, and liabilities the hull policy excludes, fall to the club. It is the standard follow-up question on limb (b) and it takes half a sentence.

blocks.h: Limb (c) - the three things a club does that an insurer does not

ol: Takes control of the defence - appoints or approves lawyers and surveyors; the member must not admit liability or settle without the club.
Works through correspondents - the local correspondent attends the ship, takes statements while the crew are aboard, and arranges joint surveys.

Provides security - the letter of undertaking that prevents or lifts an arrest, instead of a cash deposit or bank guarantee. This is the club's most valuable practical service, and under the Admiralty Act 2017 arrest is a live risk in an Indian port.

blocks.p: The classic mutual principle is that the member must first discharge the liability and is then indemnified. In practice clubs exercise discretion and pay claimants directly, especially seafarers and coastal States. Naming the principle and then noting the practice is exactly the kind of two-layer answer that scores in an oral.

Report immediately, preserve the machinery evidence and records before anything is disturbed, write down what happened while it is fresh, admit nothing. Most claims that fail on the facts fail because nobody took the evidence in the first twenty-four hours. Ending limb (c) on the candidate's own responsibility rather than on the club's procedure is a strong close.

Club retentions, pool layers, reinsurance attachment points, overspill limits, oil-pollution sub-limits and deductibles are reset every policy year. Describe the structure - retention, pool, collective reinsurance, overspill - and give no numbers. The one count worth using is that the International Group comprises twelve clubs, and even that moves with mergers, so phrase it as "the twelve clubs of the International Group" rather than as a permanent truth.

ul: Describing a club as an insurance company. It is a mutual association owned by its members.
Saying "premium" instead of "call", which signals the mutuality has not been understood.
Answering limb (a) on what a club is and never explaining how it collects money - half the limb.
Omitting the release call, or being unable to say why open policy years require one.
Putting cargo claims under "protection".
Claiming P&I covers loss of hire or damage to the member's own ship.
Writing limb (c) as "you inform the club and they pay" - six marks, the largest limb.
Quoting pool limits or reinsurance figures.
"Premium or call - and why does it matter?" A call. Because the members are the association, so the contribution can be adjusted after the event.
"What is a release call for?" Buying out future supplementary calls on policy years that are still open, because liability claims take years to mature.
"How much of the collision liability does the hull policy cover?" Classically three-fourths; the balance falls to the club.
"Does the club cover your loss of hire?" No - that is the owner's own trading loss, not a liability.
"What is a letter of undertaking and why does it matter to you?" The club's promise to satisfy a judgment, which releases the ship instead of a cash deposit - and it is what gets you out of arrest.
"What is a blue card?" The club's evidence of cover that produces the CLC, Bunkers and MLC financial security certificates. No entry, no certificates, no trading.
"What is 'pay to be paid'?" The member must discharge the liability first and is then indemnified - subject to the club's discretion in practice.
"An unpaid call - can the ship be arrested in India?" Yes - Admiralty Act 2017, section 4(1)(s).
Who is your club and where are the correspondent's details kept?
A stevedore is injured in your engine room. What do you do in the first hour?
Your ship is arrested for an unpaid bunker bill. How does the club get you out?

FOUR CALLS: advance, supplementary, release, deductible - then pool, reinsurance, overspill above. TWO WORDS: protection is people and the world; indemnity is cargo. THREE SERVICES in limb (c): controls the defence, sends the correspondent, issues the letter of undertaking.

questions.understand_first: Everything in this question falls out of one fact: a P&I club has no customers. An ordinary insurer sells you a policy and keeps the profit; if the year goes badly, that is the insurer's problem. A club is an association of shipowners who have agreed to carry each other's liabilities, so there is nobody outside the group to absorb a bad year. That single structural difference explains all of limb (a). It is why the money is called a call and not a premium - a call is what a member of an association contributes, and it can be adjusted after the event, which a premium cannot. It is why there is a supplementary call at all: if the year cost more than expected, the members pay the difference, because there is nobody else. It is why a release call exists when you leave: liability claims take years to mature, so the years you were a member are still open and still capable of costing money. And it is why the cover has no fixed sum insured - the members decided to cover each other's liabilities, whatever they turn out to be, rather than to buy a stated amount of protection. Limb (b) is then just a division of labour: your hull policy looks after your ship, and the club looks after what you owe to everyone else - people and the world under protection, cargo under indemnity. And limb (c) is the part worth understanding rather than memorising: what the club actually sells is not money, it is control and credit - a lawyer and surveyor on the quay within hours, and a piece of paper that gets your ship out of arrest without you finding cash in a foreign port.

steps.title: What a P&I club is
points: A mutual association of shipowners, charterers and operators covering third-party liabilities from the operation of their ships
The members are the club - no external shareholders, no profit extracted
Surplus retained for the members; deficit met by them - hence calls, not premiums
Liability cover, with no fixed sum insured
Governed by a board drawn from the membership; run by professional managers
Twelve clubs participate in the International Group - phrase it as a current figure, not a permanent one

steps.title: Why it is not ordinary marine insurance
points: Premium against call; property loss against legal liability; fixed sum insured against none
Narrow defined perils against very wide cover, extensible by the board's omnibus discretion
Profit to shareholders against surplus retained for members
The three the corpus itself names: mutuality, breadth of cover, absence of a fixed sum insured

steps.title: How the club collects funds - the tiers
points: Advance call - on entry for the policy year, in instalments; the estimated cost collected up front
Supplementary call - where claims and expenses exceed advance calls plus investment income. Not a penalty
Release call - on leaving, buying out exposure to future supplementary calls on open policy years
Say why years stay open: liability claims take years to mature
Deductible - the member's first amount on every claim; suppresses small-claim frequency
Rated on entered tonnage, then ship type, trade and area, crew nationality and terms, management standard - and above all the claims record
One Indian line: Admiralty Act 2017 s.4(1)(s) makes an unpaid mutual insurance call a maritime claim supporting arrest

steps.title: Above the club - the International Group
points: The club's own retention
The International Group Pooling Agreement - claims above retention shared among the participating clubs
The Group's collective reinsurance, and above it an overspill layer met by members through an overspill call
Why it matters: cover of a magnitude no single insurer would write, and a solvent target for a coastal State after a major casualty
Give no figures - retentions and layers are reset annually

steps.title: "Protection" - liabilities to people and to the world
points: Crew - injury, illness, death, medical, hospital and funeral, repatriation, personal effects, wages in defined circumstances
Other persons - stevedores, pilots, visitors, passengers, third parties
Collision - the proportion not covered by hull, which classically covers only three-fourths
Fixed and floating objects - piers, jetties, berths, buoys, cables, pipelines, navigational aids
Pollution - liability, clean-up and preventive measures beyond the hull cover
Wreck removal where compulsory by law
Stowaways, refugees, persons rescued at sea; quarantine and disinfection
Fines - pollution, cargo shortage, immigration and customs, safety breaches, so far as the rules permit
Towage and salvage liabilities under approved contracts; legal costs throughout

steps.title: "Indemnity" - liability to cargo
points: Loss, damage, shortage and contamination of cargo carried, from breach of the contract of carriage
Cargo's proportion of general average unrecoverable because of the owner's breach - the link to Q8
Liabilities under approved bills of lading and charterparty terms
Disposal of damaged or unclaimed cargo; through and transhipment liabilities

steps.title: The boundary - what P&I does not cover, and why
points: NOT damage to the member's own ship - that is hull and machinery
NOT the member's own trading loss - delay and loss of hire is a separate cover. P&I covers liabilities, not your own losses
NOT war risks; NOT liabilities under unapproved contracts; NOT where trading in breach of class or terms of entry
The corollary: the club issues the blue cards behind the CLC and Bunkers certificates, the MLC financial security, and the Nairobi wreck-removal certificate
No entry, no certificates, no trading - link to Q1 and Q6

steps.title: How the club handles a claim
points: Takes control of the defence - appoints or approves lawyers, surveyors and experts; no admission or settlement without the club
Works through correspondents - attendance on board, statements while the crew are aboard, surveys and joint surveys
Provides security - the letter of undertaking that prevents or lifts arrest, in place of cash or a bank guarantee
'Pay to be paid' - the member discharges first and is indemnified; in practice the club pays claimants directly, especially seafarers and coastal States
Utmost good faith - full disclosure, and nothing done to prejudice the club's position

steps.title: The procedure for filing a claim
points: Notify immediately - club and local correspondent; rules impose time limits and late notice can defeat the claim. Notify on suspicion
Preserve and gather evidence at once - logs, engine and bridge data, Oil Record Book, crew statements, photographs, damaged items, cargo and stowage records, soundings, SMS records
Arrange survey, and a joint survey where cargo or a third party is involved
Do not admit liability, do not settle; sign nothing beyond a factual receipt or protest
Note protest and issue letters of protest or holding replies
Submit the formal claim with incident report, surveys, invoices, wage and medical records, B/L and charterparty, legal correspondence
Request security where arrest threatens, so the LOU can issue and the ship can sail
Cooperate through the defence - witnesses, documents, the club's instructions
Settlement and reimbursement, less the deductible, with the club pursuing recovery by subrogation under the Marine Insurance Act, 1963
Close on the Chief Engineer's own part: report at once, preserve the evidence, write it down while fresh, admit nothing

questions.memory_cue: MUTUAL - four calls - two words - three services. MUTUAL: members are the club, so calls not premiums and no fixed sum insured (1-2). FOUR CALLS: advance, supplementary, release, deductible (3); above them POOL, REINSURANCE, OVERSPILL (4). TWO WORDS: protection is people and the world (5), indemnity is cargo (6). THREE SERVICES: controls the defence, sends the correspondent, issues the letter of undertaking (8).

quick_revision.recall_15s: A P&I club is a mutual association of shipowners covering third-party liabilities; the members are the club, so there are calls, not premiums, no fixed sum insured, and surplus is retained for the members. It collects in tiers: advance call on entry, assessed on entered tonnage and rated above all on the claims record; supplementary call if the year overruns; release call on leaving, because policy years stay open while liability claims mature; and a deductible on every claim. Above the club sit the International Group pooling agreement, the Group's collective reinsurance and an overspill layer. Protection covers people and the world - crew injury and death, other persons, the collision liability the hull policy's three-fourths leaves, fixed and floating objects, pollution, wreck removal, stowaways, quarantine, fines and legal costs. Indemnity covers cargo - loss, damage, shortage, contamination, and cargo's GA contribution unrecoverable through the owner's breach. It does not cover your own ship or your own loss of hire. On a claim: notify at once, preserve evidence, correspondent attends, joint survey, admit nothing, submit with documents, take a letter of undertaking to lift arrest, settle less deductible, and the club recovers by subrogation. In India an unpaid call is a maritime claim supporting arrest - Admiralty Act 2017, s.4(1)(s).
critical_numbers: Hull and machinery classically covers three-fourths of collision (running-down) liability; the balance falls to the club
Twelve clubs participate in the International Group - a current figure that moves with mergers, not a permanent fact
NO retention, pool layer, reinsurance attachment, overspill limit or deductible figure is quoted - all are reset every policy year
Admiralty Act 2017, section 4(1)(s) - insurance premium including mutual insurance calls, as a maritime claim
quick_revision.critical_regulation: There is no convention governing P&I - it is market practice, and saying so is correct rather than evasive. The Indian statutory hooks are what anchor the answer: the Admiralty (Jurisdiction and Settlement of Maritime Claims) Act, 2017, whose section 4(1)(s) makes an unpaid mutual insurance call a maritime claim supporting arrest, and the Marine Insurance Act, 1963 for utmost good faith and subrogation.
quick_revision.major_trap: Saying premium instead of call, which signals that the mutuality has not been understood - and then being unable to explain the supplementary or release call, both of which exist only because the members carry the risk themselves. Second trap: claiming P&I covers loss of hire or damage to the member's own ship. It does not - P&I covers liabilities, not the owner's own losses. Third: writing limb (c) as "tell the club and they pay". It is the largest limb at six marks, and what the club actually supplies is control and credit - a lawyer and surveyor on the quay, and a letter of undertaking that lifts an arrest without cash. Fourth: quoting pool or reinsurance figures, which are reset every policy year.
