retrieval_cards.prompt: What is a P&I club, and why does the word "mutual" matter?
retrieval_cards.answer: A mutual association of shipowners, charterers and operators covering the third-party liabilities arising from operating their ships. The members are the club - no external shareholders and no profit extracted, so a surplus is retained for them and a deficit is met by them. That single fact produces everything else: calls not premiums (a call can be adjusted after the event), no fixed sum insured (the liability incurred is what is covered), and very wide cover extensible by the board's omnibus discretion.
retrieval_cards.why: Every feature of the cover is derivable from mutuality. Answering from that one word makes the rest of the limb reconstructable rather than memorised.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How does a club collect funds? Give the tiers.
retrieval_cards.answer: Advance call - on entry for the policy year, assessed on entered tonnage and rated for ship type, trade, crew terms and above all the member's claims record. Supplementary call - if claims and expenses exceed advance calls plus investment income; the mutual mechanism working as designed, not a penalty. Release call - on leaving, buying out future supplementary calls on policy years still open because liability claims take years to mature. Deductible - the member's first amount on every claim.
retrieval_cards.why: Half of limb (a) is 'how they collect fund', and the release call is the tier candidates cannot account for unless they know why years stay open.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What sits above the individual club?
retrieval_cards.answer: The club's own retention; then the International Group Pooling Agreement, under which claims above that retention are shared among the participating clubs; then the Group's collective reinsurance placed in the market; and above that an overspill layer met by the members through an overspill call. This is why liability cover of a magnitude no ordinary insurer would write is available at all. No figures - retentions and layers are reset every policy year.
retrieval_cards.why: It answers the obvious oral follow-up - how can a mutual of shipowners possibly pay for a major pollution casualty?

retrieval_cards.prompt: Divide the risks between "protection" and "indemnity".
retrieval_cards.answer: Protection = people and the world. Crew injury, illness and death; stevedores, pilots and passengers; the collision liability the hull policy's three-fourths leaves; fixed and floating objects; pollution and clean-up; wreck removal; stowaways; quarantine; fines so far as the rules permit; legal costs. Indemnity = cargo. Loss, damage, shortage and contamination of cargo; cargo's proportion of general average unrecoverable through the owner's breach; liabilities under approved bills of lading.
retrieval_cards.why: The marks in limb (b) are for putting risks on the correct side of the line, not for the length of the list.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Does P&I cover your loss of hire, or damage to your own ship?
retrieval_cards.answer: Neither. Damage to the member's own ship is the hull and machinery policy's subject. Delay and loss of hire after a casualty is the owner's own trading loss - not a liability to anyone - and falls to a separate loss-of-hire cover if it was bought. War risks are separately insured too. The governing principle: P&I covers liabilities, not the owner's own losses.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the commonest misconception on the topic, and the MIW corpus flags it by name.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does the club actually do when a claim arises?
retrieval_cards.answer: Three things an ordinary insurer does not. It takes control of the defence - appointing lawyers and surveyors, with the member forbidden to admit liability or settle. It works through worldwide correspondents, who attend the ship, take statements while the crew are aboard, and arrange joint surveys. And it provides security - a letter of undertaking promising to satisfy any judgment, which prevents or lifts an arrest without a cash deposit.
retrieval_cards.why: What the club really sells is control and credit, not money. That reframing is what makes the six-mark limb worth six marks.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Set out the procedure for filing a claim.
retrieval_cards.answer: Notify immediately - club and correspondent, on suspicion rather than certainty, because late notice can defeat the claim. Preserve evidence at once - logs, engine data, Oil Record Book, crew statements, photographs, cargo records. Arrange survey, jointly where a third party is involved. Admit nothing and settle nothing. Submit the formal claim with documents. Request security if arrest threatens. Settlement follows, less the deductible, with recovery by subrogation.
retrieval_cards.why: Nine steps in the order they actually happen. Most claims that fail on the facts fail because nobody took the evidence in the first twenty-four hours.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the Indian statutory hook on this question?
retrieval_cards.answer: The Admiralty (Jurisdiction and Settlement of Maritime Claims) Act, 2017 lists at section 4(1)(s) "insurance premium (including mutual insurance calls)" among the maritime claims for which a vessel may be arrested in rem under section 5 - so an unpaid call can put the ship under arrest. Section 11 protects against wrongful arrest. The Marine Insurance Act, 1963 supplies utmost good faith and subrogation. Both were in force at this sitting; the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 commenced 15 March 2026 and has no application here.
retrieval_cards.why: One sentence naming an Indian statute that recognises the exact mechanism just described is worth more in an Indian examination than another paragraph on mutuality.

blocks.p: It is worth opening with the distinction, because the paper puts salvage and general average in one question and candidates blur them. Both arise from the same casualty and they answer different questions. Salvage asks: what does the outsider who saved the property get paid? General average asks: how do the owners of the property that was saved share the cost between themselves? One is a reward to a stranger; the other is an apportionment among the adventure. They also differ in source - salvage is convention and law, general average is contract.

blocks.h: 2. Limb A - the principles of modern salvage law

blocks.p: Modern salvage law is governed by the International Convention on Salvage, 1989, in force 14 July 1996, which replaced the 1910 Brussels Convention. Its principles are:

ol: Voluntariness. The service must be given voluntarily - there must be no pre-existing duty to render it. A tug under a towage contract, a crew member doing his job, or a State body under a public duty is not a salvor for these purposes.
Real danger. The property must be in danger. The danger need not be immediate or absolute, but it must be real and not fanciful.

Maritime property. The subject must be a vessel or other property in navigable waters, and the salvage must be of property rather than of life alone. Life salvage attracts no reward of itself, but a life salvor shares in a reward payable for the property saved in the same operation.

No cure, no pay - Article 12. A salvage operation that has had a useful result gives a right to a reward; one that has not gives no payment. This is the foundation of the whole regime and it is what makes salvage a commercial risk rather than a service contract.

The reward is fixed on criteria, and is capped - Article 13. The reward is assessed on ten listed criteria in sub-paragraphs (a) to (j): the salved value of the vessel and property; the skill and efforts of the salvors in preventing or minimising damage to the environment; the measure of success; the nature and degree of the danger; the skill and efforts in salving the vessel, other property and life; the time used and expenses and losses incurred; the risk of liability and other risks run; the promptness of the services; the availability and use of vessels or other equipment intended for salvage; and the state of readiness and efficiency of the salvor's equipment and its value. The reward may not exceed the salved value of the vessel and other property.

Encouragement of environmental protection - Article 14. Where a salvor has carried out operations on a vessel which by herself or her cargo threatened damage to the environment, and has failed to earn a reward at least equivalent to the special compensation, he is entitled to special compensation from the shipowner equivalent to his expenses. If he has actually prevented or minimised environmental damage, that may be increased by up to 30 per cent of his expenses, and a tribunal may go to a maximum of 100 per cent. This is the deliberate qualification of no cure no pay: a salvor who protects the environment and saves nothing is not left unpaid.

Duties run both ways - Article 8. The salvor must carry out the operation with due care, exercise due care to prevent or minimise damage to the environment, seek assistance from other salvors where reasonably required, and accept the intervention of other salvors when reasonably requested. The owner and master must co-operate fully with the salvor, exercise the same environmental due care, and accept redelivery when the property is brought to a place of safety.

Freedom of contract, subject to control. Parties are free to agree salvage terms, but an agreement may be annulled or modified where it was entered into under undue influence or the influence of danger and its terms are inequitable, or where the payment is excessively large or small for the services actually rendered.

blocks.p: In practice these principles are delivered through Lloyd's Open Form, the standard no cure no pay salvage agreement, which allows a master to engage a salvor in minutes without negotiating terms and refers the reward to arbitration afterwards. Attached to it, the SCOPIC clause supplies a contractual alternative to Article 14: instead of arguing about actual expenses after the event, the salvor may invoke SCOPIC and be remunerated on an agreed tariff with an uplift, backed by security from the owner's P&I club. Article 14 remains the legal fallback; SCOPIC is how the market avoids litigating it.

blocks.h: 3. Limb B - what general average is

blocks.p: General average is the ancient principle that where a sacrifice or expenditure is made intentionally and reasonably for the common safety of the maritime adventure, the loss is shared rateably by all the interests that were saved by it. It is older than insurance and it survives because it removes a perverse incentive: without it, the master would hesitate to jettison one shipper's cargo to save the rest, and the shipper whose cargo happened to be nearest the hatch would bear the whole loss of a decision taken for everyone's benefit.
Rule A of the York-Antwerp Rules gives the definition, and it is best written as five elements every one of which must be present:

rows: Extraordinary
The sacrifice or expenditure is outside the ordinary course of the voyage
Bunkers burned on a normal passage; ordinary wear; anything the ship was going to do anyway
Intentional
It is deliberately made, not merely suffered
Cargo washed overboard by a sea. Cargo jettisoned by decision is general average
Reasonable
It is a reasonable response in the circumstances as they appeared
A grossly disproportionate or panicked act
For the common safety
Made to preserve the whole adventure from peril, not one interest
An act benefiting only the ship, or only one parcel of cargo
Property preserved
Something must in fact be saved - there must be a fund to contribute
A total loss. If nothing is saved, there is nothing to apportion

blocks.p: Classic examples: jettison of cargo to refloat a grounded ship; water damage to cargo from fighting a fire in the hold; deliberate beaching to prevent foundering; the cost of engaging salvors; damage to machinery from working engines hard in a refloating attempt; and the expenses of putting into a port of refuge.

One point of law that must be stated because it explains everything in limb C: the York-Antwerp Rules are not law. They are a set of rules produced by the Comite Maritime International and they apply only because the bill of lading or charterparty incorporates them. Which edition applies is therefore a question of what the contract says, and editions differ in substance. In Indian law, general average is recognised by section 66 of the Marine Insurance Act, 1963, which is what makes it enforceable domestically rather than merely contractual.
Entitlement is the question of who may claim and who must contribute.

ul: The party who made the sacrifice or incurred the expenditure is entitled to a contribution from the other interests saved.

The contributing interests are ship, cargo and freight at risk - and, where applicable, bunkers and containers owned separately. Each contributes in proportion to the contributory value of its property at the termination of the adventure, not at the time of the act - so a cargo that has deteriorated for other reasons contributes on its arrived value.
The party who sacrificed also contributes on the value of what it saved, so it does not recover the whole of its loss - it recovers all but its own share.
The loss must be the direct consequence of the general average act. Indirect losses - demurrage, market loss, loss of the voyage - are excluded.

Actionable fault defeats the claim. A party whose fault caused the peril cannot recover a general average contribution from those who could sue him for that fault. This is the most important defence in the subject, and it is why a general average declaration after an engine-room fire is so often disputed: if the fire arose from unseaworthiness for which the owner is answerable, the owner's claim can fail entirely.

Security: the shipowner has a lien on the cargo for its general average contribution and will not release it without security. In practice cargo interests provide an average bond from the receiver together with an average guarantee from their cargo underwriter, or a cash deposit where there is no insurance. That is the mechanism by which the cargo actually leaves the terminal.

blocks.p: State the honest position first: "artificial general average" is practitioner terminology and is not a term defined in the York-Antwerp Rules. Saying so is worth a mark; presenting it as a defined category is a small but real error.

What it describes is this. Rule A sets a strict test - the act must be for the common safety. But the numbered Rules that follow expressly allow certain further items into general average which do not satisfy that strict test, because they are incurred for the common benefit of completing the adventure rather than to escape an immediate peril. Practitioners call those allowances artificial general average, or general average by convention, because they are general average by the agreement of the Rules rather than by the principle.

The standard examples all arise at a port of refuge. Once the ship is safely in the port, the immediate peril has passed - so the cost of discharging, storing and reloading cargo to permit repairs, the port charges, and the wages and maintenance of the crew during the detention are not common-safety expenditure at all. The adventure is no longer in danger; it is merely interrupted. The numbered Rules nonetheless allow them, because the alternative is to abandon the voyage and leave everyone worse off. The same reasoning supports temporary repairs made to enable the voyage to be completed, and the cost of substituting a cheaper expense for an allowable one.

The practical significance, and the reason candidates should understand rather than memorise this, is that artificial general average is where most of the money usually is. The jettison is dramatic and cheap; the four months in a port of refuge, with crew wages, storage and reloading, is undramatic and expensive. It is also the part most often argued about, and the part where the edition of the Rules incorporated by the contract matters most, because successive editions have moved these allowances in and out.
Adjustment is the process of turning a casualty into a set of numbers, and it is done by an average adjuster.

ul: The adjuster is appointed by the shipowner but is required to act impartially between all the interests. That combination - paid by one party, neutral between all - is the single most misunderstood feature of the role, and stating it correctly is worth a mark.
He does not declare general average; the shipowner declares it. He does not decide liability either; questions of fault and of the contract of carriage are for the courts or arbitrators.
He determines which losses and expenses are allowable under the applicable edition of the Rules, and on what basis they are valued.
He ascertains the contributory values of ship, cargo and freight at the termination of the adventure.
He calculates the rate of contribution and apportions the general average fund between the interests.
He collects the securities - average bonds, guarantees and deposits - and issues the general average statement, which sets out the allowances, the values, the apportionment and each party's balance.
Adjustment is slow. A statement can take years on a major casualty, because contributory values cannot be fixed until the cargo is delivered and its arrived value known.

blocks.p: Contestation is the challenging of the adjustment, and the first point is the one that makes it possible at all: the general average statement is evidence, not a judgment. The adjuster has no judicial authority. A party who disputes the statement is not appealing against a decision; it is declining to accept a document. Grounds of challenge fall into five groups:

ol: There was no general average act. The sacrifice was not extraordinary, or not intentional, or not reasonable, or not made for the common safety - one of Rule A's elements fails.
The allowance is not permitted under the applicable Rules, or the wrong edition has been applied - which is a live argument precisely because the Rules are contractual and editions differ.
The values or the apportionment are wrong - contributory values misstated, the wrong basis of valuation used, or arithmetical error.

Actionable fault. The most powerful ground: the peril was caused by the fault of the party claiming - typically unseaworthiness for which the shipowner is answerable and which is not excepted under the contract of carriage. If it succeeds, the claim can fail entirely, not merely in part.
The claim is time-barred, or the security was given under protest and its terms are not met.

blocks.p: Resolution follows the contract: negotiation between the adjuster and the underwriters first, which settles the great majority; then arbitration where the bill of lading or charterparty so provides; and litigation in the agreed forum where it does not. Cargo underwriters are the real parties in interest on the cargo side, and it is usually they, rather than the receivers, who contest.

The connection worth making at the end, because it shows the question was read as one question rather than two: the salvage award is itself a general average expenditure. Money paid to salvors to save the whole adventure is extraordinary, intentional, reasonable and for the common safety, so it goes into general average and is shared between ship, cargo and freight - which is why the same casualty produces a salvage arbitration and a general average adjustment running in parallel, and why the P&I club and the cargo underwriters end up providing security in both. In Indian law the general average side of that is anchored by section 66 of the Marine Insurance Act, 1963, and the domestic shipping statute at this examination is the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958.

4 + 4 + 8. The eight-mark limb is half the question and it has four named sub-items, so it needs four visible answers of roughly two marks each. That is the whole time-management problem here: candidates write beautifully on salvage, which they enjoy, and then give one paragraph to entitlement, artificial, adjustment and contestation combined. Budget half the answer for limb C before you start, and give each roman numeral its own heading.

Salvage asks what the outsider who saved the property gets paid. General average asks how the owners of the saved property share the cost between themselves. One is a reward to a stranger, the other an apportionment among the adventure. One is convention and law, the other is contract. Two sentences, and the whole question is framed.

blocks.h: Limb A - the four Articles that carry it

rows: Duties - of the salvor, and of the owner and master
Duties run both ways
No useful result, no payment
No cure, no pay
Criteria for fixing the reward
Ten criteria, (a) to (j), capped at the salved value
Special compensation where the environment was threatened
Expenses, +30%, and up to 100% at a tribunal's discretion

blocks.p: Salvage Convention 1989, in force 14 July 1996, replacing the 1910 Brussels Convention. Those two dates and those four Articles are four marks' worth on their own.

blocks.h: Why Article 14 exists - say it in one line

blocks.p: Pure no cure no pay produced a perverse result: a salvor who spent a fortune preventing a spill from a ship that was ultimately lost got nothing, so salvors declined environmental casualties - which are exactly the ones society most wants attended. Article 14 pays his expenses, with an uplift for success in protecting the environment. SCOPIC is then the market's way of avoiding an argument about what those expenses were: an agreed tariff with an uplift, invoked by the salvor and secured by the owner's club. Article 14 is the law; SCOPIC is the practice.

blocks.h: Rule A - five elements, and lose one and it fails

blocks.p: EXTRAORDINARY - INTENTIONAL - REASONABLE - COMMON SAFETY - SOMETHING SAVED. Every one must be present. Learn the failure case for each: bunkers burned on a normal passage is not extraordinary; cargo washed overboard is not intentional (cargo jettisoned is); a panicked disproportionate act is not reasonable; an act benefiting only the ship is not for the common safety; and a total loss leaves no fund to apportion.

blocks.h: The honesty point that earns a mark

blocks.p: "Artificial general average" is not a term defined in the York-Antwerp Rules. It is practitioner terminology for allowances the numbered Rules permit on a common-benefit basis although they fail Rule A's strict common-safety test - port of refuge expenses, crew wages and maintenance during detention, discharging, storing and reloading to permit repairs, temporary repairs, substituted expenses. Say it is not a defined term, then explain what it describes. Presenting it as a defined category of the Rules is a small error that a good examiner will notice.

blocks.h: And the practical point behind it

blocks.p: Artificial general average is where most of the money usually is. The jettison is dramatic and cheap; four months in a port of refuge with crew wages, storage and reloading is undramatic and expensive. It is also where the edition of the Rules matters most, because successive editions have moved these allowances in and out.

blocks.h: The adjuster - what he is and is not

ul: Appointed by the shipowner, but acts impartially between all interests. State both halves.
He does not declare general average - the shipowner does.
He does not decide liability - fault and contract questions are for courts or arbitrators.
He decides allowances under the applicable edition, ascertains contributory values at the termination of the adventure, apportions, collects securities and issues the statement.

blocks.h: Actionable fault - the answer to two sub-items at once

blocks.p: A party whose fault caused the peril cannot recover a general average contribution from those who could sue him for it. It appears under entitlement as the thing that defeats the claim, and again under contestation as the most powerful ground of challenge - and if it succeeds the claim can fail entirely, not merely in part. Using it in both places, and saying it is the same point, is efficient and shows the four sub-items are understood as one subject.

blocks.h: The security chain - know the three words

blocks.p: The shipowner has a lien on the cargo for its contribution. Cargo interests provide an average bond (from the receiver) plus an average guarantee (from the cargo underwriter), or a cash deposit where the cargo is uninsured. That is the mechanism by which cargo actually leaves the terminal, and it is the direct link to the P&I question on this same paper.

blocks.h: The York-Antwerp Rules are not law

blocks.p: They are Comite Maritime International rules that apply only because the bill of lading or charterparty incorporates them, and which edition applies is a question of what the contract says. In Indian law general average is recognised by section 66 of the Marine Insurance Act, 1963. Do not say "under the York-Antwerp Rules it is the law that..." - it is not.

ul: Confusing salvage with general average, or treating them as one doctrine.
Giving no cure no pay without Article 14 - and so missing why the environmental exception exists at all.
Saying salvage requires a contract. It does not; it requires voluntariness, danger and a useful result.
Losing an element of Rule A, usually 'extraordinary' or 'something must be saved'.
Saying cargo washed overboard is general average. Jettisoned is; washed is not.
Presenting 'artificial general average' as a defined term of the Rules.
Saying the adjuster declares general average, or that he decides liability.
Contributing on values at the time of the act rather than at the termination of the adventure.
Spending the answer on limb A and giving limb C - half the marks - a single paragraph.
"Can the reward exceed the salved value?" No - Article 13 caps it there.
"Is life salvage rewarded?" Not of itself; a life salvor shares in the reward payable for the property saved in the same operation.
"Your ship is under tow and gets into difficulty. Is the tug a salvor?" Only if the service goes beyond the towage contract - otherwise there is a pre-existing duty and no voluntariness.
"What is SCOPIC and why was it needed?" A contractual tariff-based alternative to arguing Article 14 expenses after the event, invoked by the salvor and secured by the owner's club.
"Who declares general average?" The shipowner. The adjuster adjusts it.
"Is the general average statement binding?" No - it is evidence, not a judgment.

"Give a general average act in your own engine room." Damage to main engine or auxiliaries from working them hard in a deliberate refloating attempt; or water damage from flooding a hold to fight a fire.
"What defeats a general average claim entirely?" Actionable fault - the peril was caused by the claimant's own fault, typically unseaworthiness for which the owner is answerable.
"Which edition of the York-Antwerp Rules applies?" The one the contract incorporates. There is no universal answer.
You are aground and the master signs Lloyd's Open Form. What happens next, and what do you do in the engine room?
General average has been declared. What does that mean for the cargo on your ship?
What is an average bond and who gives it?
Your engines are damaged refloating the ship. Is that general average, and who pays?
Why would the cargo underwriter contest the adjustment?
What is the difference between salvage and towage?

blocks.p: Two doctrines - four Articles - five elements - four sub-items. TWO DOCTRINES: salvage pays the stranger; GA shares among the adventure. FOUR ARTICLES: 8 duties, 12 no cure no pay, 13 ten criteria capped at salved value, 14 special compensation +30% up to 100%. FIVE ELEMENTS of Rule A: EXTRAORDINARY, INTENTIONAL, REASONABLE, COMMON SAFETY, SOMETHING SAVED. FOUR SUB-ITEMS: who pays (entitlement) - what counts (artificial) - who works it out (adjustment) - who argues (contestation).

ul: International Convention on Salvage, 1989, in force 14 July 1996 - Article 8 duties; Article 12 no useful result, no payment; Article 13 the ten criteria and the salved-value ceiling; Article 14 special compensation, 30 per cent and up to 100 per cent.
York-Antwerp Rules, Rule A - the general average act. Contractual, not law; the edition is whichever the bill of lading or charterparty incorporates.
The numbered Rules of the York-Antwerp Rules - the source of the allowances called artificial general average.
Marine Insurance Act, 1963 (India), section 66 - general average loss.
Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 (India) - the domestic shipping statute in force at this sitting.
Lloyd's Open Form and the SCOPIC clause - industry practice, not law.
LLMC 1976 / 1996 Protocol - the limitation regime that can cap what is ultimately recoverable.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: Three tasks, with the third carrying half the marks and four named sub-items. Limbs A and B are definitional and test whether the candidate can state a doctrine as a set of principles rather than as a story. Limb C is the discriminator: four practitioner-level terms - entitlement, artificial, adjustment, contestation - which test whether the candidate understands how a general average claim is actually processed and resisted, rather than what general average is in the abstract. 'Artificial' is the one most candidates cannot place at all.
decomposition_gate.mark_allocation: 16, set as 4 + 4 + 8. Printed marks are unambiguous. Limb C is half the paper and has four sub-items, so roughly two marks each - which means four separate headed answers, not one paragraph. The commonest failure on this question is a full answer to limbs A and B and a compressed limb C.

For C: who contributes and on what values, what actionable fault does, an honest account of artificial general average as a practitioner term, the adjuster's impartial but owner-appointed role and the fact that he neither declares GA nor decides liability, and the grounds on which a statement is contested.

questions.understand_first: A ship goes aground with cargo on board. Two entirely separate money questions arise from that one event, and the paper is asking about both. Question one: somebody outside the adventure - a salvage tug - came and pulled her off. What is he owed? That is salvage, and the answer is governed by an international convention with one dominant rule: if he achieves nothing, he is paid nothing. That rule is brutal and deliberate, because it makes the salvor carry the risk instead of the shipowner - and it produced one perverse consequence that had to be fixed, which is that a salvor who spent everything preventing a spill from a ship that sank anyway got nothing at all. Article 14 fixes that. Question two: the ship's owner and the twelve cargo owners were all in this adventure together. Getting off the ground cost money and destroyed some property. Who bears it? That is general average, and the answer is that everyone who was saved pays a share, in proportion to what they saved. The principle is ancient and it exists to stop the master hesitating: if he must jettison one shipper's cargo to save the rest, that shipper should not bear the whole loss of a decision taken for everybody. Then limb C is simply the four practical stages of making that sharing happen: who pays (entitlement), what counts (artificial), who works out the numbers (adjustment), and who argues about them (contestation). And the two halves of the question meet at the end - what you paid the salvor is itself a general average expenditure, shared by everyone he saved.

steps.title: Two doctrines, two questions
points: Salvage: what does the outsider who saved the property get paid?
General average: how do the owners of the saved property share the cost between themselves?
Reward to a stranger against apportionment among the adventure
Convention and law against contract

steps.title: Limb A - the principles of modern salvage law
points: Salvage Convention 1989, in force 14 July 1996, replacing the Brussels Convention 1910
Voluntariness - no pre-existing duty; a tug under a towage contract or a crew member is not a salvor
Real danger - need not be immediate, but must be real not fanciful
Maritime property - life salvage attracts no reward of itself, but a life salvor shares in the property reward
Article 12 - no cure, no pay: a useful result gives a right to a reward, no result gives nothing

Article 13 - ten criteria (a) to (j): salved value, environmental skill and efforts, measure of success, danger, skill in salving, time and expenses, risk of liability, promptness, availability of equipment, readiness and value of equipment. Capped at the salved value
Article 14 - special compensation where the environment was threatened: expenses, plus up to 30 per cent, and up to 100 per cent at a tribunal's discretion
Article 8 - duties both ways: salvor's due care and environmental care; owner and master to co-operate and accept redelivery
Freedom of contract, subject to annulment for undue influence or inequitable terms
In practice: Lloyd's Open Form, and SCOPIC as the tariff-based contractual alternative to arguing Article 14

steps.title: Limb B - what general average is
points: Sacrifice or expenditure made intentionally and reasonably for the common safety, shared rateably by all interests saved
Why it exists: it stops the master hesitating, and stops one shipper bearing a loss taken for everyone
Rule A - five elements: extraordinary, intentional, reasonable, for the common safety, and property preserved
Give the failure case for each - washed overboard is not intentional; jettisoned is
Examples: jettison, water damage fighting a fire, deliberate beaching, engaging salvors, machinery damage refloating, port of refuge expenses
The Rules are NOT law - CMI rules incorporated by the bill of lading or charterparty; the edition depends on the contract
In India, recognised by section 66 of the Marine Insurance Act, 1963

steps.title: Limb C(i) - Entitlement
points: The party who sacrificed or spent is entitled to a contribution from the interests saved
Contributors: ship, cargo and freight at risk, on contributory values at the termination of the adventure
The sacrificing party contributes too - it recovers all but its own share
The loss must be the direct consequence; demurrage and market loss are excluded
Actionable fault defeats the claim - the party whose fault caused the peril cannot recover from those who could sue him
Security: lien on cargo, discharged by an average bond from the receiver plus an average guarantee from the cargo underwriter, or a cash deposit

steps.title: Limb C(ii) - Artificial general average
points: Say first that it is practitioner terminology, NOT defined in the Rules
It describes allowances the numbered Rules permit on a common-benefit basis although they fail Rule A's strict common-safety test
Standard examples all arise at a port of refuge - the peril has passed, the adventure is interrupted not endangered
Discharging, storing and reloading cargo to permit repairs; port charges; crew wages and maintenance during detention; temporary repairs; substituted expenses
The practical point: this is where most of the money usually is - the jettison is cheap, four months in a port of refuge is not
And where the edition of the Rules matters most, because editions have moved these allowances in and out

steps.title: Limb C(iii) - Adjustment
points: The average adjuster - appointed by the shipowner but acting impartially between all interests
He does NOT declare general average - the shipowner does
He does NOT decide liability - fault and contract are for courts or arbitrators
He determines allowances under the applicable edition and their valuation
He ascertains contributory values at the termination of the adventure
He calculates the rate and apportions, collects bonds, guarantees and deposits
He issues the general average statement - allowances, values, apportionment, balances
It is slow: values cannot be fixed until cargo is delivered and its arrived value known

steps.title: Limb C(iv) - Contestation
points: The statement is evidence, not a judgment - the adjuster has no judicial authority
Ground 1 - no general average act: not extraordinary, intentional, reasonable, or for the common safety
Ground 2 - the allowance is not permitted, or the wrong edition applied
Ground 3 - values or apportionment wrong - misstated contributory values, wrong basis, arithmetic
Ground 4 - actionable fault: the peril was the claimant's own fault. Can defeat the claim entirely
Ground 5 - time bar, or security given under protest whose terms are not met
Resolution: negotiation with underwriters first, then arbitration or litigation per the contract
Cargo underwriters, not receivers, are usually the real contestants

steps.title: Where the two doctrines meet
points: The salvage award is itself a general average expenditure - extraordinary, intentional, reasonable, for the common safety
So one casualty produces a salvage arbitration and a GA adjustment in parallel
And the P&I club and the cargo underwriters provide security in both - link to Q7
Indian anchor: section 66 Marine Insurance Act, 1963; domestic statute the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958

questions.memory_cue: Two doctrines, four Articles, five elements, four sub-items. DOCTRINES: salvage pays the stranger, GA shares among the adventure (1). ARTICLES: 8 duties, 12 no cure no pay, 13 ten criteria capped at salved value, 14 special compensation +30% up to 100% (2). RULE A: EXTRAORDINARY, INTENTIONAL, REASONABLE, COMMON SAFETY, SOMETHING SAVED (3). LIMB C: who pays (4), what counts (5), who calculates (6), who argues (7).

quick_revision.recall_15s: Salvage - International Convention on Salvage, 1989, in force 14 July 1996. Principles: the service must be voluntary (no pre-existing duty), the property in real danger, and under Article 12 there is no cure, no pay - a useful result earns a reward, no result earns nothing. Article 13 fixes the reward on ten criteria and caps it at the salved value. Article 14 gives special compensation where the environment was threatened - expenses, plus up to 30 per cent, and up to 100 per cent at a tribunal's discretion. Article 8 imposes duties both ways. In practice: Lloyd's Open Form with SCOPIC as the tariff alternative to Article 14. General average - Rule A of the York-Antwerp Rules: an extraordinary, intentional, reasonable sacrifice or expenditure for the common safety, with property preserved, shared rateably. The Rules are contractual, not law; India recognises GA at section 66, Marine Insurance Act, 1963. Entitlement: ship, cargo and freight contribute on contributory values at the termination of the adventure; actionable fault defeats the claim; security by average bond and guarantee against the owner's lien. Artificial GA: not a defined term - practitioner shorthand for common-benefit allowances the numbered Rules permit though they fail Rule A's common-safety test, chiefly port of refuge expenses and crew wages. Adjustment: the average adjuster, appointed by the owner but impartial, does not declare GA and does not decide liability; he fixes allowances and values and issues the statement. Contestation: the statement is evidence, not a judgment - challenge on no GA act, allowance not permitted or wrong edition, wrong values, actionable fault, or time bar.
critical_numbers: Salvage Convention 1989, in force 14 July 1996, replacing the Brussels Convention 1910
Article 13 - TEN criteria, sub-paragraphs (a) to (j); the reward may not exceed the SALVED VALUE
Article 14 - special compensation: expenses, increased by up to 30 per cent, and to a maximum of 100 per cent
Rule A - FIVE elements, all of which must be present
Contributory values are taken at the TERMINATION OF THE ADVENTURE, not at the time of the act
Marine Insurance Act, 1963 section 66 - general average loss in Indian law
NO salvage award, percentage of salved value, SCOPIC tariff rate or security figure is quoted
quick_revision.critical_regulation: Salvage Convention 1989 Articles 12, 13 and 14 carry the whole of limb A - no cure no pay, the ten criteria capped at salved value, and the environmental exception that qualifies the first. York-Antwerp Rule A carries limb B, and it must be introduced as CONTRACTUAL rather than legal, because that single fact is what makes limb C(ii) and the wrong-edition ground in limb C(iv) intelligible.
quick_revision.major_trap: Spending the answer on salvage, which candidates enjoy, and compressing limb C - which is half the marks and has four named sub-items needing four separate answers. Second trap: presenting "artificial general average" as a term defined in the York-Antwerp Rules. It is not - it is practitioner shorthand for common-benefit allowances the numbered Rules permit although they fail Rule A's common-safety test. Say so, and gain the mark the error costs. Third: saying the adjuster declares general average - the shipowner declares it, and the adjuster neither declares it nor decides liability. Fourth: taking contributory values at the time of the act rather than at the termination of the adventure. Fifth: treating the York-Antwerp Rules as law, when they apply only because the contract incorporates them - which is also why "which edition?" is a real question. Sixth, specific to this sitting: reaching for the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025, which commenced 15 March 2026, twenty-one months after this examination.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the salvage and general average question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 Frame the two doctrines. 2 Limb A - principles of salvage. 3 Limb B - what general average is, with Rule A. 4 C(i) Entitlement. 5 C(ii) Artificial. 6 C(iii) Adjustment. 7 C(iv) Contestation. 8 Where the two meet - the salvage award is itself a GA expenditure.
retrieval_cards.why: Limb C is half the marks and has four named sub-items. One headed section each is the only way to make all four visible.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the difference between salvage and general average?
retrieval_cards.answer: Salvage asks what the outsider who saved the property is paid - a reward to a stranger, governed by the Salvage Convention 1989. General average asks how the owners of the property that was saved share the cost between themselves - an apportionment among the adventure, governed by the York-Antwerp Rules, which are contract, not law. Both arise from the same casualty and they answer different questions.
retrieval_cards.why: Two sentences that frame the whole answer and stop the two doctrines being blurred, which is the commonest structural failure here.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Limb A - state the principles of modern salvage law.
retrieval_cards.answer: Salvage Convention 1989, in force 14 July 1996. Voluntariness - no pre-existing duty. Real danger to maritime property. Article 12 no cure, no pay - a useful result earns a reward, no result earns nothing. Article 13 - ten criteria, capped at the salved value. Article 14 - special compensation where the environment was threatened: expenses, plus up to 30 per cent, and 100 per cent at a tribunal's discretion. Article 8 - duties both ways. In practice, Lloyd's Open Form with SCOPIC.
retrieval_cards.why: Four Articles carry four marks. Naming them with their effects is more efficient than any narrative.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why does Article 14 exist?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because pure no cure no pay produced a perverse result: a salvor who spent a fortune preventing a spill from a ship that was ultimately lost recovered nothing, so salvors declined the environmental casualties society most wanted attended. Article 14 pays his expenses, increased by up to 30 per cent - and 100 per cent at a tribunal's discretion - where he prevented or minimised damage. SCOPIC is the market's contractual alternative: an agreed tariff with an uplift, secured by the owner's club.
retrieval_cards.why: Explaining why a rule exists is worth more than stating it, and it sets up the SCOPIC point which is the standard oral follow-up.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State Rule A - the five elements of a general average act.
retrieval_cards.answer: EXTRAORDINARY - outside the ordinary course of the voyage. INTENTIONAL - deliberately made, not merely suffered. REASONABLE - a proportionate response in the circumstances as they appeared. FOR THE COMMON SAFETY - to preserve the whole adventure from peril, not one interest. PROPERTY PRESERVED - something must in fact be saved, or there is no fund to apportion. All five must be present.
retrieval_cards.why: Learn the failure case for each: bunkers on a normal passage is not extraordinary; cargo washed overboard is not intentional, cargo jettisoned is; a total loss leaves nothing to share.

retrieval_cards.prompt: C(i) - who contributes to general average, and on what values?
retrieval_cards.answer: Ship, cargo and freight at risk, each in proportion to its contributory value at the termination of the adventure - not at the time of the act. The party who sacrificed also contributes, so it recovers all but its own share. The loss must be the direct consequence; demurrage and market loss are excluded. Actionable fault defeats the claim. The owner has a lien on the cargo, released against an average bond plus an average guarantee.
retrieval_cards.why: The timing of the valuation and the security chain are both routinely asked, and the security chain is the direct link to the P&I question.

retrieval_cards.prompt: C(ii) - what is "artificial general average"?
retrieval_cards.answer: It is practitioner terminology and is NOT a term defined in the York-Antwerp Rules - say that first. It describes allowances the numbered Rules permit on a common-benefit basis although they fail Rule A's strict common-safety test. The examples arise at a port of refuge: discharging, storing and reloading cargo, port charges, crew wages and maintenance during detention, temporary repairs. In practice this is where most of the money is.
retrieval_cards.why: The sub-item most candidates cannot place at all, and the honesty about it being undefined is itself worth a mark.

retrieval_cards.prompt: C(iii) - what does the average adjuster do, and what does he not do?
retrieval_cards.answer: Appointed by the shipowner but required to act impartially between all interests. He determines which losses and expenses are allowable under the applicable edition and how they are valued, ascertains the contributory values at the termination of the adventure, calculates the rate and apportions, collects bonds, guarantees and deposits, and issues the general average statement. He does NOT declare general average - the shipowner does - and he does NOT decide liability; fault and contract questions are for courts or arbitrators.
retrieval_cards.why: 'Appointed by one party, neutral between all' is the single most misunderstood feature of the role, and the two things he does not do are standard traps.

retrieval_cards.prompt: C(iv) - on what grounds is an adjustment contested?
retrieval_cards.answer: Starting from the fact that the statement is evidence, not a judgment: (1) there was no general average act - one of Rule A's elements fails; (2) the allowance is not permitted, or the wrong edition was applied; (3) the values or apportionment are wrong; (4) actionable fault, which can defeat the claim entirely; (5) time bar. Resolved by negotiation with the underwriters, then arbitration or litigation.
retrieval_cards.why: Five grounds for two marks, and actionable fault is the same point that appears under entitlement - using it twice shows the four sub-items are one subject.

questions.verification_status: Authored on the QP2411-Q9 route with the interpretation and corrective-measures material written fresh for this sitting's enlarged stem, and with the donor's evidential discipline inherited whole. This is instrumental analysis and machinery condition monitoring: NO IMO OR STATUTORY INSTRUMENT PRESCRIBES A LUBRICATING OIL ANALYSIS PROGRAMME, and none is named, so the answer does not borrow authority from an unrelated instrument. The techniques are described at mechanism level and carried as engineering and analytical-chemistry reference: atomic emission spectrometry by plasma or rotating-disc electrode; the particle-size limitation arising from incomplete atomisation of large particles in the excitation source; infrared absorption at characteristic wavenumbers with Fourier transformation of the interferogram and differential comparison against the unused oil; particle counting by optical light obscuration, pore blockage or microscopy, reported in cumulative size bands; and Base Number and Acid Number as separate titrations expressed in milligrammes of potassium hydroxide per gramme. THE NO-FIGURES RULE IS ABSOLUTE AND IS THE MOST IMPORTANT EVIDENTIAL FEATURE OF THIS ANSWER: no condemning limit, alarm level, ppm value, ISO cleanliness code, base number figure or wear rate is quoted as a general rule anywhere, because every one is engine-builder, oil, application and service specific, and a figure carried between installations is a genuine hazard as well as an evidential defect. No standard number is asserted for either Base Number titration method; the two methods are distinguished by their chemistry and by the direction of the discrepancy between them. No oil company, analyser manufacturer, engine builder, laboratory or proprietary condition-monitoring programme is named. The single dated fact is the 0.50 per cent m/m global sulphur limit for fuel outside emission control areas, in force since 1 January 2020, four and a half years before this sitting, used only to explain cylinder oil base number selection; no MARPOL Annex VI provision is quoted or numbered, consistent with the corpus holding that Annex as citation-ready only.

blocks.h: 1. Why the oil is analysed, and what the four techniques are for

blocks.p: Used lubricating oil is the only sample on the ship that has been in continuous contact with every working surface in the machine. Everything that wears, everything that leaks in, and every change in the oil itself is carried in it. That is why oil analysis is the foundation of condition-based maintenance rather than an adjunct to it.

The four techniques in this question are not four ways of doing the same thing. They answer three separate questions, and seeing that before describing any of them is what makes the rest of the answer coherent:

rows: Is the machine wearing?
Elemental spectrometry and particle count
Is the oil still fit for service?
FTIR, and Base Number and Acid Number
Is anything getting in?
All four, from different directions

blocks.p: And one rule governs the use of every one of them: the trend against the machine's own history matters more than any single value. An absolute number means very little without knowing where that machine normally sits.

Principle. A measured sample is excited - in a plasma, or across a rotating-disc electrode arc. Excited atoms of each element emit light at wavelengths characteristic of that element, and the intensity at each wavelength is proportional to the concentration of that element present. The instrument reads many elements simultaneously and reports each in parts per million.
What the elements mean. They sort into three families, and reading them as families rather than as a list is what turns a report into a diagnosis:

rows: Wear metals
Iron; copper, lead and tin; chromium; aluminium; silver; nickel

Iron from liners, rings, gears and shafts. Copper, lead and tin from bearings and bushes. Chromium from rings and plated surfaces. Aluminium from pistons and some bearings. Each points at a different part of the machine
Contaminants
Silicon; sodium and boron; vanadium and nickel; water-related indicators

Silicon from airborne dirt through a defective filter or seal - and it is abrasive. Sodium and boron from coolant leakage. Vanadium and nickel from residual fuel, so their presence indicates fuel dilution
Additive elements
Calcium and magnesium; zinc and phosphorus; barium

Calcium and magnesium from detergent and dispersant additives; zinc and phosphorus from anti-wear additives. A falling trend means additive depletion; a rising one usually means the wrong oil has been added

blocks.p: Silicon deserves a note of its own because it is read two ways: dirt ingress, but also silicone antifoam or sealant residue after an overhaul. A single high silicon result shortly after a major job is usually the second; a rising trend in service is the first, and the first is serious because silicon is abrasive.

blocks.h: 3. What spectrometry cannot see - and why that governs its use

blocks.p: This is the most important qualification in the whole question and it is regularly omitted. The method depends on the complete atomisation of the particles in the excitation source. Large particles are not fully atomised, so the response falls away progressively with increasing particle size. In practice the technique reports essentially the fine fraction only.

The consequence is severe and must be stated plainly. Normal rubbing wear produces fine debris and is seen well. Bearing fatigue, spalling, scuffing and gear pitting produce coarse debris and may not be seen at all. So a satisfactory spectrometric report is not evidence that the machine is healthy - it is evidence that the fine fraction is normal, which is a much weaker statement. This is precisely why particle count, ferrography and magnetic plug inspection must sit alongside it rather than being treated as alternatives to it.

Principle. An infrared beam is passed through a thin film of the oil. Molecular bonds absorb infrared energy at wavenumbers characteristic of the bond, so the absorption pattern is a fingerprint of what molecules are present. Rather than scanning one wavelength at a time, the instrument gathers all wavelengths at once as an interferogram and applies a Fourier transform to convert it into a spectrum - which is what makes the technique fast and what the name describes.

It is a differential measurement, and this is the point candidates miss. The spectrum of the used oil is compared against the spectrum of the same oil unused, and it is the difference that is reported. Without a new-oil reference the result is very much weaker - which is a practical instruction as well as a technical one: keep a retained sample of every new oil delivered.
What it detects, each at its own characteristic absorption region:

ul: Oxidation - at the carbonyl region, the principal measure of the oil's thermal and chemical ageing.
Nitration - from combustion products, characteristic of gas and dual-fuel engines in particular.
Sulphation - from sulphur oxides, and directly related to fuel sulphur and to the acid attack discussed at Q4 on this paper.
Water - at the hydroxyl region.
Soot - seen as a broad rise in the baseline rather than as a discrete peak, because soot scatters rather than absorbs selectively.
Fuel dilution, glycol ingress from coolant, and additive depletion.

blocks.p: Strengths and limits. It is fast, needs a very small sample, requires no reagents and returns several parameters at once, which makes it ideal for routine screening. But it is semi-quantitative - excellent at trends, weaker at absolute values - and it is blind to wear metals and to particles entirely. It tells you about the oil, not about the machine.

Principle. Solid particles suspended in the oil are counted and sized. The usual method is automatic optical light obscuration - the oil passes through a cell across a light beam and each particle casts a shadow whose magnitude gives its size. Where the oil is too dark or too heavily sooted for light to pass, pore-blockage methods are used instead, and microscopic counting remains the referee method.

Reporting. Results are given as counts per millilitre in cumulative size bands - the number of particles larger than each of several sizes - and those bands are condensed into a cleanliness code for trending and for specification. The ISO cleanliness code is the usual convention; no code or band table is reproduced here because MIW does not hold the standard, and in service the target code is set by the equipment manufacturer.

Why it matters. It is decisive for hydraulic, servo and control systems, where clearances are measured in microns and a particle population that is harmless in a crankcase will destroy a servo valve. It is also the direct measure of filtration and centrifuge performance and of ingress through seals and breathers - a rising count with unchanged wear metals usually means the filtration has failed, not that the machine has. And crucially it sees the large particles that spectrometry misses, which is why the two are complementary rather than alternative.

Limits. Optical counters count water droplets and air bubbles as particles, so a wet or aerated sample reads falsely high - the sample must be settled and, where necessary, the water content measured separately. And the technique says how many and how big, never what: it cannot distinguish steel from sand from soot.

blocks.h: 6. D) Base Number against Acid Number

blocks.p: These two are confused more often than any other pair in oil analysis, and for a good reason: both are titrations and both are reported in the same units - milligrammes of potassium hydroxide per gramme of oil. They are nonetheless separate measurements of opposite things.

rows: What it measures
The alkaline reserve conferred by overbased detergent additives
The quantity of acidic constituents present
Where it comes from
Deliberately formulated into the oil
Combustion products (sulphuric and nitric acids) and oxidation of the oil itself
Direction in service
FALLS as acid is neutralised and additive is consumed
RISES as acid accumulates
Units
mg KOH per gramme
mg KOH per gramme - the same units, which is why they are confused
What a bad value means
Alkaline reserve exhausted - the oil can no longer protect against acid attack
Acid is present and is attacking the metal, or the oil is heavily oxidised

blocks.p: Three points that separate a good answer:

ul: An oil can show a significant Base Number and a significant Acid Number at the same time. They are separate titrations of separate species, and weak organic acids can coexist with the alkaline reserve. Candidates who assume the two must be mutually exclusive misread every report of this kind.

Two standard titration methods for Base Number are in use, one employing a strongly acidic titrant and one a weaker one, and they give systematically different results on the same oil - the stronger method returning the higher value. Values from the two methods must never be trended together, and a change of laboratory or method can look exactly like a change in the oil.

Which number governs depends on the oil. For cylinder oils and trunk-piston engine oils, which carry a deliberate alkaline reserve to neutralise combustion acids, BN is the controlling parameter and is matched to the sulphur of the fuel actually burned. For turbine, hydraulic, gear and stern tube oils, which have no alkaline reserve at all, BN is meaningless and AN is the governing parameter - a rising AN is the direct measure of oxidative degradation.

blocks.p: On cylinder oils specifically, the relationship with fuel changed after the 0.50 per cent m/m global sulphur limit outside emission control areas took effect on 1 January 2020. Less sulphur means less acid and in principle a lower base number - but over-alkalinity is not a safe error either: unconsumed calcium detergent forms hard deposits which are abrasive and polish the liner. Base number is therefore matched to the fuel actually in use, and adjusted at fuel changeover.

blocks.h: 7. Correct interpretation - reading the four together

blocks.p: This is what the stem's opening sentence is asking for, and it is where the four techniques stop being a list. The rule is that no single result diagnoses anything; pairs and trends do.

rows: Iron rising, residual Base Number falling toward zero
Corrosive wear - the alkaline reserve is being consumed faster than it is supplied. In a cylinder, this is cold corrosion
High - this is the clearest signature in the subject
Iron rising, Base Number still healthy
Not corrosion. Look for abrasive ingress, scuffing, or a mechanical cause - and note that increasing the feed rate will make it worse
High
Wear metals normal, particle count rising sharply
Filtration or centrifuge failure, or ingress - the machine is not necessarily wearing more, the oil is simply not being cleaned
High
Particle count rising with wear metals normal AND spectrometry clean
Suspect coarse debris that spectrometry cannot see - bearing fatigue or spalling. Go physical immediately
Medium - and the most dangerous case, because the spectrometric report looks reassuring
Silicon rising with iron and chromium
Abrasive dirt ingress through a defective air filter, seal or breather, causing three-body abrasive wear
High
Silicon high alone, immediately after an overhaul
Silicone sealant or antifoam residue, not dirt. Re-sample before acting
High
Sodium and boron rising, FTIR showing glycol and water
Coolant leak. Find it before the bearings do - glycol is far more damaging to bearing metal than water alone
High
Vanadium and nickel present, FTIR showing fuel dilution, viscosity falling
Fuel dilution from leaking injection equipment or poor combustion
High
FTIR oxidation rising, Acid Number rising, no wear metals
The oil is degrading - overheating, over-extended drain interval, or air entrainment. The machine is fine; the oil is not
High
Copper, lead or tin rising alone
Bearing distress. Copper alone can also mean cooler-tube corrosion, so identify the source before condemning a bearing
Medium
Additive elements falling steadily
Additive depletion - the oil is at the end of its useful life
High
Additive elements rising
The wrong oil has been added. Check the topping-up records
High

blocks.p: Two interpretive disciplines govern all of it. First, trend, do not spot-read: a value is meaningful only against that machine's own history, on samples taken the same way from the same point. Second, rate of change matters more than level: a moderate iron figure that has doubled in a month is far more serious than a higher figure that has been stable for a year.

The stem asks for corrective measures, so the answer must say what is actually done. The general sequence on any adverse result is: verify the result, confirm it physically, correct the cause, and only then correct the oil.

ol: Verify before acting. Re-sample properly - same point, same method, machine at operating temperature and circulating - and re-test. A large proportion of alarming results are sampling artefacts, and shutting a machine down on a bad sample is an expensive mistake.

Confirm physically. Where wear is indicated, go and look: magnetic plugs and chip detectors, filter elements cut open and examined, centrifuge sludge, ferrography for particle morphology, and where accessible a direct inspection - scavenge ports, crankcase, gear teeth, bearing clearances. Ferrography is the technique that tells you the shape of the debris and therefore the wear mechanism, which no elemental figure can.

Treat abrasive ingress by finding the entry path - air filters, seals, breathers, hatch and cover joints - rather than by increasing filtration alone. Filtration removes the consequence; the seal is the cause.

Treat coolant leaks at once. Locate by pressure-testing coolers, jackets and covers. Glycol attacks bearing metals and forms sludge, and a coolant leak left running will destroy bearings long before the wear metals reach an alarm value.
Treat fuel dilution by attending to injection equipment, timing and combustion, and by checking for leakage past pumps and pipes. Then renew the oil - diluted oil cannot be recovered.

Treat water by locating the source - cooler leaks, condensation, steam coils, stern tube ingress - and by running the purifier correctly: right gravity disc, right throughput, right temperature. Water is the one contaminant the ship can usually remove itself.

Treat a rising particle count by checking and renewing filters, verifying filter differential pressure and bypass operation, and reviewing purifier and centrifuge operation - throughput, temperature, discharge interval. Then look for the ingress path.

Treat low Base Number in a cylinder oil by increasing the feed rate or moving to a higher-BN oil, matched to the fuel sulphur actually burned - and re-check by scrape-down analysis rather than assuming the change worked. Do the reverse if residual BN is high, because over-alkalinity deposits abrasive calcium ash.

Treat high Acid Number and high oxidation in a system oil by investigating the cause - overheating, air entrainment, contamination, an over-extended drain interval - then by partial or complete renewal, and by cleaning the system before recharging so the new oil is not immediately contaminated.
Treat additive depletion by renewal. Additives cannot be topped up in service and an attempt to do so usually creates incompatibility.

Record and close the loop. Every action taken, and the analysis result that follows it, goes into the machine's history under the planned maintenance system. Unrecorded corrective action is indistinguishable from no corrective action, and it destroys the trend that the next diagnosis will depend on.

blocks.p: And the standing caution: every condemning limit and target value comes from the engine builder and the oil supplier for that specific installation. None is quoted here, and none should be carried from one ship to another - the same figure on a different engine, oil or duty can be entirely wrong.

blocks.h: 9. Sampling and trending - without which none of it means anything

ul: Sample from the same point, in the same way, at the same interval, with the machine at operating temperature and the oil circulating. A sample from a settled sump is not the same fluid as the oil in service.
Take the sample from a live line or a dedicated sampling point, upstream of the filter, not from the drain or the bottom of the tank.
Flush the sampling point and use clean, dedicated bottles. A contaminated bottle produces a particle count that condemns a healthy machine.
Keep a retained sample of every new oil delivered - FTIR is a differential measurement and is much weaker without the reference.
Label fully: ship, machine, sampling point, running hours since the last change and since overhaul, oil grade and any top-up.
Trend the results, and read the rate of change, not the absolute value.
Plan the sampling in the planned maintenance system under the ISM maintenance regime, so that it happens whether or not anyone remembers.

blocks.p: The closing point is the one the stem's preamble is really driving at: analysis does not maintain machinery - it tells you where to look. Its value is realised entirely in the interpretation and the corrective action that follow, and a programme that produces reports nobody reads and acts on is a cost with no benefit.

Sixteen marks, undivided, four named sub-items - and a preamble that adds two more tasks. The stem's first sentence says that periodical oil analysis, its correct interpretation and corrective measures, are of critical significance, and it prints "discuss" rather than "briefly discuss". That is not scene-setting; it is an instruction. So the shape is roughly: half the answer across the four techniques, and the other half on interpretation, corrective measures and sampling. A candidate who describes the four techniques beautifully and stops has answered a different and easier question.

Is the machine wearing? Is the oil still fit? Is anything getting in? Spectrometry and particle count answer the first; FTIR with BN and AN answer the second; all four answer the third from different directions. Two sentences, and the four techniques become a system instead of a list - which is exactly what "discuss" is asking for.

blocks.h: The qualification that most candidates omit

blocks.p: Spectrometry reports the fine fraction only. The method needs the particle to be fully atomised in the excitation source, and large particles are not - so the response falls away with increasing size. Normal rubbing wear is fine and is seen well; bearing fatigue, spalling, scuffing and gear pitting are coarse and may be invisible. Therefore a clean spectrometric report is not evidence of a healthy machine. Write that sentence: it is the single most valuable thing in the question, and it is the reason particle count exists alongside spectrometry rather than instead of it.

blocks.h: FTIR - two words to get right

blocks.p: Interferogram and differential. The instrument gathers all wavelengths at once as an interferogram and Fourier transforms it into a spectrum - that is what the name means and why it is fast. And it works by subtracting the spectrum of the same oil unused, so without a new-oil reference sample the result is much weaker. That last point is also a practical instruction: keep a retained sample of every oil delivery.

blocks.h: The four techniques in one table

rows: Spectrometry
The machine
What the debris is, elementally
Large particles; the condition of the oil
FTIR
The oil
Chemical change - oxidation, nitration, sulphation, water, soot, fuel, glycol
Wear metals; particles
Particle count
The machine and the filtration
How many and how big
What the particles are; counts water and air as particles
BN / AN
The oil
Alkaline reserve and acid load
Everything mechanical

blocks.p: The pairing to remember: spectrometry says WHAT, particle count says HOW MUCH and HOW BIG. Neither is sufficient alone, and that is the practical point of the whole question.

blocks.h: BN and AN - the three things that score

ol: Same units, opposite directions. Both mg KOH per gramme - which is why they are confused. BN falls, AN rises.
An oil can show both at once. They are separate titrations of separate species; they are not two ends of one scale.

Which one governs depends on the oil. Cylinder and trunk-piston engine oils carry an alkaline reserve, so BN governs. Turbine, hydraulic, gear and stern tube oils have no reserve, so AN governs and is the measure of oxidative degradation.

blocks.p: And the trap within the trap: two standard BN titration methods are in use and they give systematically different values on the same oil, the stronger titrant returning the higher figure. Never trend them together - a change of laboratory can look exactly like a change in the oil.

blocks.h: Interpretation - learn the pairs, not the values

blocks.p: The examiner asking for "correct interpretation" wants diagnostic pairs:

ul: Iron up + residual BN near zero = corrosive wear. In a cylinder, cold corrosion.
Iron up + BN still healthy = not corrosion. More oil will make it worse.
Particle count up + wear metals normal = filtration or centrifuge failure, or ingress.
Particle count up + spectrometry clean = coarse debris spectrometry cannot see. The most dangerous case, because the report looks reassuring.
Silicon up + iron and chromium up = abrasive dirt ingress.
Sodium and boron up + FTIR glycol and water = coolant leak.
Vanadium and nickel + fuel dilution on FTIR + viscosity down = fuel dilution.
Oxidation up + AN up + no wear metals = the oil is degrading, the machine is fine.
Additive elements up = somebody added the wrong oil.

blocks.p: Verify - confirm physically - correct the cause - then correct the oil. Re-sample before acting, because a large proportion of alarming results are sampling artefacts. Then go and look: magnetic plugs, filters cut open, centrifuge sludge, ferrography - ferrography being the one that tells you the shape of the debris and therefore the wear mechanism. Then attack the cause - the leaking seal, the failing cooler, the injection equipment - and only then renew or adjust the oil. Increasing filtration to deal with dirt ingress treats the consequence and leaves the cause running.

blocks.h: Quote no numbers - and say why

blocks.p: No condemning limit, alarm level, ppm value, cleanliness code, base number or wear rate should be given as a general rule. Every one is engine-builder, oil, application and service specific, and a figure carried from one installation to another is a genuine hazard as well as an examination risk. Saying "the limit comes from the engine builder's service letter and the oil supplier's recommendation for this installation" scores better than a remembered figure that may belong to a different machine - and it is the answer a Chief Engineer should give.

ul: Describing the four techniques and never answering the stem's demand for interpretation and corrective measures - roughly half the marks.
Omitting the particle-size limitation of spectrometry, and so implying a clean report means a healthy machine.
Treating spectrometry and particle count as alternatives rather than complements.
Saying FTIR measures wear metals. It is blind to them.
Forgetting that FTIR is a differential measurement needing a new-oil reference.
Assuming BN and AN cannot both be significant in the same sample.
Applying BN to a turbine or hydraulic oil, which has no alkaline reserve.
Quoting condemning limits, ppm values or cleanliness codes as general rules.
Ignoring sampling technique, without which every result is unreliable.
"Your spectrometric report is clean. Is the engine healthy?" No - it says the fine fraction is normal. Coarse debris from fatigue or spalling may not appear at all.
"What does FTIR see that spectrometry cannot, and vice versa?" FTIR sees the chemical condition of the oil; spectrometry sees the elements. Neither sees the other's subject.
"Why is water a problem for a particle counter?" Optical counters count droplets and air bubbles as particles, so a wet or aerated sample reads falsely high.
"BN is 40 and AN is 3. Is that possible?" Yes - separate titrations of separate species.
"Would you trend BN results from two different laboratories?" No - two standard methods exist and give systematically different values.
"Iron is up. Do you increase the cylinder oil feed rate?" Only if residual BN is low. If BN is healthy the cause is not corrosion and more oil will make it worse.
"What tells you the shape of the wear debris?" Ferrography - and shape identifies the wear mechanism.
"Where do your condemning limits come from?" The engine builder's service letters and the oil supplier for this installation. Not from a textbook.
Show me where you take your main engine system oil sample and talk me through doing it.
Your last report shows sodium and boron rising. What do you do?
What is in a scrape-down analysis and how does it differ from a system oil analysis?
How does your purifier remove water, and how would you know it was working?
Which of your oils has no base number, and what do you monitor instead?
You have an alarming result on a Sunday at sea. What is your first action?

blocks.p: Three questions, four techniques, two pairs, one sequence. THREE QUESTIONS: is it wearing, is the oil fit, is anything getting in. FOUR TECHNIQUES: spectrometry says WHAT, particle count says HOW MUCH and HOW BIG, FTIR says what the OIL has become, BN/AN says how much fight is LEFT. TWO PAIRS for diagnosis: iron with residual BN, and particle count with spectrometry. ONE SEQUENCE for action: verify - confirm physically - correct the cause - then correct the oil.

ul: NO IMO OR STATUTORY INSTRUMENT PRESCRIBES A LUBRICATING OIL ANALYSIS PROGRAMME. None has been named, because naming one would give the answer false authority.

MARPOL Annex VI - the 0.50 per cent m/m global sulphur limit for fuel oil used outside emission control areas, in force since 1 January 2020. Used only to explain cylinder oil base number selection; no provision is quoted or numbered.
ISO cleanliness code - named as the reporting convention for particle counts. NOT HELD by MIW; no code, band or table reproduced.
The two standard titration methods for Base Number - described by chemistry and by the direction of the discrepancy. NOT HELD by MIW and no standard number asserted.

Engine builder service letters and the oil supplier's recommendation for the specific installation - the only correct sources for condemning limits, alarm levels and target values. Not held; none reproduced.
ISM Code chapter 10 - maintenance of the ship and equipment, under which sampling and analysis are planned and recorded.

blocks.p: This question carries no statutory content and the answer says so expressly rather than borrowing authority from an unrelated instrument. Atomic emission spectrometry, infrared spectroscopy, particle counting and acid-base titration are not dated law and carry no amendment boundary; the answer would be identical at any sitting in this period.

The no-figures rule is absolute here and is the most important evidential feature of the answer. No condemning limit, alarm level, ppm value, ISO cleanliness code, base number figure or wear rate is quoted as a general rule. Every one is engine-builder, oil, application and service specific, and a figure carried between installations is a genuine hazard as well as an evidential defect. The engine builder's service letters and the oil supplier's recommendation for the specific installation are the governing sources, and MIW holds neither.

The characteristic infrared wavenumbers are approximate - they are properties of the molecular bonds and vary with the chemical environment, and the integration windows are instrument and method specific. The two standard Base Number titration methods are not identified by standard number; they are distinguished by their chemistry and by the direction of the discrepancy between them. The ISO cleanliness code is named as a reporting convention only. No oil company, analyser manufacturer, engine builder, laboratory or proprietary condition-monitoring programme is named anywhere.

The interpretation and corrective-measures material is engineering judgement, reasoned from the properties of the techniques. It is the material this sitting's enlarged stem demands and that the November 2024 donor paper was not asked for, so it is new work rather than adapted work. It is not a manufacturer's recommendation and is not presented as one.
