questions.understand_first: Every machine on the ship is sealed, and you cannot see inside it while it runs. But the oil can - it touches every working surface, continuously, and it carries away a sample of everything that happens in there. Oil analysis is simply the business of reading that sample. The reason there are four techniques and not one is that they are answering different questions, and they are blind to each other's subjects. Two of them look at the machine: spectrometry tells you what the debris is made of, and particle count tells you how much of it there is and how big - and you need both, because spectrometry physically cannot see large particles, so a clean spectrometric report on a spalling bearing is a false reassurance rather than good news. The other two look at the oil: FTIR tells you what the oil has chemically become, and Base and Acid Number tell you how much fight it has left in it. Once you see it that way, the interpretation the question demands stops being a memory exercise. You are not reading numbers - you are reading pairs. Iron rising tells you almost nothing on its own; iron rising with the base number gone tells you the oil stopped protecting the metal, while iron rising with the base number healthy tells you something entirely different and means that adding more oil will make it worse. And the last idea, which is what the stem's preamble is driving at: the analysis does not maintain anything. It tells you where to look. A programme that produces reports nobody reads is a cost with no benefit.

steps.title: Why the oil is analysed, and what the four techniques are for
points: Used oil is the only sample in continuous contact with every working surface
The four techniques are not four ways of doing one thing
Is the machine wearing? - spectrometry and particle count
Is the oil still fit? - FTIR, and BN and AN
Is anything getting in? - all four, from different directions
The governing rule: trend against the machine's own history, not the absolute value

steps.title: A) Elemental (spectrometric) analysis
points: Sample excited in a plasma or across a rotating-disc electrode arc
Each element emits at characteristic wavelengths; intensity gives concentration in ppm
Wear metals - iron from liners, rings, gears, shafts; copper, lead, tin from bearings; chromium from rings and plating; aluminium from pistons
Contaminants - silicon from dirt (abrasive); sodium and boron from coolant; vanadium and nickel from residual fuel
Additive elements - calcium and magnesium (detergent), zinc and phosphorus (anti-wear)
Additives falling = depletion; rising = the wrong oil was added
Silicon reads two ways - dirt ingress in service, or sealant and antifoam residue right after an overhaul

steps.title: What spectrometry cannot see - and why that governs its use
points: The method needs complete atomisation of the particle in the excitation source
Large particles are not fully atomised, so response falls away with increasing size
It therefore reports essentially the fine fraction only
Normal rubbing wear is fine and is seen well
Bearing fatigue, spalling, scuffing and gear pitting are coarse and may not be seen
So a clean spectrometric report is NOT evidence of a healthy machine
Which is exactly why particle count, ferrography and plug inspection sit alongside it

steps.title: B) Fourier Transform Infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy
points: Infrared through a thin film; molecular bonds absorb at characteristic wavenumbers
All wavelengths gathered at once as an interferogram, Fourier transformed to a spectrum - hence fast
A DIFFERENTIAL measurement - subtracted from the spectrum of the same oil unused
Practical consequence: keep a retained sample of every new oil delivery
Detects oxidation (carbonyl), nitration, sulphation, water (hydroxyl)
Soot as a broad baseline rise, not a discrete peak
Also fuel dilution, glycol ingress, additive depletion
Fast, small sample, no reagents - but semi-quantitative and blind to wear metals and particles

steps.title: C) Particle count
points: Solid particles counted and sized, usually by optical light obscuration
Pore blockage where the oil is too dark; microscopy is the referee method
Reported as counts per millilitre in cumulative size bands, condensed to a cleanliness code
Decisive for hydraulic and servo systems where clearances are microns
The direct measure of filtration and centrifuge performance and of ingress
It sees the large particles spectrometry misses - the two are complementary
Limits: counts water droplets and air bubbles as particles; cannot say what the particles are

steps.title: D) Base Number against Acid Number
points: Both titrations, both in mg KOH per gramme - which is why they are confused
BN = alkaline reserve from overbased detergent additives; it FALLS in service
AN = acidic constituents from combustion and oxidation; it RISES
An oil can show both at once - separate titrations of separate species
Two standard BN methods give systematically different values - never trend them together
BN governs for cylinder and trunk-piston oils, matched to the sulphur actually burned
AN governs for turbine, hydraulic, gear and stern tube oils, which have no reserve
Since the 0.50 per cent limit of 1 January 2020, BN is matched to the fuel in use - and over-alkalinity deposits abrasive calcium

steps.title: Correct interpretation - reading the four together
points: No single result diagnoses anything; pairs and trends do
Iron up + residual BN near zero = corrosive wear (in a cylinder, cold corrosion)
Iron up + BN healthy = NOT corrosion; more oil will make it worse
Particle count up + wear metals normal = filtration or centrifuge failure, or ingress
Particle count up + spectrometry clean = coarse debris - the most dangerous case
Silicon up + iron and chromium up = abrasive dirt ingress
Sodium and boron up + FTIR glycol and water = coolant leak
Vanadium and nickel + FTIR fuel + viscosity down = fuel dilution
Oxidation up + AN up + no wear metals = the oil is degrading, the machine is fine
Additive elements up = the wrong oil was added
Two disciplines: trend do not spot-read; and rate of change beats level

steps.title: Corrective measures
points: The sequence: verify - confirm physically - correct the cause - then correct the oil
Re-sample before acting - many alarming results are sampling artefacts
Confirm physically - magnetic plugs, filters cut open, centrifuge sludge, ferrography for debris shape, direct inspection
Abrasive ingress - find the entry path (filters, seals, breathers), not just more filtration
Coolant leak - pressure-test coolers, jackets, covers; glycol destroys bearings
Fuel dilution - injection equipment, timing, combustion; then renew, because diluted oil cannot be recovered
Water - find the source and run the purifier correctly (gravity disc, throughput, temperature)
Rising particle count - filters, differential pressure, bypass, purifier operation; then the ingress path
Low BN in cylinder oil - raise feed rate or move to higher BN, matched to fuel sulphur, and re-check by scrape-down
High AN and oxidation - find the cause, then renew, and clean the system before recharging
Additive depletion - renew; additives cannot be topped up
Record and close the loop in the PMS - unrecorded action destroys the trend
Standing caution: every limit comes from the builder and the oil supplier for THAT installation

steps.title: Sampling and trending - without which none of it means anything
points: Same point, same way, same interval; machine at temperature and oil circulating
From a live line upstream of the filter, not the drain or tank bottom
Flush the point; use clean dedicated bottles - a dirty bottle condemns a healthy machine
Retain a sample of every new oil - FTIR needs the reference
Label fully: ship, machine, point, hours since change and since overhaul, grade, top-ups
Trend, and read the rate of change
Plan it in the PMS under the ISM maintenance regime
Close: analysis does not maintain machinery - it tells you where to look

questions.memory_cue: Three questions, four techniques, two pairs, one sequence. QUESTIONS: is it wearing, is the oil fit, is anything getting in (1). TECHNIQUES: spectrometry says WHAT (2, limited by step 3), particle count says HOW MUCH and HOW BIG (5), FTIR says what the OIL has become (4), BN/AN says how much FIGHT is left (6). PAIRS: iron with residual BN; particle count with spectrometry (7). SEQUENCE: verify, confirm physically, correct the cause, then correct the oil (8).

quick_revision.recall_15s: Four techniques answering three questions. Elemental spectrometry - the sample is excited in a plasma or rotating-disc arc, each element emits at characteristic wavelengths and intensity gives ppm; reads wear metals (iron, copper, lead, tin, chromium, aluminium), contaminants (silicon from dirt, sodium and boron from coolant, vanadium and nickel from residual fuel) and additive elements (calcium, magnesium, zinc, phosphorus). Its critical limitation: large particles are not fully atomised, so it reports the fine fraction only - fatigue, spalling and scuffing debris may be invisible, so a clean report is not a healthy machine. FTIR - bonds absorb at characteristic wavenumbers, all gathered as an interferogram and Fourier transformed; a differential measurement against the same oil unused; detects oxidation, nitration, sulphation, water, soot (baseline rise), fuel dilution, glycol, additive depletion; fast but semi-quantitative and blind to wear metals. Particle count - light obscuration, or pore blockage on dark oil, microscopy as referee; counts per millilitre in cumulative bands, condensed to a cleanliness code; decisive for hydraulics, the measure of filtration performance, and it sees what spectrometry misses - but counts water and air as particles and cannot say what they are. BN and AN - both mg KOH/g, BN falls, AN rises, both can be present at once; two standard BN methods differ systematically so never trend them together; BN governs cylinder and trunk-piston oils, AN governs turbine, hydraulic, gear and stern tube oils. Interpret by pairs: iron up with BN gone = corrosion; iron up with BN healthy = not corrosion; count up with metals normal = filtration failure. Then verify, confirm physically, correct the cause, correct the oil.
critical_numbers: 0.50 per cent m/m global sulphur limit for fuel oil outside emission control areas, in force 1 January 2020 - the only figure quoted in this answer
NO condemning limit, alarm level, ppm value, ISO cleanliness code, base number or wear rate is quoted as a general rule
Both BN and AN are expressed in milligrammes of potassium hydroxide per gramme of oil - the same units, opposite meanings
The governing sources for all limits: the engine builder's service letters and the oil supplier's recommendation for the specific installation
quick_revision.critical_regulation: None. No IMO or statutory instrument prescribes a lubricating oil analysis programme, and saying so expressly is correct rather than evasive. MARPOL Annex VI is named only for the 0.50 per cent sulphur limit that changed cylinder oil base number selection. Sampling and analysis are planned and recorded under ISM Code chapter 10 as part of the maintenance regime.
quick_revision.major_trap: Describing the four techniques and never answering the stem's express demand for correct interpretation and corrective measures - which the preamble states and which "discuss" rather than "briefly discuss" reinforces. That is roughly half the marks. Second trap: omitting the particle-size limitation of spectrometry, and so implying that a clean spectrometric report means a healthy machine. It does not - coarse debris from bearing fatigue, spalling and scuffing may not be seen at all. Third: assuming BN and AN cannot both be significant in the same sample, or applying BN to a turbine or hydraulic oil that has no alkaline reserve. Fourth: trending base numbers from two different laboratories or methods - the two standard methods give systematically different values on the same oil. Fifth: quoting condemning limits, ppm values or cleanliness codes as general rules. Every one is engine-builder, oil and application specific, and a figure carried between installations is a genuine hazard.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the lubricating oil analysis question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 Why analyse, and the three questions. 2 Elemental spectrometry. 3 Its particle-size limitation. 4 FTIR. 5 Particle count. 6 BN against AN (2-6 are the four printed sub-items). 7 Correct interpretation - the diagnostic pairs. 8 Corrective measures. 9 Sampling and trending.
retrieval_cards.why: The stem's preamble expressly demands interpretation and corrective measures, and prints 'discuss' not 'briefly discuss'. Sections 7 and 8 are roughly half the marks and are what most candidates never write.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What are the four techniques each for?
retrieval_cards.answer: Is the machine wearing? - elemental spectrometry and particle count. Is the oil still fit for service? - FTIR, and Base and Acid Number. Is anything getting in? - all four, from different directions. The pairing to remember: spectrometry says WHAT the debris is; particle count says HOW MUCH and HOW BIG. FTIR and BN/AN say nothing about the machine at all - they describe the oil.
retrieval_cards.why: Framing them as a system rather than a list is what 'discuss' is asking for, and it makes the interpretation section reconstructable.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Your spectrometric report is clean. Is the engine healthy?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. The method depends on complete atomisation of the particle in the excitation source, and large particles are not fully atomised - so the response falls away with increasing size and the technique reports essentially the fine fraction only. Normal rubbing wear is seen well; bearing fatigue, spalling, scuffing and gear pitting are coarse and may not be seen at all. That is exactly why particle count, ferrography and magnetic plug inspection sit alongside it.
retrieval_cards.why: The single most valuable point in the question, and the one most often omitted. It is also the standard oral trap.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Explain FTIR and why it needs a reference sample.
retrieval_cards.answer: An infrared beam passes through a thin film of oil; molecular bonds absorb at characteristic wavenumbers. All wavelengths are gathered at once as an interferogram and Fourier transformed into a spectrum, which is what makes it fast. It is a differential measurement against the same oil unused, so without a new-oil reference it is much weaker. It detects oxidation, nitration, sulphation, water, soot (a baseline rise), fuel dilution and glycol - and is blind to wear metals.
retrieval_cards.why: 'Differential' is the word candidates miss, and it carries a practical instruction: retain a sample of every oil delivery.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How does particle counting work and what is it blind to?
retrieval_cards.answer: Solid particles are counted and sized, usually by optical light obscuration. Pore-blockage methods are used where the oil is too dark; microscopy is the referee method. Results are counts per millilitre in cumulative size bands, condensed to a cleanliness code. It is decisive for hydraulic and servo systems, measures filtration performance, and sees the large particles spectrometry misses. Blind spots: it counts water and air as particles, and never says what they are.
retrieval_cards.why: Complementary to spectrometry, not an alternative - and the water-and-air limitation explains many false alarms.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Distinguish Base Number from Acid Number.
retrieval_cards.answer: Both are titrations reported in mg KOH per gramme of oil, which is why they are confused. BN is the alkaline reserve from overbased detergent additives and it FALLS in service. AN is the acidic constituents present and it RISES. An oil can show both at once - separate titrations of separate species. BN governs cylinder and trunk-piston oils; AN governs turbine, hydraulic, gear and stern tube oils, which carry no reserve.
retrieval_cards.why: Three separate marks live here: same units, opposite directions, and which one governs which oil.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Would you trend Base Number results from two different laboratories?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. Two distinct standard titration methods for Base Number are in use - one employing a strongly acidic titrant, one a weaker one - and they give systematically different results on the same oil, the stronger method returning the higher value. Trending them together makes a change of laboratory or method look exactly like a change in the oil.
retrieval_cards.why: A quiet trap that catches experienced engineers as often as candidates, because the report looks identical either way.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the diagnostic pairs for interpreting a report.
retrieval_cards.answer: Iron up + residual BN near zero = corrosive wear; in a cylinder, cold corrosion. Iron up + BN healthy = not corrosion - more oil will worsen it. Particle count up + wear metals normal = filtration failure or ingress. Particle count up + spectrometry clean = coarse debris; the most dangerous case. Silicon with iron and chromium = dirt ingress. Sodium and boron with glycol = coolant leak. Oxidation and AN up, no wear metals = the oil is degrading, not the machine.
retrieval_cards.why: The stem demands 'correct interpretation'. No single result diagnoses anything - pairs and trends do, and rate of change beats absolute level.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the corrective sequence on an adverse result?
retrieval_cards.answer: Verify - confirm physically - correct the cause - then correct the oil. Re-sample and re-test first, because many alarming results are sampling artefacts. Then go and look: magnetic plugs, filters cut open, centrifuge sludge, ferrography for debris shape. Then attack the cause - the leaking seal, the failing cooler - because filtration removes the consequence and leaves the cause running. Only then renew or adjust. And record every action, or the trend is destroyed.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the second half of what the stem asks for, and 'correct the cause before the oil' is the sentence that shows it is understood.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Where do condemning limits come from?
retrieval_cards.answer: From the engine builder's service letters and the oil supplier's recommendation for that specific installation - never from a textbook and never from another ship. Every condemning limit, alarm level, ppm value, cleanliness code and base number target is engine, oil, application and service specific, and a figure carried between installations is a genuine hazard as well as an examination risk.
retrieval_cards.why: Saying this scores better than a remembered number, and it is the answer a Chief Engineer is supposed to give.
